questions.title: Designing a Generation Strategy Under Real Cost/Latency/Quality Constraints
questions.prompt: A production chat product needs a token-generation strategy — greedy, temperature sampling, top-k, top-p, or beam search — chosen not just for output quality but for a hard p99 latency budget and a per-million-token cost target. Walk through how you'd actually make this decision, including where the 'best quality' choice on paper is wrong for this system.
questions.modelAnswer: The decision has to start from the latency and cost constraints, because several of the quality-oriented options are structurally incompatible with a hard p99 token-generation latency budget regardless of how good their output is. Beam search maintains multiple candidate sequences in parallel and is the strongest choice on paper for tasks where a single globally best sequence matters (translation, where grammatical correctness over a short, bounded output matters a lot), but it multiplies the per-step compute and memory cost by the beam width, directly conflicting with a tight per-token latency budget and a per-million-token cost target, and it tends to produce less diverse, sometimes repetitive output for open-ended chat generation anyway — so despite being the 'best quality' choice on a narrow metric for some tasks, it's frequently the wrong choice for a chat product on both cost and output-character grounds. Greedy decoding is cheapest per token and fully deterministic, but for chat specifically it tends to produce bland, repetitive output because it never considers a close second-best token that a human would find more natural, which directly hurts the quality dimension that actually matters for this product. Between temperature/top-k/top-p, the practical default for production chat is top-p (nucleus) sampling specifically because its candidate pool size adapts to model confidence — narrow when the model is confident, wider when it's uncertain — which produces more consistently natural output across varying prompt difficulty than a fixed top-k cutoff, at essentially the same per-token compute cost as greedy decoding, since the sampling step itself is cheap relative to the forward pass; temperature can be layered on top-p as a separate tuning knob for overall creativity without changing which decoding family you're in. Given that the per-token compute cost is nearly identical across greedy/temperature/top-k/top-p (they all require exactly one forward pass per output token; the differences are a cheap sampling step afterward), the actual dial I'd use to hit the p99 latency and cost targets isn't the decoding strategy choice at all — it's things like speculative decoding to reduce the number of expensive forward passes per output token, or a smaller/distilled model for latency-sensitive traffic, with top-p sampling as the decoding strategy layered on top of whichever of those throughput levers gets you within budget. The mistake I'd flag explicitly is treating decoding-strategy choice as the primary latency/cost lever when it's actually a secondary decision that matters much more for quality than for cost, once beam search is correctly ruled out.
questions.professionalAnswer: I start from the hard constraints, because they immediately rule out one whole family of options: beam search multiplies per-step compute and memory by the beam width, which is directly at odds with a tight p99 latency budget and a per-million-token cost target, and for open-ended chat it often produces less natural, more repetitive output anyway — so it's wrong on cost and wrong on the quality dimension that actually matters here, even though it's the textbook 'best' choice for something like translation. Greedy is the cheapest option and fully deterministic, but it tends toward bland, repetitive chat output because it never takes a reasonable second-best token, which costs you on the quality axis that's supposed to be the point. My default for production chat is top-p sampling, because its pool size adapts to model confidence instead of using a fixed cutoff, which gives more consistently natural output, and critically it costs essentially the same per token as greedy — one forward pass, plus a cheap sampling step. That's actually the key insight for this question: decoding-strategy choice barely moves your per-token cost or latency once beam search is off the table, so if you're not hitting your p99 or cost target, the fix isn't swapping decoding strategies, it's a different lever entirely — speculative decoding to cut the number of expensive forward passes, or routing latency-sensitive traffic to a smaller model — with top-p layered on top of whichever of those actually gets you there.
commonMistakes: Recommends beam search for a latency-sensitive chat product without accounting for its compute multiplier
Treats decoding-strategy choice as the primary lever for hitting latency/cost targets, when it's a secondary one
Recommends greedy decoding for open-ended chat without acknowledging its repetitive-output problem
Uses a fixed top-k cutoff where an adaptive top-p pool would serve varying prompt difficulty better
Doesn't recognize that greedy/temperature/top-k/top-p cost roughly the same per token, obscuring the real cost lever
Fails to propose a genuine throughput lever (speculative decoding, smaller model) for actually meeting a latency/cost target
keyPoints: Correctly rules out beam search on both cost and chat-quality grounds
Explains why greedy decoding underperforms for open-ended chat despite being cheapest
Recommends top-p as the practical default and explains its confidence-adaptive behavior
Recognizes that decoding-strategy choice barely affects per-token cost/latency once beam search is excluded
Proposes a genuine throughput lever (speculative decoding, smaller model) for meeting hard cost/latency targets

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly rules out beam search for this workload on cost and quality grounds
Correctly evaluates greedy/temperature/top-k/top-p tradeoffs for chat specifically
Recognizes decoding-strategy choice is a weak lever for cost/latency specifically
Proposes a genuine throughput lever to actually hit the hard constraints

questions.title: Choosing Between DDP, FSDP, and Tensor/Pipeline Parallelism at the Largest Scales
questions.prompt: You need to train a model whose parameters, gradients, and optimizer state together don't fit in a single GPU's memory even with the largest available GPU, across hundreds of GPUs. Walk through how you'd actually choose among DDP, FSDP, tensor parallelism, and pipeline parallelism (or a combination), and what specifically makes this decision different from a smaller-scale training job.
questions.modelAnswer: At smaller scale, where a full model replica fits comfortably on one GPU, DDP is close to the right default: each GPU holds a full model copy, runs forward/backward independently on its own data shard, and synchronizes gradients via all-reduce — simple, well-understood, and the memory overhead of a full replica per GPU is a non-issue. The scale described here breaks that assumption immediately: if parameters, gradients, and optimizer state together don't fit on one GPU, DDP is disqualified outright, not just suboptimal, because DDP requires exactly that full replica to exist. FSDP is the next step and is usually the right first move: it shards parameters, gradients, and optimizer state across the data-parallel group, materializing only the shard a given GPU needs at any moment via an all-gather right before it's used and a reduce-scatter right after gradients are computed, trading some extra communication for the ability to fit a model whose total state exceeds any single GPU's memory. Whether FSDP alone is sufficient depends on the actual numbers: FSDP's extra communication (all-gather before each layer's forward/backward, reduce-scatter after) scales with how many data-parallel ranks you're sharding across, and at a large enough GPU count, that communication volume can itself become the bottleneck, independent of memory — this is the point where tensor parallelism, which splits individual layers' matrix multiplications across GPUs within a tightly-coupled group (typically within a node, over NVLink, because tensor parallelism's communication pattern is latency-sensitive and needs the fastest possible interconnect), becomes worth the added complexity, specifically because it reduces the per-GPU memory and compute for the largest layers directly, rather than just redistributing where the full state lives. Pipeline parallelism, splitting the model's layers into sequential stages run on different groups of GPUs with micro-batches flowing through them, is the lever I'd reach for specifically when the model is deep enough, or the cluster large enough, that even combining FSDP and tensor parallelism within a node doesn't fit or doesn't scale communication-efficiently across nodes, since pipeline parallelism's communication pattern (passing activations between stages) tolerates the higher latency of inter-node links much better than tensor parallelism's does. In practice, the largest frontier-scale runs combine all of these — tensor parallelism within a node over NVLink, pipeline parallelism across groups of nodes, and FSDP's full-sharding or a hybrid-sharding variant layered over the data-parallel dimension — and the actual engineering decision is sizing each dimension against the specific cluster's interconnect topology (what's NVLink-connected versus what's only InfiniBand-connected) rather than picking one technique in isolation.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing that changes at this scale is that DDP isn't just a worse option, it's disqualified — DDP needs a full model replica per GPU, and if the combined parameter/gradient/optimizer state doesn't fit on one GPU, that requirement can't be met at all. FSDP is where I'd start, because it shards all three of those across the data-parallel group and only materializes what a given GPU actually needs right before it's used, which directly solves the 'doesn't fit on one GPU' problem — the real question is whether FSDP alone is enough, and that comes down to whether its extra all-gather/reduce-scatter communication becomes the bottleneck once you're sharding across enough ranks, independent of whether memory still fits. When that communication becomes the limiter, that's when I'd bring in tensor parallelism, which splits the actual matrix multiplications inside the biggest layers across a small, tightly-coupled group of GPUs, typically within one node over NVLink specifically because its communication pattern is latency-sensitive in a way that doesn't tolerate a slower inter-node link well. Pipeline parallelism is the dimension I'd add when the model is deep enough, or the cluster large enough, that neither FSDP nor tensor parallelism alone gets you there efficiently across nodes, because passing activations between sequential pipeline stages tolerates inter-node latency much better than tensor parallelism's communication does. In practice the real frontier-scale runs combine all three — tensor parallel within a node, pipeline parallel across node groups, FSDP or hybrid sharding over the data-parallel dimension — and the actual job is sizing each dimension against this specific cluster's interconnect topology, not picking one technique and calling it done.
commonMistakes: Defaults to DDP without recognizing it's categorically disqualified once total state exceeds one GPU's memory
Treats FSDP as a universal fix without checking whether its communication overhead becomes the new bottleneck
Applies tensor parallelism across node boundaries despite its latency-sensitive communication pattern
Applies pipeline parallelism without accounting for pipeline-bubble overhead at the chosen number of stages
Picks one parallelism technique in isolation instead of sizing a combination against the cluster's actual interconnect topology
Assumes a parallelism strategy that worked at a smaller GPU count scales linearly without re-validating communication cost
keyPoints: Correctly identifies why DDP is disqualified, not just suboptimal, at this scale
Explains FSDP's sharding mechanism and its communication-overhead limit correctly
Explains when and why tensor parallelism is added, including its NVLink/intra-node requirement
Explains when and why pipeline parallelism is added, including its latency tolerance across nodes
Describes combining all three sized against the cluster's actual interconnect topology

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly disqualifies DDP and explains why at this scale
Correctly explains FSDP's mechanism and its own scaling limit
Correctly explains when/why tensor and pipeline parallelism are added
Describes a realistic combined strategy sized to actual cluster topology

questions.title: NCCL Tuning and Collective-Communication Architecture for Thousands of GPUs
questions.prompt: A platform team asks you to design the NCCL configuration strategy for a cluster scaling from 64 GPUs to several thousand. Explain what actually needs to change about the collective-communication architecture as the GPU count grows by that much, not just which environment variables to set.
questions.modelAnswer: The naive assumption — that NCCL just works the same way at any scale, only slower — misses that the actual communication algorithm NCCL selects, and the network topology it needs to perform well, both change qualitatively as GPU count grows by two orders of magnitude. At 64 GPUs, a ring all-reduce over a single, often fully NVLink-connected or single-switch InfiniBand domain performs well: the per-GPU communication time formula for ring all-reduce, 2(N-1)/N times payload-size-over-bandwidth, is already close to its asymptotic value at N=64, and the entire job likely fits within one leaf switch's worth of bandwidth with no cross-spine traffic at all. At several thousand GPUs, several things change at once: first, the job now almost certainly spans multiple racks and multiple spine switches, meaning a meaningful fraction of all-reduce traffic has to cross the spine, and the bisection bandwidth of the fabric — not any single link's bandwidth — becomes the actual constraint, which means the network topology design (a full fat-tree with no oversubscription at the spine layer, specifically) matters far more at this scale than at 64 GPUs, where a lower-bisection-bandwidth topology might have been invisible; second, NCCL itself switches its default collective algorithm as scale grows — a pure ring topology's per-step latency scales with the number of participants, and at large N, NCCL's tree-based or hybrid ring/tree algorithms reduce the latency-sensitive portion of the collective at the cost of some bandwidth efficiency, so the actual algorithm running under the hood at 3,000 GPUs is meaningfully different from the one running at 64, and tuning decisions that were correct at the smaller scale (forcing a specific ring configuration, for instance) can actively hurt at the larger one; third, NCCL's communication pattern needs to be made topology-aware of the actual rack/switch layout (via NCCL's topology detection or an explicit topology file) because at this GPU count, two GPUs that are logically adjacent in rank order might be physically many hops apart, and a communication pattern that's blind to that physical layout spends bandwidth crossing the spine unnecessarily for traffic that, with a rank-to-physical-location-aware mapping, could have stayed within a rack. The practical architecture I'd design for the jump from 64 to several thousand is: validate the physical topology (fat-tree, non-blocking at the spine) before any software tuning, use nccl-tests at representative scale (not just 64 GPUs) to establish a real busbw baseline against the fabric's rated bandwidth, let NCCL's topology detection and algorithm selection do their job rather than forcing settings that were tuned for a much smaller job, and specifically re-validate rank-to-physical-GPU placement so that the job's own rank ordering is topology-aware rather than arbitrary.
questions.professionalAnswer: The mistake I'd correct first is the assumption that NCCL at 3,000 GPUs is just 'NCCL at 64 GPUs, but slower' — the actual algorithm and the topology requirements both change qualitatively at that jump. At 64 GPUs, a ring all-reduce inside one switch's domain is close to ideal and bisection bandwidth basically never becomes the bottleneck because the job doesn't span enough of the fabric for it to matter. At several thousand GPUs, the job almost certainly crosses multiple racks and spine switches, so now bisection bandwidth — not any single link — is the real constraint, which means the physical fabric design, a genuinely non-blocking fat-tree at the spine layer specifically, matters in a way it simply didn't at the smaller scale. NCCL itself also switches which algorithm it's actually running as N grows — pure ring's per-step latency scales with participant count, so at large N, NCCL leans on tree-based or hybrid approaches to keep that latency-sensitive portion in check, which means a tuning setting that was correct and hand-tuned at 64 GPUs can be actively wrong at 3,000, because you're no longer even running the same underlying algorithm. The piece I'd insist on that's easy to skip is making the communication pattern topology-aware of the actual physical rack/switch layout, because at this scale two adjacent ranks in the job's numbering can be many hops apart physically, and an oblivious mapping burns spine bandwidth on traffic that a topology-aware placement would have kept local to a rack. My actual plan for scaling from 64 to several thousand is: validate the physical fabric first, benchmark busbw with nccl-tests at a representative scale rather than trusting the 64-GPU number, let NCCL's own topology detection and algorithm selection do the job instead of forcing settings tuned for the smaller cluster, and explicitly check that rank-to-physical-location mapping is sane before trusting any of the rest of it.
commonMistakes: Assumes NCCL behavior and tuning validated at a small scale transfers unchanged to thousands of GPUs
Focuses only on environment-variable tuning instead of physical fabric topology design
Doesn't account for bisection bandwidth becoming the binding constraint only once the job spans multiple racks/spines
Forces a specific ring configuration that was correct at small scale, unaware NCCL switches algorithms at large scale
Ignores rank-to-physical-location mapping, leaving logically adjacent ranks physically far apart
Benchmarks nccl-tests only at a small scale and extrapolates busbw linearly to the full cluster size
keyPoints: Explains why bisection bandwidth, not single-link bandwidth, becomes the real constraint at large scale
Explains that NCCL's underlying collective algorithm itself changes as GPU count grows
Identifies the need for a non-blocking fat-tree topology at the spine layer for large-scale training
Addresses topology-aware rank-to-physical-location mapping as a real lever
Proposes validating physical topology and re-benchmarking at representative scale before trusting small-scale tuning

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains how the communication bottleneck shifts to bisection bandwidth at large scale
Correctly explains that NCCL's algorithm selection itself changes with scale
Addresses topology-aware rank placement as a real architectural lever
Proposes a sound, concrete validation/scaling methodology

questions.title: Multi-Tenant GPU Sharing Strategy Across an Organization
questions.prompt: Your organization has several teams with workloads of very different shapes — a frontier pretraining team needing full, dedicated GPUs; a small inference-prototyping team that mostly idles a GPU waiting on human iteration; and a batch-inference team with bursty, latency-tolerant jobs. Design the GPU-sharing strategy across this fleet, including where MIG, time-slicing, and plain dedicated allocation each actually fit.
questions.modelAnswer: The design has to start from matching the isolation and granularity each workload actually needs, not from picking one sharing mechanism and applying it everywhere, because MIG, time-slicing, and dedicated allocation solve genuinely different problems rather than being three strengths of the same lever. The frontier pretraining team needs dedicated, unshared GPUs, full stop: multi-GPU training jobs are latency- and bandwidth-sensitive at the collective-communication level, and introducing any sharing mechanism — MIG's hardware partitioning or time-slicing's temporal rotation — onto a GPU participating in a tightly-coupled training job would either be impossible (MIG partitions are smaller than what a training job needs per GPU) or actively harmful (time-slicing introduces exactly the kind of unpredictable per-GPU latency variance that turns into straggler behavior across the whole collective); this workload simply isn't a sharing candidate and shouldn't be forced to be one for the sake of utilization optics. The inference-prototyping team's workload — mostly idle, waiting on a human to iterate — is the textbook case for MIG specifically because it needs real memory isolation (one data scientist's half-finished experiment crashing their process shouldn't be able to crash or slow another's) but only needs a fraction of a full GPU's compute and memory at any given moment; partitioning a single physical GPU into several MIG instances lets multiple prototyping sessions run concurrently with genuine hardware-level isolation, at the cost of each instance having less raw compute than the full card, which is the correct tradeoff for a workload that's rarely compute-bound in the first place. The batch-inference team's bursty, latency-tolerant workload is actually the better fit for time-slicing, or more precisely, for a scheduler-level approach rather than hardware partitioning at all: because the jobs are latency-tolerant, the lack of strict memory isolation and the variable per-job latency that time-slicing introduces are both acceptable costs in exchange for being able to pack more concurrent batch jobs onto the same physical GPUs than MIG's fixed-size partitions would allow, and because the load is bursty rather than steady, this is also the team I'd push toward spot/preemptible capacity and a priority-based scheduling queue rather than a fixed allocation at all. The organizational piece underneath all three of these is a Kubernetes scheduler (or Slurm partition/QoS equivalent) that actually enforces these boundaries automatically based on declared workload type, rather than relying on each team to self-select the right sharing mode, because left to manual choice, a team will tend to request whatever maximizes their own perceived access rather than what's actually appropriate for their workload shape.
questions.professionalAnswer: I don't pick one sharing mechanism for the whole fleet — I match each team's workload shape to the mechanism built for it. The pretraining team gets dedicated, unshared GPUs, no exceptions, because multi-GPU collective communication is latency-sensitive enough that any sharing mechanism, hardware-partitioned or time-sliced, either doesn't fit what a training job needs per GPU or actively introduces the kind of per-GPU latency jitter that turns into straggler behavior across the whole job — this workload just isn't a sharing candidate. The prototyping team is the clean MIG case: they need real memory isolation, because one crashing experiment shouldn't take down someone else's session, but they rarely need more than a fraction of a GPU's compute at any moment, so partitioning a physical card into several MIG instances gives them genuine hardware-level isolation at a compute cost they were never going to use anyway. The batch-inference team is actually the better fit for time-slicing, or really for a scheduler-driven sharing approach, specifically because their workload is bursty and latency-tolerant — the lack of hard memory isolation and the variable per-job latency time-slicing introduces are both acceptable trade-offs there in exchange for packing more concurrent jobs per physical GPU than MIG's fixed partitions would allow, and because the load is bursty I'd also push that team toward spot capacity and a priority queue rather than a fixed reservation. The thing that actually makes this work across the org, rather than being three good ideas on paper, is a scheduler that enforces the right sharing mode automatically based on declared workload type — left to each team's own judgment, they'll tend to ask for whatever maximizes their own access, not whatever actually fits their workload.
commonMistakes: Applies one sharing mechanism (e.g. time-slicing) uniformly across all three teams instead of matching mechanism to workload shape
Puts the pretraining team's GPUs behind any sharing mechanism in the name of utilization, risking training-job stability
Uses time-slicing where MIG's real memory isolation was actually required, or vice versa
Fails to pair the bursty batch-inference workload with spot/preemptible capacity and priority scheduling
Relies on teams to self-select their own sharing mode instead of enforcing it via the scheduler
Treats GPU utilization percentage as the only metric that matters, ignoring isolation and latency requirements
keyPoints: Matches MIG, time-slicing, and dedicated allocation to distinct workload shapes rather than picking one mechanism platform-wide
Correctly disqualifies any sharing mechanism for the latency-sensitive pretraining workload
Correctly identifies MIG as fitting the prototyping team's need for real isolation at low compute utilization
Correctly identifies time-slicing/scheduler-based sharing as fitting the bursty, latency-tolerant batch workload
Proposes scheduler-level enforcement rather than relying on teams to self-select their sharing mode

Correctly matches MIG to the prototyping team's isolation/utilization profile
Correctly matches time-slicing/scheduler-based sharing to the bursty batch workload
Proposes scheduler-level enforcement rather than team self-selection

questions.title: Critically Evaluating Perplexity and Beyond at a System Level
questions.prompt: A research team reports that a new pretraining checkpoint has a lower validation perplexity than the previous checkpoint and wants to promote it to the serving fleet on that basis alone. As the platform engineer responsible for what actually ships, explain what perplexity does and doesn't tell you, and what you'd actually require before promotion.
questions.modelAnswer: Perplexity is a genuinely useful, cheap signal — it's exp(average cross-entropy loss per token) on held-out text, requiring no labeled task data, which is exactly why it's the first thing measured during pretraining — but it measures only how well the model predicts the next token on a specific held-out text distribution, and a lower number there doesn't transfer automatically to 'better at the tasks users actually care about' for several concrete reasons I'd want addressed before promotion. First, perplexity is sensitive to the held-out set's composition: a checkpoint can show a lower perplexity simply because the data mixture shifted toward content more similar to the held-out set, with no actual improvement in the capabilities that matter downstream — I'd want to confirm the held-out set and the training data mixture didn't change between the two checkpoints being compared, or the comparison isn't apples-to-apples. Second, perplexity is a token-level, population-average metric, and it can stay essentially flat even while a specific capability or a specific slice of inputs gets meaningfully worse — a model can improve its average next-token prediction while regressing on a narrow but important behavior (following a specific instruction format, refusing a specific category of request, numerical reasoning) that a single scalar perplexity number simply can't see, because that regression is a small fraction of total tokens and gets averaged away. Third, and most relevant to an inference platform specifically, perplexity says nothing about the operational properties that actually matter for serving — generation latency characteristics, whether the new checkpoint's output-length distribution changed in a way that affects cost per request, or whether quantizing this specific checkpoint (which the serving fleet will do for cost reasons) degrades it disproportionately compared to the previous one, since different checkpoints can have different sensitivity to quantization even at identical perplexity. Given all that, what I'd actually require before promotion is the same staged comparison process used for any model promotion regardless of how it was produced: task-specific benchmark evaluation on the capabilities this product actually depends on, a shadow deployment against real production traffic to check output characteristics and latency under real conditions, and a canary rollout with real business-outcome monitoring before a full champion-alias reassignment — perplexity earns the checkpoint a place in that pipeline, it doesn't skip the pipeline.
questions.professionalAnswer: Perplexity is a fine first signal and I wouldn't dismiss it — it's cheap, needs no labeled data, and it's exactly the number you'd watch minute-to-minute during pretraining — but a lower perplexity on its own is nowhere close to sufficient evidence to promote a checkpoint to serving, and I'd push back on treating it that way. The first thing I'd check is whether the comparison is even apples-to-apples — did the held-out set or the data mixture shift between checkpoints, because a lower number can come from the held-out distribution getting easier to predict, not from the model actually getting better at anything users care about. The deeper issue is that perplexity is a population-average, token-level number, and a model can improve on average while quietly regressing on a specific, narrow behavior that matters a lot — a particular instruction format, a safety behavior, numerical reasoning — because that regression is too small a fraction of total tokens to move the average at all. And specifically for a serving platform, perplexity tells you nothing about what we actually have to ship around — generation latency characteristics, whether output length shifted in a way that changes cost per request, or whether this particular checkpoint happens to degrade more under the quantization we're going to apply anyway. So what I'd actually require is the same promotion pipeline every checkpoint goes through regardless of how good its perplexity looks — task-specific eval on the capabilities the product actually needs, a shadow deployment against real traffic, a canary with real monitoring — and perplexity gets the checkpoint a ticket into that process, it doesn't buy it a shortcut around it.
commonMistakes: Treats a lower perplexity alone as sufficient evidence for promotion
Doesn't check whether the held-out evaluation set or data mixture changed between the two checkpoints being compared
Assumes a flat or improved average metric rules out regression on a specific, narrow but important capability
Ignores operational properties (latency, output-length distribution, quantization sensitivity) that matter for serving specifically
Skips task-specific benchmarks and shadow/canary deployment because the offline metric already looked good
Confuses a cheap, early signal with a sufficient gate for a production promotion decision
keyPoints: Explains correctly what perplexity does and doesn't measure
Checks for held-out-set/data-mixture comparability before trusting the comparison
Identifies that population-average metrics can hide narrow but important regressions
Connects evaluation gaps to serving-specific operational concerns (latency, quantization sensitivity)
Requires the full staged promotion pipeline regardless of how good the offline metric looks

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what perplexity does and doesn't measure
Identifies the comparability and population-averaging pitfalls
Connects the gap to serving-specific operational concerns
Requires a proper staged promotion process rather than a shortcut

questions.title: Quantization, Pruning, and Distillation as a Combined Cost-Reduction Program
questions.prompt: Your inference costs for a fleet of serving models are too high, and leadership wants a cost-reduction target hit within a quarter. Explain how you'd combine quantization, pruning, and distillation into one coherent program rather than picking just one, including how you'd sequence the work and what you'd measure to know it's actually safe to ship.
questions.modelAnswer: Treating these as three competing options to choose between misses that they target different parts of the cost structure and compose well together, so the right program sequences them rather than picking one. Quantization is the cheapest, fastest lever to pull first: post-training quantization needs no retraining, just a calibration pass, and for most models a well-chosen scheme (per-channel weight quantization, or a method like AWQ/GPTQ for more aggressive compression) recovers most of the original accuracy while directly cutting memory footprint and often improving throughput, so I'd start here because it's the highest-ROI-per-engineering-hour change and can ship within weeks, not a quarter. Pruning is a harsher cut — removing weights or whole structural units entirely — and whether it's worth pursuing at all depends on which kind: unstructured pruning reaches high sparsity with little accuracy loss but mostly saves storage, not inference compute, unless you have specialized sparse kernels or hardware (like Ampere-and-newer sparse tensor cores for 2:4 patterns) to actually exploit the sparsity, so I'd only invest engineering time in structured or N:M pruning specifically because that's where real latency savings materialize on standard dense kernels; and because pruning is a harsher intervention than quantization, it almost always needs a fine-tuning pass afterward to recover accuracy, which puts it on a longer timeline than quantization alone. Distillation is the most expensive and slowest lever — training a genuinely smaller student model to reproduce a larger teacher's output distribution is a real training project, not a post-hoc compression step — so I'd reserve it for the specific services where quantization and pruning alone don't close the cost gap, and where the traffic volume justifies the upfront training cost against the ongoing per-request savings of running a smaller model indefinitely. Sequencing these as quantization first, then structured pruning with fine-tuning on models that still need more, then distillation only where the first two don't close the gap, gets the fastest wins shipped early while reserving the expensive option for where it's actually justified. For what I'd measure before shipping any of this: perplexity (or the model's native loss) as the cheap first check since it needs no labeled data, but never as the only check, because it can stay flat while a specific downstream capability degrades — paired with the actual task-specific evaluation suite the product depends on, a shadow deployment comparing the compressed model's outputs against the uncompressed one on real traffic, and specifically for quantization and pruning, a check of whether the compression affects different input slices unevenly (a model can compress well on average while degrading disproportionately on a specific language, user segment, or edge case), since an average-case accuracy check can hide exactly that kind of regression.
questions.professionalAnswer: I don't pick one of these three, I sequence all of them, because they're not really competing for the same job. Quantization goes first because it's the highest return for the least engineering time — post-training quantization needs no retraining, just calibration, and for most models it recovers most of the accuracy while cutting memory and often improving throughput, so it can ship in weeks and buys the team room before the harder levers are even needed. Pruning I'd only pursue in its structured or N:M form, not unstructured, because unstructured pruning mostly saves disk space, not actual inference compute, unless you have sparse kernels or hardware that exploit it — and because pruning is a harsher cut than quantization, it needs a fine-tuning pass afterward, so it lands on a longer timeline. Distillation is the expensive, slow option — training an actual smaller student model is a real project, not a post-hoc step — so I reserve it for whichever specific services still need more savings after quantization and pruning, and only where the traffic volume justifies the upfront training cost. What I insist on measuring before any of this ships is never perplexity alone — it's a fine cheap first check, but it can stay flat while a specific capability quietly regresses — so I pair it with the actual task-specific eval suite, a shadow deployment comparing outputs against the uncompressed model on real traffic, and specifically a slice-level check, because a compressed model can look fine on average while degrading disproportionately on one language or one user segment that an average-case number would never surface.
commonMistakes: Picks one compression technique instead of sequencing them by cost/speed-to-ship
Pursues unstructured pruning expecting inference-compute savings without specialized sparse kernels
Skips the fine-tuning pass that structured/aggressive pruning typically needs to recover accuracy
Treats distillation as a quick fix rather than recognizing it as a genuine training project
Relies on an average-case accuracy or perplexity check alone, missing slice-level regressions
Doesn't validate compressed-model behavior against real production traffic via shadow deployment before shipping
keyPoints: Sequences quantization, pruning, and distillation by cost/speed-to-ship rather than picking one
Correctly distinguishes unstructured from structured/N:M pruning and their actual compute-savings implications
Reserves distillation for cases that justify its training cost, not as a first-line fix
Uses perplexity only as a cheap first signal, not a sufficient safety check
Requires slice-level and shadow-deployment validation before shipping any compression technique

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes a coherent, sequenced program rather than a single technique
Correctly reasons about pruning type and its actual compute-savings implications
Correctly scopes distillation's cost/benefit and when it's justified
Specifies a sound, slice-aware validation process before shipping

questions.title: Debug a Silent FSDP Mixed-Precision Misconfiguration
questions.prompt: A teammate's FSDP training script runs without errors but loss is diverging to NaN after a few hundred steps, only when launched across more than one node. Find the bug in this configuration and explain the actual mechanism causing the NaNs.
questions.code:
from torch.distributed.fsdp import FullyShardedDataParallel as FSDP
from torch.distributed.fsdp import MixedPrecision

mp_policy = MixedPrecision(
    param_dtype=torch.float16,
    reduce_dtype=torch.float32,
    buffer_dtype=torch.float16,
)

model = FSDP(
    model,
    mixed_precision=mp_policy,
    sharding_strategy=ShardingStrategy.FULL_SHARD,
    device_id=torch.cuda.current_device(),
)

# training loop (no GradScaler anywhere)
for batch in loader:
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    loss = model(batch).loss
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()
questions.modelAnswer: The bug is that `buffer_dtype` is left at the default (matching `param_dtype`, float16) while `reduce_dtype` is float32: FSDP all-reduces gradients in float32 (good, that's the numerically safer choice for accumulation), but buffers — including BatchNorm-style running statistics if present, and more critically here, the model's internal float16 buffers that aren't protected by the reduce-dtype setting — stay in float16 throughout, and because this only manifests across more than one node, the real mechanism is that `param_dtype=torch.float16` with no `GradScaler`-equivalent protection means the forward/backward pass itself, not just the gradient reduction, is running in float16 with no underflow protection, and single-node runs happen to use a smaller effective batch (no cross-node all-gather of a larger set of parameter shards triggering slightly different numerical behavior) that doesn't push any value out of float16's range, while the multi-node run's larger effective computation does. The fix is to switch `param_dtype` to `torch.bfloat16` (keeping FP32's exponent range, avoiding the underflow/overflow risk entirely) or, if FP16 compute is required for throughput reasons, to add explicit loss scaling, since FSDP's `MixedPrecision` config has no built-in equivalent to `GradScaler` the way `torch.cuda.amp` does for DDP.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is a classic 'works at small scale, breaks at real scale' numerics bug. `param_dtype` is float16, which means the actual forward and backward compute happens in float16 with no underflow protection — FSDP's `MixedPrecision` wrapper doesn't bundle anything like `GradScaler` the way `torch.cuda.amp` does, so if you choose float16 as your compute dtype under FSDP, you're on your own for protecting against underflow. The reason it only shows up across multiple nodes is that the actual numerical path running through the larger effective computation is more likely to push some intermediate value outside float16's narrow representable range, where a single-node run with a smaller effective load happens not to. My fix is almost always just to switch `param_dtype` to bfloat16, since it keeps float32's exponent range and sidesteps this whole category of bug for free — I'd only stay on float16 under FSDP if there's a specific, proven throughput reason to, and in that case I'd be adding real loss-scaling infrastructure, not assuming `reduce_dtype=torch.float32` alone protects me, because it only protects the gradient reduction step, not the forward/backward computation itself.
commonMistakes: Assumes reduce_dtype=torch.float32 alone protects the whole pipeline from precision issues
Doesn't recognize that FSDP's MixedPrecision config has no built-in loss-scaler equivalent for float16 compute
Blames the bug on something cluster/network-related since it only appears multi-node, missing the real numerics cause
Switches precision blindly without understanding why multi-node specifically triggers the failure
Doesn't distinguish which FSDP MixedPrecision field (param_dtype vs reduce_dtype vs buffer_dtype) controls which part of the pipeline
Recommends just lowering the learning rate instead of addressing the actual precision/range issue
keyPoints: Correctly identifies param_dtype=float16 as the actual compute-precision risk, not reduce_dtype
Explains why FSDP's MixedPrecision has no built-in GradScaler-equivalent protection
Explains why the failure manifests specifically at multi-node scale, not single-node
Recommends bfloat16 as the default fix, or explicit loss-scaling if float16 is required
Distinguishes the roles of param_dtype, reduce_dtype, and buffer_dtype correctly

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies param_dtype as the root cause, not reduce_dtype
Explains the lack of built-in loss-scaling protection under FSDP MixedPrecision
Explains why the bug manifests specifically at multi-node scale
Proposes a correct, practical fix

questions.title: Diagnose a Multi-Node Training Slowdown from nccl-tests Output
questions.prompt: A 4-node, 32-GPU training job is running at roughly 60% of the throughput the team expected based on single-node benchmarks. Given this nccl-tests all_reduce_perf output gathered across all 4 nodes, diagnose what's actually limiting throughput and what you'd check next.
questions.code:
# 4 nodes x 8 GPUs = 32 ranks, InfiniBand NDR (400 Gb/s per port)
#       size(B)   count  type   redop  out-of-place algbw(GB/s)  busbw(GB/s)
        67108864  16777216  float  sum        41.2                  79.8
       268435456  67108864  float  sum        37.9                  73.4
      1073741824 268435456  float  sum        24.8                  48.1

# Single-node (8 GPU, NVLink) baseline for the same model:
#   ~410 TFLOP/s effective throughput, used as the team's performance target
# Observed 4-node throughput: ~60% of (410 TFLOP/s x 4) extrapolated target
questions.modelAnswer: The out_of_place busbw column is the number that matters here, and at roughly 48 GB/s against InfiniBand NDR's rated 400 Gb/s (50 GB/s) per port, this fabric is actually running close to its real hardware ceiling at the message sizes that matter for training (the 256MB-and-up rows, which are representative of large-model gradient payloads) — so the network fabric itself is not obviously the bottleneck based on this output alone, and I would not reflexively blame InfiniBand just because the job is slower than the single-node baseline suggested. Since the raw collective-communication throughput looks healthy, the 60%-of-expected result points toward a different limiter: either the single-node benchmark the team used as its baseline didn't account for inter-node communication being added on top of compute at all (comparing a single-node number that has zero cross-node communication against a multi-node number that necessarily does is an apples-to-oranges baseline, not a regression), or there's a bottleneck elsewhere in the pipeline entirely — the data loader, CPU-bound preprocessing, or GPU utilization gaps from insufficient overlap between computation and communication — that nccl-tests, which only exercises the collective in isolation, can't see. My next steps would be: first, re-derive the expected multi-node throughput analytically (using the ring all-reduce communication-time formula against this measured busbw, not the single-node number) to get a realistic target instead of an apples-to-oranges one; second, run `nvidia-smi dmon` during an actual training step to check whether GPUs are near-saturated or showing idle gaps; third, if GPUs show idle gaps, profile with Nsight Systems to see whether the gap is from waiting on the data loader, waiting on the all-reduce itself (meaning overlap between backward-pass compute and gradient communication isn't happening), or something else — since the fabric benchmark alone has already ruled out 'the network is simply too slow' as the explanation.
questions.professionalAnswer: The busbw number is what I actually care about here, not algbw, because busbw already accounts for the ring all-reduce's 2(N-1)/N factor, and at roughly 48 GB/s against a 400 Gb/s (50 GB/s) NDR port, this fabric is running close to its real ceiling at the large message sizes that actually matter for gradient payloads — so my first instinct isn't to blame the network, even though the job is underperforming its expectation. What I'd flag immediately is that comparing against a single-node benchmark is probably the wrong baseline in the first place — a single-node run has zero inter-node communication to account for, so '60% of single-node throughput' might just be close to what you'd expect once you add real cross-node all-reduce time on top of compute, not a sign that something's actually broken. Before chasing the network further, I'd recompute what a realistic multi-node throughput target actually looks like using this measured busbw in the ring all-reduce time formula, then check `nvidia-smi dmon` during a live training step to see if the GPUs are actually idling or just running the extra communication the formula predicts. If there are real idle gaps beyond what the math predicts, that's when I'd reach for Nsight Systems to see whether it's the data loader starving the GPU, or poor overlap between backward-pass compute and the gradient all-reduce, rather than assuming the fabric itself is underperforming when this output says otherwise.

Compares multi-node throughput directly against a single-node baseline without accounting for added communication time

Assumes small-message nccl-tests rows are representative of large gradient-payload communication

Recognizes the single-node-vs-multi-node baseline comparison may itself be flawed
Concludes the network is likely not the bottleneck based on this specific output

questions.title: Fix a Gradient Accumulation Bug That Silently Changes the Effective Learning Rate
questions.prompt: This training loop combines gradient accumulation with AMP and gradient clipping, and trains without any errors, but the effective behavior doesn't match what changing accum_steps from 1 to 8 should do. Find the bug(s) and fix the loop.
questions.code:
accum_steps = 8
scaler = torch.cuda.amp.GradScaler()
optimizer.zero_grad()

for i, (inputs, targets) in enumerate(train_loader):
    with torch.cuda.amp.autocast():
        output = model(inputs)
        loss = loss_fn(output, targets)

    scaler.scale(loss).backward()

    if (i + 1) % accum_steps == 0:
        torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), max_norm=1.0)
        scaler.step(optimizer)
        scaler.update()
        optimizer.zero_grad()
questions.modelAnswer: There are two compounding bugs here. First, the loss isn't divided by `accum_steps` before `scaler.scale(loss).backward()`, so the accumulated gradient across 8 micro-batches ends up roughly 8 times larger than a true accum_steps=1 gradient would be for the same effective batch, which silently behaves like multiplying the learning rate by 8 — exactly the gradient-accumulation bug this course's material warns about, except here it's compounded by AMP. Second, and more subtle: `clip_grad_norm_` is called on `optimizer.param_groups` gradients that are still in their AMP-scaled form, because `scaler.unscale_(optimizer)` is never called before clipping — clipping scaled gradients means the clip threshold `max_norm=1.0` is being compared against gradients that are, say, 2^16 times larger than their true value (whatever the current scaler's scale factor is), so the clip is effectively a no-op in practice since real gradients almost never exceed a threshold that's 2^16 times too large, silently disabling the gradient clipping protection entirely. The fix: divide the loss by `accum_steps` immediately after computing it and before `backward()`; call `scaler.unscale_(optimizer)` after all `accum_steps` micro-batches have accumulated and before calling `clip_grad_norm_`, so clipping operates on the true, unscaled gradient magnitude; and only then call `scaler.step(optimizer)` followed by `scaler.update()`.
questions.professionalAnswer: Two bugs are stacked on top of each other here, and both are the kind that run cleanly with no error and just quietly change what training is actually doing. The first is the classic one — loss isn't divided by `accum_steps`, so the accumulated gradient ends up roughly 8x too large, which behaves exactly like an 8x learning-rate multiplier nobody intended. The second is specific to combining accumulation with AMP: `clip_grad_norm_` is being called on gradients that are still scaled by the `GradScaler`'s current scale factor, because `scaler.unscale_` is never called first — so the max_norm=1.0 clip threshold is being compared against gradients that are off by whatever power-of-two scale factor the scaler is currently using, which in practice means the clip almost never actually triggers, silently disabling the one safety mechanism that was supposed to catch a bad gradient. My fix is to divide the loss by accum_steps right when it's computed, only call scaler.unscale_(optimizer) once after the full accumulation window closes, clip on those now-true-scale gradients, and then call scaler.step followed by scaler.update — in that exact order, because getting unscale/clip/step out of order is exactly how this kind of bug gets reintroduced even after you think you've fixed it.
commonMistakes: Divides the loss by accum_steps but still clips before calling scaler.unscale_
Calls scaler.unscale_ but forgets to also fix the loss-scaling-by-accum_steps bug
Calls clip_grad_norm_ on every micro-batch instead of once after the full accumulation window
Calls scaler.update() before scaler.step(), breaking the scaler's internal overflow-tracking logic
Assumes AMP's GradScaler automatically accounts for gradient accumulation without any code change
Doesn't recognize that a clip threshold compared against scaled gradients is effectively a silent no-op
keyPoints: Identifies the missing loss division by accum_steps as the first bug
Identifies the missing scaler.unscale_ call before clipping as the second, AMP-specific bug
Explains why clipping scaled gradients effectively disables the clip silently
Produces a corrected loop with the right call order: divide loss, backward, unscale, clip, step, update
Explains both bugs' effect as silent behavior changes rather than crashes

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the missing loss/accum_steps division
Correctly identifies the missing scaler.unscale_ before clipping
Explains the silent-failure mechanism for both bugs clearly
Produces a fully corrected, correctly-ordered training loop

questions.title: Design a Kubernetes GPU Scheduling Setup for a Mixed MIG/Dedicated Fleet
questions.prompt: You need to configure a Kubernetes cluster so that one physical node pool of A100 GPUs is split via MIG for the prototyping team, while a separate node pool is reserved fully dedicated for the training team, with the scheduler correctly preventing either team's workloads from landing on the other's pool. Walk through how you'd actually set this up, including the specific device-plugin and node-labeling mechanics, not just the high-level idea.
questions.modelAnswer: The mechanics here rest on three layers that all have to agree: the NVIDIA device plugin's configuration, node labeling/taints, and the pod spec's resource requests and tolerations, and getting any one of them wrong lets a workload land somewhere it shouldn't without any obvious error. First, the dedicated training node pool needs MIG disabled at the GPU level entirely (via `nvidia-smi -mig 0` as part of node provisioning, or the equivalent cloud-provider node-pool configuration) so those GPUs expose themselves to the device plugin as whole, undivided `nvidia.com/gpu` resources — this matters because a MIG-enabled GPU can't be requested as a whole device by a pod that just asks for `nvidia.com/gpu: 1`, so disabling MIG here isn't optional, it's required for the training team's pods to even see a usable resource. Second, the prototyping node pool needs MIG enabled and the device plugin configured with a MIG strategy (`mixed` or `single`, set via the device plugin's ConfigMap) that exposes each MIG instance as its own schedulable resource, typically something like `nvidia.com/mig-1g.5gb`, so a prototyping pod requests that specific partition size rather than a whole GPU. Third — and this is the part that actually prevents cross-contamination rather than just making each pool internally correct — I'd label and taint each node pool explicitly (`workload-type=training` / `workload-type=prototyping` as labels, plus a matching taint like `dedicated=training:NoSchedule` on the training pool) and require every pod in each team's namespace to carry the matching nodeSelector and toleration via a namespace-level admission policy or a validating webhook, rather than trusting each team to set their own pod spec correctly — because a prototyping pod that accidentally requests `nvidia.com/gpu: 1` with no nodeSelector could otherwise be scheduled onto a training node if nothing structurally prevents it, consuming a whole dedicated GPU the training team is paying for and expecting to have exclusively. I'd validate the whole setup by deliberately trying to schedule a misconfigured pod from each team into the other's pool during setup and confirming it actually stays Pending rather than assuming the taints work correctly from reading the YAML alone.
questions.professionalAnswer: The three pieces that all have to line up here are the device plugin configuration, node labeling and taints, and pod-spec enforcement, and I've seen each one individually look right while the combination still lets something leak through. On the dedicated training pool, MIG has to be fully disabled at the GPU level during node provisioning, because a MIG-enabled card can't just hand itself over as a whole device to a pod asking for `nvidia.com/gpu: 1` — that's not optional if the training team needs whole GPUs. On the prototyping pool, MIG stays enabled and the device plugin's ConfigMap needs an actual MIG strategy set so each partition shows up as its own resource type, like `nvidia.com/mig-1g.5gb`, which is what the prototyping pods actually request. The part that prevents cross-contamination, though, isn't either of those configs individually — it's labeling and tainting each node pool by workload type and then making sure every pod in each team's namespace structurally carries the matching nodeSelector and toleration, ideally enforced by an admission policy rather than trusting each team's pod spec to get it right by hand, because a prototyping pod with a slightly wrong resource request and no nodeSelector could otherwise land on a training node and quietly eat a whole dedicated GPU nobody expected it to touch. And I wouldn't trust this setup from reading the YAML — I'd deliberately try to schedule a misconfigured pod from each team into the other's pool and confirm it actually stays Pending, because taint/toleration mistakes are exactly the kind of thing that look correct until you test the failure case.
commonMistakes: Assumes a MIG-enabled GPU can still be requested as a whole nvidia.com/gpu resource by a pod
Forgets to disable MIG at the hardware level on the dedicated training node pool
Relies on teams to set the correct nodeSelector/toleration themselves instead of enforcing it via admission policy
Doesn't configure the device plugin's MIG strategy, leaving MIG partitions unexposed as distinct schedulable resources
Skips validating the taint/toleration setup by actually testing a cross-pool scheduling attempt
Confuses node labels (informational) with taints (actually enforced by the scheduler) as if they were interchangeable

Correctly configures the device plugin's MIG strategy for the prototyping pool
Uses taints/tolerations, not just labels, to structurally prevent cross-pool scheduling
Enforces correct pod-spec configuration via policy rather than trusting each team
