questions.title: Fix a torch.distributed.checkpoint Resharding Script That Loses Optimizer State
questions.prompt: This checkpoint-loading code is meant to let a 64-GPU training run resume on a different GPU count (32 GPUs) after a node failure, using torch.distributed.checkpoint. It loads without error but the optimizer's momentum state is silently reset, causing a visible loss spike after every resume. Find the bug.
questions.modelAnswer: The bug is that `dcp.load` is called with a `state_dict` built from only `model.state_dict()`, never including the optimizer's state dict, so DCP has nothing to resize or reshard for the optimizer at all — the optimizer silently starts from its freshly-initialized state (zeroed momentum buffers) because `optimizer.load_state_dict` is never called with anything loaded from the checkpoint, and there's no error because an optimizer starting from scratch is a perfectly valid, if undesired, program state. This is exactly the failure mode DCP is designed to avoid when done correctly: `torch.distributed.checkpoint`'s whole value is that each rank saves and loads only the shard of state it holds, with metadata that lets the shapes reconcile across a different rank count on load, but that resharding only happens for whatever's actually included in the `state_dict` passed to `dcp.load` — model parameters and optimizer state have to both be included, typically via `get_state_dict(model, optimizer)` from `torch.distributed.checkpoint.state_dict`, which returns a combined, DCP-compatible state dict for both, or by explicitly adding an `'optim'` key alongside `'model'` before calling `dcp.load`. The fix: build the state dict to include both model and optimizer state before calling `dcp.load`, and call `optimizer.load_state_dict` (or use `set_state_dict` from the same module, which handles both model and optimizer in one call) with the loaded optimizer state after load completes, so the momentum buffers actually reshard and resume rather than silently reinitializing.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is a 'ran without error, quietly wrong' bug, which is the worst kind, because a fresh optimizer state is a completely valid program state — nothing crashes, you just get a loss spike every time a resume happens, which looks like normal training noise if you're not watching closely. The actual bug is that the state dict passed into `dcp.load` only has the model's weights in it — the optimizer's momentum and variance buffers were never included, so DCP has literally nothing to reshard or restore for the optimizer, and `optimizer.load_state_dict` never gets called with anything meaningful. DCP's entire value proposition is resharding whatever you hand it across a different number of ranks, but that only applies to what's actually in the state dict you pass — model and optimizer both need to be in there, which in practice means using `get_state_dict(model, optimizer)` from `torch.distributed.checkpoint.state_dict` to build a properly DCP-compatible combined dict, or at minimum adding an explicit `'optim'` key before the load call, then loading it back into the optimizer afterward. Once I fixed that, the loss-spike-on-resume symptom should disappear entirely, because the momentum buffers are now actually resuming instead of restarting cold every single time.
commonMistakes: Only checks model.state_dict() for the bug, missing that optimizer state was never included at all
Assumes an error would be raised if optimizer state failed to load, so looks elsewhere for the bug
Adds optimizer.load_state_dict() with the wrong source dict instead of fixing what's loaded via dcp.load
Doesn't recognize DCP only reshards whatever keys are present in the state_dict passed to it
Fixes the save path but doesn't verify the load path actually passes the optimizer state dict too
Confuses this bug with a learning-rate-scheduler state issue instead of optimizer momentum state
keyPoints: Correctly identifies that optimizer state was never included in the DCP state dict at all
Explains why this produces no error, only a silent, visible symptom (loss spike) after resume
Explains that DCP only reshards whatever is present in the passed-in state dict
Proposes using get_state_dict/set_state_dict (or an explicit 'optim' key) to properly include optimizer state
Produces a corrected save/load flow that actually restores momentum buffers on resume

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies missing optimizer state in the DCP state dict as root cause
Explains why this fails silently rather than erroring
Explains DCP's resharding scope correctly
Produces a correct, working fix

questions.title: Interpret DCGM Metrics to Separate a Communication-Bound Step from a Data-Bound One
questions.prompt: A training job's step time has doubled with no code change. You pull these DCGM metrics sampled during a training step on one node. Determine whether this points to a communication-bound, compute-bound, or data-loading-bound problem, and what you'd check next to confirm it.
questions.modelAnswer: The combination here — GPU_UTIL at 94% (the GPU is almost always 'doing something'), PIPE_TENSOR_ACTIVE down at 22% (very little of that busy time is actual tensor-core compute), and NVLINK/network throughput counters flat near their floor — rules out both a classic compute-bound signature and a purely data-starved signature, pointing specifically at communication time dominating the step without that communication actually being network-bound. A compute-bound step would show PIPE_TENSOR_ACTIVE tracking close to GPU_UTIL, which isn't happening here, so this isn't 'the model is just doing more math.' A data-loading-bound step typically shows GPU_UTIL itself dropping (the GPU goes idle waiting for the next batch), which also isn't what's shown — GPU_UTIL staying high while PIPE_TENSOR_ACTIVE is low specifically means the GPU is busy running some kernel, just not a tensor-core-heavy one, and the flat, low NVLink/network counters rule out the obvious 'the collective communication itself got slower' explanation, since if NCCL were actually pushing more bytes or hitting degraded link speed, the network throughput counters would show it. That combination points toward time spent in non-tensor-core work that doesn't show up as network traffic at all — the most likely candidates are a kernel-launch or synchronization-heavy portion of the step (excessive host-device sync calls, a non-fused sequence of small elementwise operations, or — given no code change — a software/driver-level regression like a CUDA or NCCL version change from an automatic node image update) rather than anything intrinsic to the model or the network fabric itself. What I'd check next, in order: first, confirm no software stack change actually happened (driver version, CUDA version, NCCL version, PyTorch version) despite 'no code change,' since an infrastructure-level update is the single most common cause of an unexplained regression with this exact signature; second, if the stack is unchanged, profile the step with Nsight Systems to get a visual timeline and find exactly which portion of the step the GPU is 'busy but not computing much' during — this is the one thing DCGM's aggregate counters can't show on their own; third, check whether NCCL fell back to a slower transport (via `NCCL_DEBUG=INFO` logs) even though raw throughput looks flat, since a fallback to a less direct path could show as 'low but not necessarily network-saturating' traffic rather than an obvious spike.
questions.professionalAnswer: I read GPU_UTIL and PIPE_TENSOR_ACTIVE together here, not separately, because that pairing is the whole diagnostic signal: GPU_UTIL at 94% but PIPE_TENSOR_ACTIVE at only 22% means the GPU looks busy but isn't doing much real tensor-core work, which already rules out a straightforward compute-bound explanation — if this were just 'more math,' those two numbers would track each other closely. It also rules out the classic data-starved signature, because a starved GPU usually shows GPU_UTIL itself dropping as it waits on the next batch, and that's not what's happening — this GPU stays busy, just not on compute. The flat, near-floor NVLink/network counters are the piece that rules out 'NCCL just got slower' as the obvious next guess, because if the collective itself were pushing more bytes or falling back to a degraded link, I'd expect that throughput number to actually move. Put together, this points at non-tensor-core work eating the step time without a visible network signature — something like excessive host-device sync calls, a chain of small unfused elementwise ops, or, since nothing in the code changed, a software-stack regression from a driver, CUDA, or NCCL version bump that happened underneath the team without anyone noticing. My first move, before touching a profiler at all, is confirming the software stack genuinely didn't change, because that's the single most common explanation for 'nothing in my code changed but everything got slower.' If the stack really is unchanged, Nsight Systems is what actually shows which part of the step is eating the time that DCGM's aggregate counters can only hint at, and I'd also check NCCL_DEBUG=INFO logs specifically for a transport fallback, since that can show up as oddly low-but-not-saturating network throughput rather than an obvious spike.
commonMistakes: Concludes the job is compute-bound from high GPU_UTIL alone, without checking PIPE_TENSOR_ACTIVE
Concludes the job is network-bound without checking whether network throughput counters actually moved
Assumes 'no code change' rules out a software-stack regression (driver/CUDA/NCCL version)
Doesn't distinguish a data-loading-bound signature (GPU_UTIL dropping) from this one (GPU_UTIL staying high)
Jumps straight to a deep Nsight Compute profile without first ruling out a simple stack-version change
Treats DCGM's aggregate metrics as sufficient on their own to pinpoint the exact offending code region
keyPoints: Correctly reads GPU_UTIL and PIPE_TENSOR_ACTIVE together to rule out a compute-bound explanation
Correctly rules out a data-starved signature based on sustained high GPU_UTIL
Correctly reads flat network counters as ruling out a straightforward network-throughput explanation
Proposes checking for an unnoticed software-stack change as a high-probability first step
Proposes a sound next diagnostic step (Nsight Systems, NCCL_DEBUG) beyond DCGM's aggregate view

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly interprets the combination of DCGM metrics to rule out compute- and data-bound explanations
Correctly rules out a straightforward network-throughput explanation
Proposes checking for an unnoticed software-stack change
Proposes a sound further diagnostic plan

questions.title: Fix a CUDA Kernel's Occupancy-Limiting Shared Memory Allocation
questions.prompt: This custom CUDA kernel for a fused layer-norm operation runs correctly but Nsight Compute reports achieved occupancy far below the theoretical maximum, with shared memory listed as the limiting resource. Fix the kernel so occupancy improves without changing its numerical behavior.
questions.modelAnswer: The kernel statically declares `__shared__ float buffer[4096]` per block regardless of how many threads are actually launched per block, which means every block reserves a fixed 16KB of shared memory (4096 floats x 4 bytes) whether it needs it or not — and since an SM's total shared memory is a fixed pool shared across all concurrently resident blocks, a 16KB-per-block reservation that's much larger than what's actually used directly limits how many blocks can be resident on an SM simultaneously, which is exactly what 'shared memory as the limiting resource' means in Nsight Compute's occupancy report. The fix is to size the shared-memory allocation to what the kernel actually needs for its launch configuration — if the kernel is launched with `blockDim.x` threads and only needs one float of scratch space per thread, declaring `extern __shared__ float buffer[]` and passing the exact required size (`blockDim.x * sizeof(float)`) as the third launch-configuration parameter at the call site, rather than a static over-allocated array, lets the compiler and runtime reserve only what's needed per block, which directly increases how many blocks can be co-resident on an SM and raises achieved occupancy. If the kernel's actual working set genuinely requires close to 4096 floats of shared memory for correctness (not just as a safety margin), then the real fix isn't to shrink the allocation dishonestly — it's to accept the occupancy ceiling that correct shared-memory usage imposes, since forcing higher occupancy at the cost of correctness or by reducing threads-per-block below what the algorithm needs would be solving the wrong problem; I'd confirm this by checking whether the kernel's actual per-block scratch usage, computed from its real launch configuration, is meaningfully smaller than 4096 before committing to the fix.
questions.professionalAnswer: Nsight Compute naming shared memory as the limiter means some fixed per-block allocation is big enough to cap how many blocks an SM can run at once — shared memory is a shared, finite pool per SM, so every byte a block over-reserves directly reduces how many other blocks can be resident alongside it. Here the kernel statically grabs 16KB per block (4096 floats) no matter what it's actually launched with, and if the real per-thread scratch need is much smaller than that for a typical launch configuration, that's pure waste capping occupancy for no reason. My fix is to switch to `extern __shared__` with a size computed from the actual launch config — blockDim.x times whatever each thread genuinely needs — and pass that exact byte count as the kernel launch's shared-memory parameter, instead of over-provisioning a static array sized for some unrelated worst case. The thing I'd check before declaring this fixed, though, is whether the kernel's real working set actually needs close to that much shared memory for correctness — if it does, then the right answer isn't to shrink the allocation and risk correctness, it's to accept that occupancy ceiling as the honest cost of what the algorithm actually requires, and I wouldn't force a 'fix' here that trades correctness for a better occupancy number on a dashboard.
commonMistakes: Reduces the shared-memory allocation without verifying the kernel's actual per-thread working-set requirement
Reduces threads-per-block to force higher occupancy instead of fixing the oversized shared-memory allocation
Doesn't recognize shared memory as a fixed, SM-wide pool shared across concurrently resident blocks
Switches to dynamic shared memory but doesn't correctly compute the required size from the launch configuration
Treats higher occupancy as an unconditional goal even if it would require sacrificing numerical correctness
Confuses shared-memory-per-block with total global memory usage when diagnosing the limiter
keyPoints: Correctly explains why an oversized static shared-memory allocation limits occupancy
Proposes extern __shared__ with a size computed from the actual launch configuration
Explains that shared memory is a fixed, SM-wide resource shared by co-resident blocks
Checks whether the kernel's real working set actually needs the larger allocation before shrinking it
Avoids sacrificing correctness or threads-per-block just to improve an occupancy number

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the oversized static shared-memory allocation as the cause
Proposes a correct, working fix (dynamic shared memory sized to actual need)
Explains the SM-wide shared-memory-pool mechanism correctly
Avoids sacrificing correctness to force a better occupancy number

questions.title: Fix a vLLM Deployment Config Causing Intermittent OOM Under Load
questions.prompt: This vLLM server launch configuration runs fine at low traffic but crashes with a CUDA out-of-memory error once concurrent request volume rises, even though the model comfortably fits in GPU memory on its own. Identify the misconfiguration and fix it.
questions.modelAnswer: The problem is `gpu_memory_utilization=0.98` combined with no `max_num_seqs` cap and a `max_model_len` of 32768: vLLM uses `gpu_memory_utilization` to decide how much of the GPU's total memory to reserve upfront for the KV cache pool after loading model weights, and setting it to 0.98 leaves almost no headroom for anything else vLLM or the CUDA runtime needs at runtime (activation memory during prefill for a newly arriving long request, CUDA context overhead, memory fragmentation from the allocator) — at low concurrency, the KV cache pool is barely touched and there's enough slack, but as concurrent requests rise toward the server's real capacity, the KV cache pool fills close to its reserved ceiling and the margin that 0.98 left for everything else is no longer enough, producing an OOM that looks like a capacity problem but is actually a configuration problem with zero safety margin. The `max_model_len=32768` with no `max_num_seqs` cap compounds this: every new request's maximum possible KV cache footprint is sized against `max_model_len`, so without a `max_num_seqs` ceiling, vLLM's admission logic can admit more concurrent long-context requests than the reserved KV cache pool can actually guarantee once they all grow toward their maximum length simultaneously. The fix: lower `gpu_memory_utilization` to a more conservative value (commonly 0.85-0.90) to leave real headroom for runtime overhead, and set an explicit `max_num_seqs` based on the server's own 'Maximum concurrency' startup-log estimate (which vLLM prints specifically to help set this) rather than leaving admission uncapped — this trades a small amount of maximum theoretical throughput for an actual safety margin that prevents OOM under realistic concurrent load.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is the classic 'worked in testing, fell over in production' pattern, because low-traffic testing never actually exercises the KV cache pool hard enough to hit the ceiling that 0.98 utilization leaves almost no margin around. `gpu_memory_utilization` controls how much of the GPU vLLM reserves upfront for the KV cache after loading weights, and setting it to 0.98 is leaving almost nothing for runtime overhead — prefill activation memory for a newly arriving request, CUDA context, allocator fragmentation — which is fine when the KV cache pool is mostly empty under light load, and not fine once concurrent requests push that pool toward what was reserved. The second half of the problem is that `max_model_len=32768` with no `max_num_seqs` cap means vLLM's admission control has no explicit ceiling on how many requests it'll let in concurrently, each one sized against that large max length, so nothing stops it from admitting more long-context requests than the KV cache pool can actually back once they all grow toward their maximum simultaneously. My fix is to bring `gpu_memory_utilization` down to something like 0.85-0.90 to leave real runtime headroom, and to set an explicit `max_num_seqs` using vLLM's own startup-log 'Maximum concurrency' estimate as the actual number to size against, instead of leaving admission open-ended — yes, that costs a bit of theoretical peak throughput, but it's the difference between a server that degrades gracefully under load and one that falls over with an OOM.
commonMistakes: Assumes gpu_memory_utilization=0.98 is safe because the model itself fits comfortably in memory
Doesn't account for KV cache pool growth under concurrent load as the actual OOM trigger
Leaves max_num_seqs uncapped, letting admission control exceed what the reserved KV cache can back
Lowers max_model_len instead of addressing the actual utilization/admission misconfiguration
Treats the crash as a hardware capacity problem rather than a configuration margin problem
Doesn't reference vLLM's own startup-log concurrency estimate when setting max_num_seqs
keyPoints: Correctly identifies gpu_memory_utilization=0.98 as leaving insufficient runtime headroom
Explains how KV cache pool growth under concurrency, not model weight size, triggers the OOM
Identifies the missing max_num_seqs cap as compounding the problem
Proposes a concrete, correct fix (lower utilization, explicit max_num_seqs)
Explains the real throughput-vs-safety-margin tradeoff of the fix

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies gpu_memory_utilization as leaving insufficient headroom
Correctly identifies the missing max_num_seqs cap as compounding the issue
Proposes a concrete, correct, production-appropriate fix
Explains the tradeoff the fix introduces honestly

questions.title: Design an Elastic Slurm Job That Survives Node Loss Without a Full Restart
questions.prompt: Your team runs multi-day training jobs on a Slurm cluster where nodes occasionally get pulled for maintenance mid-run. Design the sbatch/srun submission and the training script's checkpoint/resume behavior so the job survives losing a node without starting over from scratch. Be specific about what Slurm can and can't do for you here versus what torch.distributed.elastic has to handle.
questions.modelAnswer: Slurm and torch.distributed.elastic solve two different halves of this problem, and conflating them is the most common design mistake. Slurm's job is allocation and scheduling: it decides which nodes a job runs on, and it has no native concept of 'the job should keep running with fewer nodes if one disappears' — a plain `sbatch`/`srun` job that loses a node simply fails, because `srun` launched a fixed-size parallel step across a fixed node allocation, and losing one of those nodes breaks that allocation's assumption. To get real elasticity, I'd submit the job requesting a range rather than a fixed count where the cluster supports it, and more importantly, launch the actual training process via `torchrun` with `--nnodes=MIN:MAX` and `--max-restarts` set to a reasonable budget, so that torch.distributed.elastic's own rendezvous and agent layer — not Slurm — handles detecting a disappeared worker, tearing down and re-forming the process group with whatever nodes remain, and restarting training from the most recent checkpoint, rather than Slurm trying to restart the whole job from scratch. The specific gotcha is that elastic's re-formation resumes from the last checkpoint, not the exact in-flight step that was running when a node dropped — so the actual resilience of this design is bounded by checkpoint frequency, not by how cleverly the elastic layer handles the node loss itself, which means checkpoint cadence has to be chosen based on how much recomputation is acceptable to lose (I'd derive this from the expected node-failure rate across the cluster size, the same blast-radius math used for a 512-GPU fault-tolerance plan, not an arbitrary 'every N steps' guess). I'd also keep the Slurm-level `sbatch` script itself simple and durable — requesting the node range, setting a generous time limit, and calling `srun torchrun ...` once — rather than trying to encode retry logic into the sbatch script itself, because Slurm-level job requeuing (`--requeue`) restarts the whole job including reloading from the cluster scheduler side, which is a much heavier, slower recovery path than letting torch.distributed.elastic handle a single node drop in-place without the job ever leaving Slurm's RUNNING state. Finally, I'd keep the rank-0 coordination role off any node pool that's more likely to be pulled for maintenance (a dedicated, more stable node for rank 0 where the cluster supports that distinction), since losing the elastic agent's coordination point is a more disruptive failure than losing an ordinary worker, even under elastic's own recovery model.
questions.professionalAnswer: I treat Slurm and torch.distributed.elastic as handling two different layers of this, and the design only works if I'm clear about which one owns what. Slurm allocates nodes and schedules the job, but it has no concept on its own of 'keep going with fewer nodes if one disappears' — a fixed `srun` step just fails outright if a node in its allocation drops. So I submit the job with a node range where the cluster supports it, and the actual elasticity comes from launching training with `torchrun --nnodes=MIN:MAX --max-restarts=N`, because that's what makes torch.distributed.elastic's agent layer, not Slurm, responsible for noticing a worker disappeared, tearing down and re-forming the process group with whoever's left, and resuming from the last checkpoint. The thing I'd be upfront about is that elastic recovery resumes from the last checkpoint, not the exact step that was interrupted — so the real resilience of this whole design comes down to checkpoint cadence, which I'd size based on the cluster's actual expected failure rate rather than picking an arbitrary interval, the same blast-radius-style math you'd use for planning fault tolerance at any real cluster scale. I'd also keep the sbatch script itself boring — request the node range, set a generous time limit, call `srun torchrun` once — rather than trying to build retry logic into Slurm's own requeue mechanism, because `--requeue` restarts the whole job from the scheduler side, which is a much heavier recovery path than letting elastic handle a single dropped node without the job ever leaving Slurm's running state. And I'd specifically avoid putting rank 0's coordination role on whatever node pool is more likely to get pulled for maintenance, since losing the elastic coordination point itself is a bigger disruption than losing an ordinary worker.
commonMistakes: Relies on Slurm's own retry/requeue mechanism to handle a single dropped node instead of torch.distributed.elastic
Assumes a fixed-size srun step will gracefully continue if one node in its allocation disappears
Doesn't account for elastic recovery resuming from the last checkpoint rather than the exact interrupted step
Picks an arbitrary checkpoint interval instead of deriving cadence from the cluster's real failure-rate math
Puts rank 0's coordination role on a node pool equally likely to be pulled for maintenance as any worker
Conflates what Slurm is responsible for (allocation/scheduling) with what torch.distributed.elastic is responsible for (in-job elasticity)
keyPoints: Correctly separates Slurm's allocation/scheduling role from torch.distributed.elastic's in-job recovery role
Specifies torchrun with --nnodes range and --max-restarts as the actual elasticity mechanism
Explains that recovery resumes from last checkpoint, not the exact interrupted step
Ties checkpoint cadence to real failure-rate math rather than an arbitrary interval
Protects the rank-0 coordination role from being placed on volatile node capacity

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly separates Slurm's role from torch.distributed.elastic's role
Specifies a concrete, correct elastic launch configuration
Correctly ties checkpoint cadence to realistic recovery-granularity reasoning

questions.title: Find and Fix a Training/Serving Skew Bug in Feature Computation Code
questions.prompt: A fraud model's production accuracy is quietly worse than its offline evaluation suggested. You're given the batch feature-computation SQL used for training and the online feature function used at serving time for the same logical feature, 'transactions_last_24h'. Find the discrepancy and propose the fix, including how you'd prevent this exact class of bug from recurring.
questions.modelAnswer: The batch SQL computes a strict trailing 24-hour window using `event_timestamp` as the anchor and includes transactions with `status IN ('completed', 'pending')`, while the online function anchors its 24-hour window on `now()` (the wall-clock time the serving request arrives) and only counts `status = 'completed'` — two separate discrepancies stacked on top of each other, not one. The timestamp-anchor difference matters because the batch training data, built from historical event logs, naturally uses each event's own timestamp as the reference point for 'the last 24 hours,' while the online function reasonably uses the current wall-clock time since there's no historical event to anchor to at serving time — this isn't a bug in either implementation individually, but it means the two code paths are answering subtly different questions ('transactions in the 24 hours before this historical event' versus 'transactions in the 24 hours before right now') that happen to look identical in the common case and diverge specifically for any transaction near a status transition or a delayed event arrival. The status-filter difference is the more serious bug: a transaction that's `pending` at serving time but later resolves to `completed` (or `failed`) by the time the historical batch job runs gets counted in training but not in serving, so the model learned a feature definition that counts pending transactions, and the production feature it actually receives systematically undercounts relative to what it saw in training whenever there's a meaningful pending-transaction rate — which is exactly the kind of training/serving skew that degrades production accuracy without showing up in any offline evaluation, since the offline evaluation also uses the batch definition. The fix is to make both code paths implement the literal same feature definition, including the status filter, and ideally to generate both from one shared, declarative feature definition (the FeatureView pattern) rather than two independently hand-maintained implementations — a batch materialization job and an online on-demand or streaming path that both derive from the same transformation logic, so a future change to the status filter or the window logic can't silently diverge between the two again. To prevent recurrence, I'd add an automated consistency check that periodically samples real production feature values and recomputes the same feature from the batch definition for the same entity and timestamp, alerting on any systematic divergence beyond a small tolerance, rather than relying on code review alone to catch a future version of this exact bug.
questions.professionalAnswer: Finding this means actually diffing the two implementations' real logic, not just their names, because 'transactions_last_24h' sounds like one feature and is actually two slightly different features wearing the same name. The timestamp-anchor difference — batch uses each historical event's own timestamp, online uses wall-clock `now()` — isn't really a bug by itself, since there's no other sensible anchor for the online path, but it does mean the two paths are quietly answering different questions that only look the same in the typical case. The real bug is the status filter: batch counts `pending` and `completed` transactions, online counts only `completed`, so any transaction that's still pending when a fraud-scoring request comes in but later resolves by the time the training data gets built gets counted in training and not in serving — the model learned a feature that includes pending transactions, and what it actually gets in production systematically undercounts relative to that, which degrades accuracy in a way no offline evaluation would ever catch, because the offline eval is built from the same batch definition that has the bug baked into it. My fix is to make both paths implement the literal same definition, and the way I'd actually prevent this specific bug class from recurring is to stop hand-maintaining two separate implementations at all — generate both the batch and online paths from one shared, declarative feature definition, so there's structurally only one place the status filter or window logic can live, plus an automated job that periodically recomputes a sampled production feature value from the batch definition and alerts on systematic divergence, instead of trusting code review to catch the next version of this same mistake.
commonMistakes: Only checks the timestamp-anchor difference and misses the more serious status-filter discrepancy
Treats the timestamp-anchor difference as a bug rather than recognizing it's not avoidable given online's lack of a historical anchor
Fixes the specific instance without proposing a structural fix (shared feature definition) to prevent recurrence
Assumes offline evaluation would have caught this, missing that the offline eval shares the same buggy batch definition
Doesn't propose any ongoing, automated consistency check between batch and online feature values
Focuses only on the SQL/code fix without explaining why this specific class of bug evades normal testing
keyPoints: Correctly identifies the status-filter discrepancy as the primary bug
Correctly distinguishes it from the timestamp-anchor difference, which isn't actually avoidable
Explains why this exact bug class evades offline evaluation entirely
Proposes a shared, declarative feature-definition fix rather than a point patch to one implementation
Proposes an ongoing automated consistency check to catch recurrence

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the real bug (status filter) versus the non-bug (timestamp anchor)
Explains why this evades offline evaluation specifically
Proposes a structural fix (shared feature definition), not just a point patch
Proposes an ongoing automated detection mechanism for recurrence

questions.title: Read a Nsight Systems Timeline to Find a Hidden Synchronization Stall
questions.prompt: You profile a single training step with Nsight Systems and the timeline shows: a long, unbroken block of GPU kernel activity, followed by a visible gap where the GPU row goes empty, followed by a short CPU-side block labeled with a cudaMemcpy or similar sync-triggering call, before the next step's GPU activity begins. Explain what this pattern tells you and what specific code change you'd look for.
questions.modelAnswer: This is the textbook signature of an unnecessary host-device synchronization point breaking up an otherwise well-overlapped training loop, and the specific shape of the timeline — not just the fact that there's a gap — is what tells you where to look. GPU kernel activity running as one long unbroken block means the forward/backward computation itself is being issued and executing efficiently with good kernel-to-kernel overlap, so the problem isn't inside the model's compute; the gap where the GPU row goes empty immediately after that block, followed by a CPU-side block that includes a synchronizing call, means the CPU was blocked waiting for the GPU to finish everything queued so far before it could do whatever's in that CPU block — and crucially, while the CPU is blocked, the GPU is sitting completely idle because nothing new has been issued to it, which is wasted time on the much more expensive piece of hardware. The specific code pattern I'd look for is any call in the training loop that forces the CPU to wait on a GPU result synchronously: `.item()` or `.cpu()` on a tensor still attached to the computation graph (common when accumulating a running loss directly instead of calling `.item()` immediately, or when logging a metric every step without detaching it first), a plain blocking `.to('cpu')` transfer instead of a `non_blocking=True` transfer paired with pinned memory, or an explicit `torch.cuda.synchronize()` call left in from debugging. The fix depends on which of those it is, but the general pattern is the same: move whatever CPU-side work is currently synchronous (logging a loss value, checking a metric for early stopping, writing a checkpoint trigger condition) to either happen less frequently (every N steps instead of every step), or to use an async-friendly pattern (accumulate the loss as a tensor and only call `.item()` once per logging interval, not once per step) so the CPU isn't forced to wait on every single step's GPU work finishing before it can move the loop forward. I'd confirm the exact call by zooming into that CPU-side block in the Nsight Systems timeline and reading which API call it's actually labeled with, rather than guessing from the training loop code alone, since several different lines of code can produce this same timeline shape.
questions.professionalAnswer: The shape of this timeline is the giveaway — a clean, unbroken block of GPU activity tells me the model's own compute is overlapping well and isn't the problem, and the empty GPU gap that shows up right after it, lined up with a CPU-side block that includes a sync-triggering call, means the CPU stalled waiting on the GPU to catch up before it could do whatever's in that block, and the GPU just sits idle the whole time it's waiting. What I'd actually go looking for in the code is whatever's forcing that synchronous wait — the usual suspects are a `.item()` or `.cpu()` call on a tensor that's still attached to the graph, often from accumulating a running loss the wrong way instead of detaching it immediately, or a blocking CPU transfer instead of a non_blocking one with pinned memory, or sometimes just a leftover `torch.cuda.synchronize()` from an earlier debugging session nobody removed. I wouldn't guess which one it is from reading the loop though — I'd zoom into that exact CPU block in the Nsight Systems timeline and read what API call it's actually labeled with, because several different lines can produce this identical gap shape, and guessing wrong means fixing the wrong thing. The general fix once I know which it is is the same shape regardless: stop forcing a synchronous wait every single step — log or check whatever that value is every N steps instead of every step, or keep accumulating as a tensor and only pull it to the CPU once per logging interval, so the CPU can keep issuing the next step's work instead of blocking on this step's GPU result finishing first.
commonMistakes: Concludes the model's compute itself is the bottleneck, missing that the long unbroken GPU block rules that out
Guesses which specific line of code causes the sync without confirming via the actual labeled call in the timeline
Recommends torch.cuda.synchronize() as a fix rather than recognizing it as a likely cause of this exact pattern
Doesn't distinguish a synchronous .item()/.cpu() call from a properly async, non_blocking transfer
Proposes reducing model size or batch size instead of addressing the actual synchronization stall
Fixes the symptom (removes one sync call) without checking for other instances of the same pattern elsewhere in the loop
keyPoints: Correctly reads the unbroken GPU block as ruling out a compute-bound explanation
Correctly identifies the gap+CPU-sync-call pattern as a host-device synchronization stall
Proposes concrete candidate code patterns (.item()/.cpu(), blocking transfer, leftover synchronize())
Recommends confirming the exact cause via the timeline's labeled call rather than guessing
Proposes a sound general fix pattern (reduce sync frequency, async-friendly accumulation)

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly reads the timeline pattern as a host-device synchronization stall
Proposes concrete, plausible code-level causes
Recommends confirming the exact cause rather than guessing
Proposes a sound general fix approach

questions.title: Fix a Fused Triton Kernel That Produces Wrong Results Only at Larger Batch Sizes
questions.prompt: This Triton kernel for a fused RMSNorm operation produces correct output at batch size 1-8 but silently produces wrong results at batch size 32 and above, with no error raised. Find the bug.
questions.code:
@triton.jit
def rmsnorm_kernel(x_ptr, out_ptr, weight_ptr, hidden_dim, eps,
                   BLOCK_SIZE: tl.constexpr):
    row = tl.program_id(0)
    offsets = tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE)
    mask = offsets < hidden_dim

    x = tl.load(x_ptr + row * hidden_dim + offsets, mask=mask, other=0.0)
    ms = tl.sum(x * x, axis=0) / hidden_dim
    rrms = 1.0 / tl.sqrt(ms + eps)

    w = tl.load(weight_ptr + offsets, mask=mask, other=0.0)
    out = x * rrms * w
    tl.store(out_ptr + row * hidden_dim + offsets, out, mask=mask)

# launched with BLOCK_SIZE=1024, grid=(batch_size,)
# hidden_dim in practice reaches 4096+ for larger model configs
questions.modelAnswer: The bug is that `BLOCK_SIZE` is fixed at 1024 and the kernel grid is launched with one program instance per row (`grid=(batch_size,)`), but the row-reduction loop inside the kernel only processes the first `BLOCK_SIZE` elements of each row via a single `tl.load` with no loop over multiple blocks when `hidden_dim` exceeds `BLOCK_SIZE` — at batch sizes 1-8 the test is presumably being run with a `hidden_dim` that happens to fit within 1024 elements, or the discrepancy from truncating the reduction is too small to notice, but the described symptom ('wrong at batch size 32+') is actually a strong hint that the real variable at play isn't batch size directly, it's that whatever test harness generates the input tensor is likely using a `hidden_dim` that scales with or correlates with batch size in the test setup, or more likely, the kernel is reusing a single program per row for the *entire* row's reduction with a hardcoded offset range `tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE)` that never advances past the first BLOCK_SIZE elements regardless of the actual row length — so for any row longer than 1024 elements, the mean and variance are computed from only the first 1024 elements and silently normalized as if that were the whole row, which is numerically 'valid' output (no NaN, no crash) but wrong relative to the true RMSNorm over the full row. The fix is to either loop over `hidden_dim` in chunks of `BLOCK_SIZE` within the kernel, accumulating the sum-of-squares across all chunks before computing the final RMS normalization and writing output in a second pass over the same chunks, or to make `BLOCK_SIZE` large enough (as a `tl.constexpr` matched to `triton.next_power_of_2(hidden_dim)`) to cover the whole row in one block if `hidden_dim` is known to be bounded — the chunked-loop version is the more general, correct fix since it doesn't depend on `hidden_dim` staying under a fixed ceiling.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is a silent-truncation bug, which is the most dangerous kind because the output isn't NaN or garbage, it's just computed from less data than it should be. The kernel's reduction only ever looks at the first `BLOCK_SIZE` (1024) elements of each row via one `tl.load` and one fixed `tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE)` offset range that never advances — so for any row whose actual length exceeds 1024, the mean and variance driving the normalization are computed from a truncated slice of the row, not the whole thing, and the output still looks like valid, finite RMSNorm output because the math itself is correct, it's just operating on the wrong amount of data. The 'works at batch size 1-8, breaks at 32+' framing is really a proxy for whatever's changing about the actual row length (hidden_dim) in however this is being tested — the real trigger is row length exceeding BLOCK_SIZE, not batch size directly. My fix is to make the kernel actually loop over the full row in BLOCK_SIZE-sized chunks, accumulating sum-of-squares across every chunk before computing the final RMS value, then doing a second pass over those same chunks to write the normalized output — that's the general fix that doesn't depend on hidden_dim staying under some fixed ceiling, versus just bumping BLOCK_SIZE up to cover today's row length and reintroducing the exact same bug the next time someone uses a bigger hidden_dim.
commonMistakes: Blames batch size directly instead of identifying hidden_dim/row length exceeding BLOCK_SIZE as the real trigger
Proposes simply increasing BLOCK_SIZE as a general fix instead of a size-independent chunked-loop approach
Doesn't recognize the bug as silent truncation rather than an indexing crash or NaN-producing error
Assumes the kernel would raise an error if the reduction were incomplete, rather than producing valid-looking wrong output
Fixes only the sum-of-squares accumulation loop but forgets the output-writing pass also needs to loop over the full row
Doesn't verify the fix against the specific case (row length > current BLOCK_SIZE) that exposed the original bug
keyPoints: Correctly identifies the fixed BLOCK_SIZE combined with no chunking loop as the root cause
Correctly reframes the trigger as row length (hidden_dim) exceeding BLOCK_SIZE, not batch size directly
Explains why this produces valid-looking but numerically wrong output rather than an error
Proposes a size-independent chunked-loop fix rather than just raising BLOCK_SIZE
Covers both the reduction (sum-of-squares) pass and the output-writing pass in the fix

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the fixed-BLOCK_SIZE truncation as root cause
Correctly reframes the real trigger as row length vs. batch size
Proposes a correct, size-independent chunked fix
Addresses both reduction and output-writing passes

questions.title: Fix a Canary Rollout Script That Can Silently Promote a Failing Model
questions.prompt: This deployment automation script is meant to canary a new model version at 5% traffic, check error rate, and either promote or roll back. Find the logic bug that lets it silently promote a model that's actually failing, and fix it.
questions.modelAnswer: The bug is in the metric query and comparison: `error_rate = get_metric('error_rate', window='5m')` fetches the error rate for *all* traffic to the service, not specifically the canary version's slice, because the query has no filter by model version or deployment label — so if the canary is only receiving 5% of traffic and is failing badly, its errors get diluted into the aggregate error rate across the other 95% of traffic still going to the stable version, and the aggregate number can easily stay under the `threshold=0.05` check even while the canary itself is failing on a majority of its own requests. This is exactly the kind of bug that passes every test run during development, because a canary deployed with a correctly-isolated test traffic split would actually need the metric query to be filtered to reproduce this bug — it only shows up in a real production topology where the canary is genuinely a small slice of a much larger traffic volume, which is precisely the scenario this script exists to handle safely. The fix is to query the error rate filtered specifically to the canary's own version label or deployment identifier (`get_metric('error_rate', window='5m', filters={'version': canary_version})`), and ideally to also compare it against the stable version's own error rate over the same window as a relative check, not just an absolute threshold, since a canary with a 4% error rate against a stable version's steady 0.1% is a real signal even if 4% happens to be under an absolute 5% threshold chosen for a different context. I'd also add a minimum-sample-size guard before trusting the canary's error rate at all, since 5% traffic over a 5-minute window might be too few requests for the measured error rate to be statistically meaningful, and promoting (or failing to catch a failure) based on a noisy small-sample estimate is its own distinct risk from the metric-isolation bug.
questions.professionalAnswer: The actual bug here is subtle because the script runs, checks something real, and still gets the wrong answer — the error-rate query isn't scoped to the canary at all, it's pulling the error rate across all traffic to the service, so the canary's own failures get averaged in with the 95% of traffic still going to the healthy stable version and diluted below the threshold. This is exactly the kind of bug that sails through any test where the canary and stable split isn't realistically small, because you'd need the metric query to actually be filtered by version to even notice the dilution in a test with, say, a 50/50 split — it only becomes dangerous in the real 5%-canary scenario this script is supposed to be safe for. My fix is to filter the error-rate query specifically to the canary's own version or deployment label, and honestly I'd go further and compare it against the stable version's error rate over the same window as a relative signal, not just an absolute threshold, because a canary running at 4% errors against a stable baseline of 0.1% is a real problem even though 4% is technically under a 5% absolute cutoff that was probably chosen without this specific canary-size scenario in mind. I'd also add a minimum-sample-size check before trusting the number at all, since 5% of traffic over a short window might just not be enough requests to make the error rate measurement itself statistically meaningful — that's a separate risk from the metric-isolation bug, but it's exactly the kind of thing that compounds with it if you don't also guard against it.
commonMistakes: Doesn't notice the error-rate query lacks a filter for the canary's specific version/deployment label
Assumes an absolute threshold check is sufficient without comparing against the stable version's baseline
Doesn't account for dilution of canary-specific errors into the aggregate traffic error rate
Misses that this bug would not reproduce in a test with a large canary traffic percentage, only a small realistic one
Doesn't add a minimum-sample-size guard, risking promotion/rollback decisions based on statistically noisy data
Fixes the query filter but doesn't also address the relative-comparison or sample-size issues
keyPoints: Correctly identifies the missing version/deployment filter on the error-rate query as the root cause
Explains why the dilution effect specifically appears at realistic small canary traffic percentages
Proposes filtering the query to the canary's specific version as the primary fix
Proposes a relative comparison against the stable baseline, not just an absolute threshold
Adds a minimum-sample-size guard as an additional, distinct safeguard

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the missing version-scoped filter as root cause
Explains why this specifically manifests at realistic small canary traffic shares
Proposes a correct fix including relative comparison against baseline
Adds a sample-size safeguard as a distinct improvement

questions.title: Write a Burn-Rate Alert for an Inference SLO Instead of a Raw Threshold Alert
questions.prompt: Your current alerting fires whenever p99 TTFT exceeds 2 seconds for even one scrape interval, and it pages on-call constantly for brief, self-resolving spikes. Rewrite this as a proper SLO burn-rate alert with both a fast-burn and a slow-burn rule, and explain the reasoning behind the specific windows and thresholds you choose.
questions.code:
# Current (bad) rule
- alert: HighTTFT
  expr: histogram_quantile(0.99, ttft_seconds_bucket) > 2
  for: 0m
  labels:
    severity: page
questions.modelAnswer: The current rule's actual flaw is treating every single scrape interval as independently alert-worthy, with no concept of how much of the monthly error budget a brief spike actually consumes — which is exactly why it pages constantly on blips that resolve before anyone could act on them anyway. A burn-rate alert instead asks 'at the rate we're currently failing the SLO, how long until we exhaust the error budget,' and fires at two different urgencies depending on how fast that consumption is happening. For the fast-burn rule, I'd use a short lookback window (5 minutes) combined with a burn-rate multiplier high enough that it only fires when the SLO is being violated badly enough to exhaust the entire monthly budget in a matter of hours if sustained — a common, defensible choice is a 14.4x burn rate over 5 minutes (which, for a 99.9% SLO with a 30-day budget, corresponds to exhausting the whole month's budget in about 2 hours if sustained at that rate), paired with a short `for:` duration (1-2 minutes) so a true, sustained fast burn pages immediately, but a single-scrape blip that resolves on its own doesn't. For the slow-burn rule, I'd use a longer lookback window (1 hour, or even 6 hours) with a lower burn-rate multiplier (around 6x, corresponding to exhausting the month's budget in about 5 days if sustained), and route it to a ticket rather than a page, since a slow burn is real and needs attention but doesn't need anyone woken up at 3am — the urgency genuinely is different, and giving both rules the same severity is exactly the kind of alert-fatigue mistake that erodes trust in the whole alerting system. I'd implement both as ratio-based burn-rate calculations against the actual SLI (the fraction of requests violating the TTFT target) rather than alerting on the raw TTFT value directly, since the raw value conflates 'how bad is this request' with 'how much of our budget is this costing us,' and it's the second question that should actually drive paging decisions.
questions.professionalAnswer: The real problem with the current rule is that it has no sense of budget at all — it treats a single bad scrape interval the same as a sustained outage, which is exactly backwards, because a blip that resolves in under a minute barely touches the actual monthly error budget and isn't worth waking anyone up for. A burn-rate alert answers a different question: at this rate of SLO violation, how long until the whole month's budget is gone, and that naturally gives you two different urgencies. My fast-burn rule uses a short window, 5 minutes, with a high burn-rate multiplier like 14.4x — which for a 99.9% SLO corresponds to blowing the whole month's budget in a couple of hours if it keeps up — plus a short `for:` duration so it still catches a genuinely sustained problem fast without firing on one noisy scrape. My slow-burn rule uses a longer window, an hour or more, with a lower multiplier like 6x, corresponding to exhausting the budget over several days rather than hours, and that one goes to a ticket, not a page, because it's real but it's not a 3am problem. Giving both of these the same severity is exactly the alert-fatigue mistake that erodes trust in the whole system over time — the entire point of having two rules is that they represent genuinely different urgency, and the paging behavior should reflect that difference, not just the rule's existence.
commonMistakes: Keeps a raw-threshold alert instead of converting to a burn-rate-based rule
Uses only one burn-rate rule instead of distinguishing fast-burn from slow-burn urgency
Gives fast-burn and slow-burn rules the same severity/paging behavior
Picks arbitrary windows/multipliers without tying them to actual budget-exhaustion math
Doesn't add a for: duration, so a single noisy scrape can still trigger a page
Alerts on the raw SLI value rather than the burn-rate ratio against the actual error budget
keyPoints: Correctly diagnoses the existing rule's lack of budget-awareness as the core flaw
Proposes a genuine fast-burn rule with a short window and high multiplier
Proposes a genuine slow-burn rule with a longer window and lower multiplier, routed to a ticket not a page
Ties the specific multipliers to real budget-exhaustion-time reasoning
Gives the two rules different severities reflecting their different urgency

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the raw-threshold rule's core flaw
Proposes a correct, well-reasoned fast-burn rule
Proposes a correct, well-reasoned slow-burn rule with different severity
Ties thresholds to real budget-exhaustion-time math

questions.title: Diagnose Why Speculative Decoding Is Making Latency Worse, Not Better
questions.prompt: After enabling speculative decoding with a small draft model, your serving fleet's actual p50 latency got slightly worse, not better, even though the draft model's token-level accuracy against the target model looked reasonable in offline testing. Walk through how you'd diagnose this and what's most likely actually happening.
questions.modelAnswer: Speculative decoding is only a net win when the draft model's acceptance rate is high enough that the throughput gained from verifying multiple tokens per large-model forward pass outweighs the extra overhead of running the draft model at all plus the rejection-sampling verification step itself — 'reasonable' offline token-level accuracy isn't the same as a high real-world acceptance rate for this specific workload's actual input distribution, and the gap between those two is the first thing I'd check. The offline accuracy number is likely measured on some representative or benchmark dataset, while production traffic may skew toward content the draft model handles worse than the target (a different domain, a different language mix, more code or more structured output where small models are known to diverge more from larger ones) — if the real acceptance rate in production is low, most speculative rounds end in rejection, meaning you paid the draft model's forward-pass cost and the verification cost for most rounds without getting the multi-token-per-verification benefit that's supposed to pay for it, which can net out worse than not speculating at all. I'd instrument and check the actual acceptance rate under real production traffic specifically (not the offline benchmark number), broken down by request characteristics if possible, since a low aggregate acceptance rate hiding a bimodal distribution (very high acceptance on some request types, very low on others) would suggest routing only some traffic through speculative decoding rather than all of it. Separately, I'd check whether the draft model's own forward pass is actually cheap relative to the target model's — if the 'small' draft model is only modestly smaller than the target (not an order of magnitude smaller), its forward-pass cost eats into the latency budget speculative decoding is supposed to save, regardless of acceptance rate, so I'd compare the draft model's actual latency contribution per round against the latency saved per accepted token. Finally, I'd check how many tokens are being drafted per round (the speculation length) — drafting too many tokens per round increases the chance that a rejection happens early in the draft sequence, wasting the compute spent drafting tokens past the rejection point, so if acceptance rate is moderate but speculation length is set aggressively high, shortening it could reduce wasted work even without changing the draft model itself.
questions.professionalAnswer: The gap I'd focus on immediately is that 'reasonable offline token accuracy' and 'high real acceptance rate on actual production traffic' are two different numbers, and the second one is the one that actually determines whether speculative decoding helps or hurts. If production traffic skews toward content the draft model handles worse than whatever it was benchmarked on — different domain, more code, different language mix — the real acceptance rate could be low enough that most speculative rounds end in rejection, and when that happens you've paid for the draft model's forward pass and the verification step without getting the multi-token payoff that's supposed to justify the whole mechanism, which nets out as pure overhead. So my first move is instrumenting the actual acceptance rate under real traffic, ideally broken down by request type, because a low aggregate number hiding a bimodal split would point toward routing speculative decoding selectively rather than applying it to everything. I'd also sanity-check that the draft model is actually cheap relative to the target — if it's only modestly smaller, its own forward-pass cost is eating into the exact latency budget this technique is supposed to save, independent of acceptance rate. And I'd look at the speculation length — how many tokens get drafted per round — because drafting too many at once increases the odds of an early rejection wasting compute on tokens past the rejection point, so if the acceptance rate turns out to be moderate rather than bad, dialing speculation length down might fix this without touching the draft model at all.
commonMistakes: Assumes offline token-accuracy is a reliable proxy for real production acceptance rate without verifying it
Doesn't check whether production traffic's content distribution differs from the offline benchmark's
Overlooks that a draft model only modestly smaller than the target can itself erode the latency benefit
Doesn't consider speculation length (tokens drafted per round) as an independent tuning lever
Concludes speculative decoding is simply the wrong technique without first instrumenting real acceptance rate
Changes multiple variables (draft model, speculation length) at once instead of isolating the actual cause
keyPoints: Distinguishes offline token-accuracy from real production acceptance rate as the key diagnostic gap
Proposes instrumenting real acceptance rate under production traffic, ideally segmented by request type
Checks whether the draft model's own forward-pass cost is genuinely small relative to the target
Considers speculation length as an independent, tunable variable
Proposes a logical, staged diagnostic process rather than guessing at a single cause

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes offline accuracy from real production acceptance rate
Proposes concrete instrumentation to measure real acceptance rate
Considers draft-model cost and speculation length as independent variables
Proposes a sound, staged diagnostic approach

questions.title: Extend a Cost-Attribution Script to Catch Underutilized Reserved GPU Capacity
questions.prompt: Your Kubecost-based chargeback script currently attributes GPU cost by namespace, proportional to each pod's GPU request. Leadership also wants it to flag any team paying for GPUs they're running at low utilization, not just report what they're spending. Describe the extension you'd actually build, including what data you'd need beyond Kubecost's default view.
questions.modelAnswer: Kubecost's namespace-proportional attribution answers 'who is being billed for what,' but it has no idea whether the GPUs a namespace is being billed for are actually being used, because Kubecost's cost model is built from resource requests/allocations, not from runtime utilization telemetry — so extending this to flag underutilization means joining a genuinely different data source (DCGM metrics, specifically `DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_UTIL` or the more precise `DCGM_FI_PROF_PIPE_TENSOR_ACTIVE` if you want to catch a GPU that's technically 'busy' but not doing much real compute) against the same namespace/pod attribution Kubecost already uses, rather than trying to get Kubecost to compute this on its own. The extension I'd build: a scheduled job that queries Prometheus (where DCGM metrics typically already land if DCGM-exporter is deployed) for average GPU utilization per pod over a trailing window (I'd use a window long enough to smooth out legitimate bursty workloads, like 24-48 hours, rather than a snapshot, since a training job that's compute-bound in bursts with brief data-loading gaps shouldn't be flagged as underutilized from a 5-minute sample), joins that utilization data to the same pod-to-namespace-to-team mapping Kubecost already uses for cost attribution, and computes a cost-weighted utilization number per namespace — specifically, dollars spent on GPU capacity multiplied by (1 minus average utilization), which gives a dollar figure representing 'cost of idle capacity' rather than just a utilization percentage that doesn't communicate the actual business stakes. I'd set the flagging threshold based on workload type, not one number platform-wide, since the prototyping team's low utilization is expected and acceptable (that's explicitly why they're on MIG-shared capacity, not dedicated GPUs) while the same low utilization on a dedicated training-pool allocation represents real wasted spend that's actually actionable — so the report needs to be workload-type-aware, pulling in the node-pool/sharing-strategy context from the scheduling design, not just a flat percentage cutoff applied uniformly. I'd deliver this as a weekly report to each team lead rather than a real-time alert, since utilization-based cost flags are a capacity-planning input, not an incident, and firing it as an urgent alert would just contribute to alert fatigue for a signal that's genuinely not time-critical.
questions.professionalAnswer: Kubecost's default view tells you who's paying for what, but it has no idea whether those GPUs are actually doing anything, because its cost model comes from resource requests and allocations, not from runtime telemetry — so this extension really means joining a different data source entirely, DCGM utilization metrics via Prometheus, against the same pod-to-namespace mapping Kubecost already has, rather than expecting Kubecost itself to grow a utilization feature. What I'd actually build is a scheduled job that pulls average GPU utilization per pod over a trailing 24-48 hour window — long enough to smooth out a legitimately bursty workload instead of flagging it from one unlucky 5-minute sample — joins that to the existing cost-attribution mapping, and reports a dollar figure, cost times (1 minus utilization), because 'this namespace is at 40% utilization' doesn't land with leadership the way 'this namespace is paying for roughly $12,000 of idle GPU capacity this week' does. The piece I'd insist on is making the threshold workload-type-aware rather than one flat cutoff for the whole fleet, because the prototyping team running at low utilization is exactly what MIG sharing is designed for and isn't a real problem, while the same low number on a dedicated training allocation is genuinely wasted spend worth acting on — so this report needs to know which node pool and sharing strategy a workload is actually on, not just compute one percentage and apply the same bar everywhere. And I'd ship this as a weekly report, not a real-time alert, because underutilization is a capacity-planning signal, not an incident, and treating it like one just adds to the alert fatigue problem instead of actually getting acted on.
commonMistakes: Assumes Kubecost's own cost model can natively answer a utilization question without joining external telemetry
Uses a short utilization sampling window that would flag legitimately bursty workloads as underutilized
Applies one flat utilization threshold uniformly across workload types with very different expected utilization
Reports utilization as a raw percentage rather than translating it into a dollar-cost-of-idle-capacity figure
Ships the utilization flag as a real-time alert rather than a periodic capacity-planning report
Doesn't account for workload-type/node-pool context (dedicated vs. MIG-shared) when deciding what's actionable
keyPoints: Correctly identifies that Kubecost's cost model has no native utilization signal and needs an external data join
Proposes a sound trailing-window utilization measurement that avoids false-flagging bursty workloads
Translates utilization into a dollar-cost-of-idle-capacity figure rather than a bare percentage
Makes the flagging threshold workload-type-aware rather than a flat platform-wide cutoff
Delivers the signal at an appropriate cadence (periodic report, not real-time alert)

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the need to join external DCGM/utilization data to Kubecost's cost attribution
Proposes a sound measurement window and dollar-cost framing
Makes the threshold workload-type-aware rather than flat
Delivers the signal at an appropriate cadence and avoids alert fatigue

questions.title: Postmortem: A Silent Accuracy Regression Spanning Data, Training Numerics, and Serving Quantization
questions.prompt: A mid-sized AI company, Northfield Labs, ships a 13B-parameter instruction-tuned model behind an internal developer-assistant product. Three weeks after a routine retraining-and-redeploy cycle, a handful of users report the assistant is 'getting worse' at multi-step reasoning tasks, but no dashboard shows a clear signal: eval suite scores are within normal noise, serving latency and error rates are flat, and GPU utilization looks unchanged. You're asked to lead the investigation. Walk through how you'd actually find the root cause and what you'd change afterward, given that the regression could plausibly originate in the data pipeline, the distributed training run itself, or the serving-side quantization applied before deployment.
commonMistakes: Treats the vague qualitative complaint as unfalsifiable instead of building a targeted eval slice to quantify it
Assumes the regression lives in whichever layer changed most recently without actually isolating layers via a 2x2-style comparison
Trusts a flat or noisy broad eval suite score as proof there's no real regression
Fixes a plausible-sounding cause without evidence it's the actual one, re-deploying without re-validating against the targeted slice
Relies on perplexity alone to validate the quantization pipeline, missing a narrower capability regression
Skips the fast rollback to last-known-good while root-causing, leaving users in a degraded state longer than necessary
keyPoints: Converts a vague complaint into a quantified, reproducible regression before investigating further
Isolates data, training, and quantization layers via a genuine before/after comparison design
Correctly interprets the 2x2 comparison evidence to localize the actual failure layer
Proposes a fast rollback to last-known-good independent of root-cause timeline
Proposes layer-specific remediation grounded in the actual evidence, not a guess
Closes the structural detection gap (targeted eval slice as a standing promotion gate) that let this go unnoticed

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Converts the vague report into a quantified, reproducible regression before investigating
