deepDive.heading: Clarify the actual signal and its boundaries
deepDive.content: Before touching any system, I'd pin down exactly what 'getting worse at multi-step reasoning' means operationally, because a vague qualitative complaint with no corroborating dashboard signal is exactly the kind of report that gets dismissed as anecdote and then turns out to be real three months later. I'd ask the reporting users for specific transcripts and task types, then build or reuse a small, targeted eval slice specifically for multi-step reasoning (chain-of-thought math, multi-hop retrieval-style questions, or whatever this product's actual usage looks like) rather than trusting the existing general eval suite, since a regression concentrated in one capability is exactly the kind of thing a broad average-case eval suite is known to hide. The first concrete deliverable isn't a root cause, it's a reproducible, quantified regression — a specific eval slice where the new model measurably underperforms the old one by more than noise — because without that, every downstream hypothesis is unfalsifiable.

deepDive.heading: Establish a clean before/after comparison across every layer
deepDive.content: Once the regression is quantified, I'd deliberately isolate each layer that changed between the two deployments, because the retraining-and-redeploy cycle touched all three: the data pipeline pulled a new training data snapshot, the training run produced a new checkpoint, and the serving deployment re-ran quantization on that new checkpoint. I'd test each layer independently rather than assuming the whole chain is guilty: run the previous checkpoint through the new quantization pipeline and the new checkpoint through the old (unquantized, full-precision) path, creating a 2x2 of {old checkpoint, new checkpoint} x {quantized, full precision}, evaluated on the targeted reasoning slice. This is the single highest-leverage move in the whole investigation, because it converts 'which of three systems is at fault' from a theory into a measured, falsifiable 2x2 result.

deepDive.heading: If the regression is checkpoint-driven: investigate the data pipeline first, then training numerics
deepDive.content: If the full-precision new checkpoint already underperforms the full-precision old checkpoint, quantization is cleared and the problem is upstream. I'd check the data pipeline's recent changes first, since it's the cheaper and faster thing to audit: did the training data mixture's proportions shift (more of one domain, less of another, which can happen silently if an upstream data source's volume changed without anyone adjusting sampling weights), did a data-quality filter change or regress, or did a feature-store-style skew issue let differently-processed data into this retraining run than into the last one. If the data pipeline checks out clean, I'd move to training numerics: pull the training run's loss curves and gradient-norm logs and check for a period of instability or a near-miss divergence that didn't fully crash the run but left the model in a worse region of the loss landscape — mixed-precision numerics issues (a BF16/FP16 misconfiguration, or a sharp gradient spike that gradient clipping dampened but didn't fully prevent from nudging training somewhere subtly worse) are exactly the kind of thing that produces a checkpoint that looks fine on broad eval averages while being specifically worse at a capability that depends on more fragile, compounding correctness, like multi-step reasoning.

deepDive.heading: If the regression is quantization-driven: isolate which operation and which scheme
deepDive.content: If instead the full-precision new checkpoint is fine but the quantized version of it regresses, the investigation shifts entirely to the quantization pipeline, and I'd check first whether the quantization scheme itself changed between deployments (a version bump in the quantization library, a different calibration dataset, a switch from one scheme to another) versus staying the same while the underlying model changed in a way that happens to interact worse with a scheme that was previously fine. Multi-step reasoning specifically is a capability known to be more sensitive to compounding small errors across a long generation than single-turn factual recall is, which makes it a plausible casualty of a quantization scheme that looks fine on perplexity (a cheap, broad signal) while degrading a narrower capability perplexity doesn't resolve. I'd re-run the calibration pass with a dataset more representative of actual multi-step reasoning traffic, and compare accuracy on the targeted eval slice between the current quantization scheme and a less aggressive one (a higher bit-width, or a scheme with per-channel rather than per-tensor scaling) to isolate whether this is a 'quantization in general is too aggressive for this checkpoint' problem or a 'this specific calibration set was a poor match' problem.

deepDive.heading: Distinguishing the three failure modes with the actual evidence
deepDive.content: The 2x2 result is the deciding evidence, and I'd treat it as definitive rather than layering in speculation once it's in hand: regression present in both quantized and full-precision new-checkpoint cells but absent in both old-checkpoint cells points at the checkpoint itself (data or training); regression present only in the new-checkpoint-quantized cell but absent in new-checkpoint-full-precision points at quantization specifically interacting badly with this particular checkpoint; and if the regression also failed to show in the full-precision old checkpoint but somehow does show in the quantized old checkpoint when re-run through the new quantization pipeline, that's actually evidence the quantization pipeline itself regressed independent of which checkpoint it's applied to, which is a different, serving-side-only incident. I'd insist the whole team see this evidence before committing to a remediation path, because the instinct to blame 'the model' when something changed during a deploy is common, and in my experience splits roughly evenly between the three layers in practice, which is exactly why guessing without the 2x2 wastes real time.

deepDive.heading: Remediation
deepDive.content: Whichever layer turns out to be responsible, the immediate remediation is the same first move: roll back to the last-known-good deployed artifact (the previous checkpoint at its previous quantization) via the registry's alias mechanism, which should be close to instantaneous and doesn't require waiting for the root cause to be fully understood. The substantive fix depends on the layer: a data pipeline cause gets a corrected data mixture and a retraining run validated against the targeted eval slice before promotion; a training-numerics cause gets a numerics audit of the training recipe (gradient-norm monitoring thresholds, mixed-precision configuration) and likely a retrain with tighter instability safeguards; a quantization cause gets either a better-matched calibration set or a less aggressive scheme specifically validated against the targeted reasoning slice, not just the broad perplexity number, before it's allowed back into the deployment pipeline.

deepDive.heading: Prevention: closing the actual gap that let this go undetected for three weeks
deepDive.content: The deepest problem exposed here isn't the regression itself — regressions happen — it's that the existing eval suite and dashboards had zero sensitivity to this specific failure mode for three weeks, and that's the gap I'd prioritize closing. I'd add the targeted multi-step-reasoning eval slice as a standing, automated gate in the promotion pipeline, run against both the full-precision and the quantized artifact separately before either reaches production, specifically so a 2x2-style comparison happens automatically on every promotion instead of being reconstructed manually after a complaint. I'd also add a lightweight, automated slice-level eval comparison as part of the standard quantization validation step, not just a perplexity check, since perplexity's blindness to this exact kind of narrow capability regression is a documented, known limitation, not a surprise, and treating it as the only pre-deployment signal is the structural mistake underneath this whole incident.

questions.title: A 512-GPU Training Run Diverges to NaN Only After 40,000 Steps
questions.prompt: A pretraining run has been stable for 40,000 steps across 512 GPUs using BF16, then the loss spikes and diverges to NaN within a handful of steps with no obvious trigger in the logs. Walk through how you'd actually diagnose the root cause of a divergence that takes this long to appear.
questions.modelAnswer: A divergence this far into a run, after tens of thousands of previously stable steps, points away from a static misconfiguration (which would typically show instability from the start) and toward something that either accumulates gradually or is triggered by a specific, rare data pattern the model hadn't encountered yet. I'd start by pulling the gradient-norm history, not just the loss curve, for the steps immediately preceding the spike, because gradient norm reaching an unusually high value a few steps before the loss itself visibly diverges is the typical early-warning signature, and if gradient clipping was active but the clip threshold was set too loosely to actually prevent the update from being too large, that's a strong, checkable lead. I'd also check whether the specific batch of training data processed at the step where things started going wrong contains anything unusual — an unusually long sequence, a sequence with repeated or degenerate tokens, or a data-quality issue that slipped past the pipeline's filters — since a model that's been stable for 40,000 steps diverging suddenly is frequently explained by hitting a specific bad data point rather than a continuous numerical drift, and I'd want the data pipeline to let me replay that exact batch in isolation to confirm or rule this out. If the specific batch looks unremarkable, I'd check for BF16-specific accumulation issues: even though BF16 avoids FP16's underflow risk, accumulated rounding error in a long-running optimizer state (particularly Adam's second-moment estimate) can, over tens of thousands of steps, drift enough to produce a pathological update in combination with a specific gradient pattern, which is a slower, harder-to-catch failure mode than a single bad batch. I'd also check cluster health signals from right around the divergence step — a straggler GPU, a degraded NIC, or a silent hardware fault (an Xid error in the driver log) on one of the 512 GPUs can, in rare cases, produce corrupted values that propagate through an all-reduce and corrupt every rank's gradients simultaneously, which would explain a sudden, cluster-wide divergence with no warning in the loss curve beforehand. The practical next step regardless of root cause is to resume training from the last good checkpoint before the spike with gradient-norm logging at finer granularity and, if a bad batch is suspected, with that specific data shard either excluded or replayed in isolation on a small-scale job to confirm the hypothesis without burning the full cluster's time.
questions.professionalAnswer: A divergence after 40,000 stable steps tells me this almost certainly isn't a basic misconfiguration, since that would usually show up far earlier — so I'm looking for either something that accumulates slowly or a specific trigger the model just happened to hit. My first pull is the gradient-norm history right before the spike, not just the loss curve, because a gradient norm climbing sharply a few steps before the visible divergence is the classic early-warning sign, and if that's what I see, the next question is whether gradient clipping was actually tight enough to have prevented the resulting update from being this large. In parallel, I'd want to know exactly what training data the model processed right at the step where things started going wrong, because a model stable for 40,000 steps suddenly diverging is very often explained by one unusual batch — an abnormally long sequence, degenerate repeated tokens, something that slipped past a data-quality filter — rather than a continuous numerical drift, and I'd want to replay that exact batch in isolation to confirm it. If the batch looks clean, I'd look at BF16 accumulation specifically, because even though BF16 avoids FP16's underflow problem, rounding error in something like Adam's second-moment estimate can drift over tens of thousands of steps and combine with a particular gradient pattern to produce a bad update — a slower, subtler failure than a single bad batch. And I wouldn't rule out hardware — a straggler GPU, a degraded NIC, or a silent Xid fault on one of 512 GPUs can corrupt a value that then propagates through an all-reduce and hits every rank at once, which would explain a sudden cluster-wide divergence with zero warning beforehand. Either way, my first practical move is resuming from the last good checkpoint with finer-grained gradient-norm logging turned on, and if I suspect a specific bad batch, replaying it in isolation on a small job rather than burning the whole 512-GPU cluster chasing a hypothesis.
commonMistakes: Assumes the divergence must be a misconfiguration despite 40,000 steps of prior stability
Only checks the loss curve and misses the gradient-norm history's earlier warning signal
Doesn't attempt to isolate and replay the specific data batch processed at the divergence point
Assumes BF16 is immune to any numerical accumulation issue simply because it avoids FP16's underflow problem
Ignores hardware-level causes (Xid errors, a straggler, a degraded NIC) as a possible explanation for a sudden cluster-wide spike
Restarts the full 512-GPU run from scratch instead of resuming from the last good checkpoint with better instrumentation
keyPoints: Recognizes the late-stage timing points away from a static misconfiguration toward an accumulating or data-triggered cause
Checks gradient-norm history, not just loss, for an early-warning signature before the spike
Proposes isolating and replaying the specific batch at the divergence point to test a bad-data hypothesis
Considers BF16 optimizer-state accumulation drift as a slower, subtler possible cause
Considers hardware-level causes (Xid faults, straggler, degraded NIC) as a plausible explanation
Proposes resuming from checkpoint with better instrumentation rather than restarting from scratch

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly uses gradient-norm history, not just loss, as the primary diagnostic signal
Proposes isolating the specific triggering data batch as a concrete hypothesis test
Considers numerical-accumulation and hardware-level causes appropriately

questions.title: Inference Fleet Latency Creeps Up Over Three Weeks With No Single Deploy to Blame
questions.prompt: Your LLM-serving fleet's p99 TTFT has crept up by roughly 40% over three weeks with no single deployment, config change, or traffic spike that obviously correlates with it. Walk through how you'd actually find the cause of a slow, creeping degradation like this.
questions.modelAnswer: A slow creep with no single correlated event rules out the easy explanations (a bad deploy, an obvious config regression) and points toward something that accumulates continuously — either a gradual shift in traffic characteristics, a resource leak or fragmentation issue that worsens the longer a server process runs, or a gradual capacity mismatch as organic traffic growth outpaces a fixed fleet size. I'd start by overlaying the p99 TTFT trend against raw request volume and against average prompt length over the same three weeks, since both are plausible, boring explanations that are easy to check first: if request volume grew 40% over the same window with no corresponding fleet scale-up, this might simply be a capacity problem that's been masquerading as a mystery, and if average prompt length grew (longer context windows being used more, a product change encouraging longer inputs), TTFT naturally rises because prefill cost scales with prompt length — either of these would be the answer and wouldn't need anything more exotic. If both of those are flat, I'd look at per-replica uptime: specifically, whether the replicas serving the slowest requests are disproportionately long-running ones versus recently restarted ones, because a GPU memory allocator fragmentation issue (where the KV cache pool's effective usable memory degrades over very long uptimes due to repeated allocation/deallocation of varying-sized blocks) is exactly the kind of thing that creeps rather than spikes, and a server that's been running continuously for three weeks without a restart is a textbook candidate for this. I'd test this directly by comparing TTFT distributions between replicas grouped by uptime, and if long-uptime replicas are measurably worse, that's strong evidence, with the practical (if temporary) fix being a rolling restart cadence while the actual fragmentation behavior gets investigated and potentially mitigated via an allocator configuration change. If uptime doesn't correlate either, I'd check whether the model or request mix shifted — a growing share of requests using a particular feature (a longer system prompt, a specific tool-use pattern generating longer context) could gradually shift the aggregate workload toward a heavier profile without any single day showing an obvious change, which is the kind of thing that only becomes visible in a three-week rolling comparison, not a day-over-day diff.
questions.professionalAnswer: No single correlated event over three weeks tells me to stop looking for an event and start looking for something continuous — either traffic itself growing, something resource-related getting worse the longer a process runs, or a slow shift in what kind of requests are actually coming in. My first check is the boring stuff, because it's usually right: I'd overlay the p99 TTFT trend against raw request volume and against average prompt length over the same window, since if either of those grew by something close to 40% with no corresponding capacity increase, that alone explains the whole thing — more load without more capacity, or longer prompts costing more prefill time, and I don't need to look any further. If both are flat, my next suspect is GPU memory allocator fragmentation, because that's a classic creeping problem rather than a spike — a server that's been running continuously for three weeks without a restart is exactly the kind of candidate where the allocator's usable KV cache memory degrades gradually from repeated allocation and deallocation of varying-sized blocks. I'd test that directly by comparing TTFT distributions between replicas grouped by how long they've been running, and if the long-uptime ones are measurably worse, that's a strong signal, with a rolling restart cadence as the immediate mitigation while the underlying allocator behavior gets a real fix. If even that doesn't correlate, I'd look at whether the request mix itself has quietly shifted — more traffic using a feature with a longer system prompt, or a tool-use pattern that generates more context than it used to — because that's exactly the kind of change that's invisible day-to-day but shows up clearly once you compare the start and end of a three-week window.
commonMistakes: Searches only for a single correlated deploy/config event instead of considering continuous, accumulating causes
Skips checking the boring explanations (request volume growth, prompt-length growth) before reaching for an exotic cause
Doesn't consider GPU memory allocator fragmentation as a creeping, uptime-correlated failure mode
Doesn't compare TTFT distributions grouped by replica uptime to test the fragmentation hypothesis
Misses a gradual shift in request/feature mix as a plausible explanation for a slow capacity-profile change
Jumps to an expensive fix (full fleet resize or re-architecture) without first testing cheaper, more specific hypotheses
keyPoints: Correctly reasons that a slow creep with no correlated event points to a continuous, not event-driven, cause
Checks request-volume and prompt-length growth as the first, most likely explanations
Proposes GPU memory allocator fragmentation as a plausible creeping cause tied to replica uptime
Proposes a concrete test (TTFT by replica uptime) to validate or rule out fragmentation
Considers a gradual shift in request/feature mix as an additional plausible explanation

questions.title: An OOM Pattern That Only Appears Once You Scale Past 256 GPUs
questions.prompt: A training job runs fine on 64 and 128 GPUs with the same per-GPU batch size and model configuration, but reliably OOMs partway through step 1 once scaled to 256 GPUs or more, with no code change between runs. Walk through why this specific pattern — fine at smaller scale, broken only past a scale threshold — happens and how you'd diagnose it.
questions.modelAnswer: Per-GPU batch size and model configuration being identical across all three runs is the key clue that rules out the most common OOM causes (the model itself is too big, or the batch size is too aggressive), and points specifically at something that scales with GPU *count* rather than with per-GPU workload — which, for a sharded-parallelism setup like FSDP, is a short list of real candidates. The first thing I'd check is whether this job uses FSDP's hybrid sharding or a sharding strategy where the sharding group size is tied to a fixed value (like sharding only within a node of 8 GPUs) while the number of nodes themselves increases — if that's the case, going from 64 to 256 GPUs with a fixed intra-node sharding group doesn't change each GPU's share of sharded state at all, but it does increase the number of concurrent all-gather operations the data-parallel dimension has to coordinate, and if there's a known or custom communication-buffering behavior that allocates temporary buffers proportional to the number of participating ranks rather than per-GPU workload, that buffer allocation alone can grow large enough to tip a GPU over its memory ceiling specifically past some rank-count threshold, independent of the actual model or batch size staying fixed. Second, I'd check the data loader's sharding behavior specifically at step 1 — if every rank's dataloader, on the very first step, needs to agree on something globally (a vocabulary size check, a dataset-length computation, a dynamic batching decision) via an all-gather or broadcast whose buffer size scales with world size, a bug in that one-time startup logic could manifest exactly as 'OOMs partway through step 1' and exactly at a larger GPU count, since it would never have been exercised at a small enough scale to show the problem, and would never recur at step 2 onward since it's a one-time startup computation. Third, I'd check activation-checkpointing and pipeline-parallelism-adjacent memory behavior if either is in play — certain configurations of pipeline parallelism have memory requirements (especially for the first and last pipeline stages, which hold extra activation buffers) that don't scale per-GPU the way people assume, and adding more pipeline stages as part of scaling to 256+ GPUs, even unintentionally through an autoscaling config, could change which GPUs are actually most memory-pressured in a way that wasn't visible at 64 or 128 GPUs if those runs happened to use fewer pipeline stages. The practical first diagnostic step is checking exactly which part of the memory allocator's history (via `torch.cuda.memory_summary()` or a memory snapshot right before the OOM) shows growth that correlates with GPU count rather than with the unchanged model/batch configuration, since that narrows the investigation to a specific allocation category rather than guessing at the mechanism blind.
questions.professionalAnswer: The fact that per-GPU batch size and model config are identical across 64, 128, and 256 GPUs is the whole clue here — it rules out 'the model's too big' or 'the batch is too aggressive' immediately, and points at something that scales with GPU count itself, not per-GPU workload, which for a sharded setup narrows this down fast. My first suspect is the sharding configuration: if this job uses a fixed intra-node sharding group (say, sharding only within each 8-GPU node) while the number of nodes keeps growing, each GPU's actual sharded-state size doesn't change at all going from 64 to 256 GPUs, but the number of concurrent communication operations the data-parallel dimension has to coordinate does grow, and if there's any communication-buffer allocation that scales with the number of participating ranks rather than with actual per-GPU data, that alone can be enough to tip memory over the edge only past some rank-count threshold. Second, I'd look hard at the data loader's step-1-only startup logic — a one-time all-gather or broadcast where every rank needs to agree on something globally, with a buffer size that scales with world size, is exactly the kind of bug that would never show up at 64 or 128 GPUs, would reliably OOM right at step 1 and nowhere else, and would only appear past whatever rank count makes that buffer big enough to matter. Third, if pipeline parallelism is involved at all, I'd check whether scaling to 256+ GPUs quietly changed the pipeline configuration, because the first and last pipeline stages often carry extra activation-buffer memory that doesn't scale the way people assume, and a stage-count change that happened as a side effect of scaling up, rather than a deliberate decision, could explain memory pressure landing somewhere different than it did at smaller scale. Regardless of which of these it is, my first concrete move is pulling a CUDA memory snapshot right before the OOM and checking which allocation category actually grew with GPU count rather than guessing at the mechanism without that evidence in hand.
commonMistakes: Assumes the model or batch size itself must be too large, despite both being unchanged across all three scales
Doesn't consider that a fixed intra-node sharding group size means per-GPU sharded state doesn't change with node count
Misses that a one-time step-1 startup computation (not steady-state training) can be the actual OOM trigger
Doesn't consider that pipeline-parallelism stage count or configuration might have quietly changed when scaling up
Guesses at a mechanism without pulling an actual memory snapshot/allocator history to confirm which allocation grew
Assumes the issue must recur every step rather than recognizing a step-1-only pattern as evidence of a startup-specific bug
keyPoints: Correctly reasons that identical per-GPU config across scales points to something scaling with GPU count, not workload
Considers fixed intra-node sharding group size with growing node count as a plausible communication-buffer cause
Considers a one-time step-1 startup/all-gather bug as a plausible, scale-threshold-specific cause
Considers pipeline-parallelism configuration changes as a plausible contributing cause
Proposes pulling a concrete memory snapshot/allocator history to confirm the actual allocation category responsible

questions.title: A Straggler GPU Silently Cuts Throughput in Half With No Error Anywhere
questions.prompt: Throughput on a 64-GPU training job has dropped to roughly half of its expected value. No error appears in any log, no job crashed, and nvidia-smi on every node shows GPUs at high utilization. Walk through how a straggler GPU can cause exactly this symptom and how you'd actually find which one it is.
questions.modelAnswer: Collective operations like all-reduce are synchronous by design — every rank has to arrive at the collective before any of them can proceed past it — which means a single straggler GPU running meaningfully slower than the other 63 doesn't cause an error at all, it just means every other GPU spends part of every step waiting at the collective barrier for the slow one to catch up, and from a per-node nvidia-smi glance, the straggler itself can look busy (high utilization, just taking longer per unit of actual work) while the other 63 GPUs look busy too, because 'waiting at a barrier inside an NCCL call' and 'actively computing' both show up as GPU utilization to a tool that only measures whether a kernel is running, not whether it's useful work or a wait. This is exactly why 'no error, no crash, uniformly high utilization everywhere' is consistent with a straggler rather than ruling one out — the aggregate symptom (halved throughput) is real and the individual-node symptom (looks fine) is also real, because nvidia-smi simply isn't the right tool to distinguish 'computing' from 'blocked waiting on a slower peer' at this level of granularity. To find which GPU is the straggler, I'd instrument per-rank step timing directly in the training loop — logging the wall-clock time each rank spends in its forward/backward compute versus the time it spends inside the collective call itself, which most distributed frameworks expose or can be instrumented around — and look for the one rank whose compute-only time is meaningfully longer than the other 63's, rather than looking at aggregate cluster-wide metrics that average the problem away. If per-rank compute timing doesn't immediately reveal an outlier, I'd check DCGM-level health metrics per GPU specifically for thermal throttling (a GPU running hotter due to a cooling issue in one specific chassis position would compute correctly but more slowly) or for ECC error counts, since a GPU accumulating correctable ECC errors can silently run slower without crashing or producing any wrong output, which exactly matches 'no error in any log.' Once the specific straggler rank is identified, the fix is usually operational rather than algorithmic: cordon and drain that specific node for hardware inspection while the job continues on remaining capacity (if using elastic training) or restart the job excluding that node's rank range, rather than spending more time trying to tune away a hardware-level problem in software.
questions.professionalAnswer: Collectives are synchronous, and that's the whole reason this symptom makes sense even with zero errors anywhere — every rank has to hit the all-reduce barrier together, so one genuinely slower GPU doesn't crash anything, it just makes the other 63 sit and wait for it at every single step, and nvidia-smi can't tell the difference between 'computing' and 'blocked inside an NCCL call waiting on a peer,' so every node including the slow one can show high utilization while the actual useful work rate has been cut in half. That's exactly why 'no error, high utilization everywhere' doesn't rule out a straggler — it's consistent with one, because the tool people reach for first here just isn't measuring the right thing. To actually find the straggler, I'd instrument per-rank timing directly — not aggregate cluster metrics, which average the problem away — logging how long each rank spends in actual forward/backward compute versus how long it spends waiting inside the collective call, and looking for the one rank whose compute-only time stands out from the other 63. If that doesn't immediately surface an outlier, I'd pull DCGM-level health data per GPU, specifically checking for thermal throttling — a cooling issue in one chassis position can leave a GPU computing correctly but slower — or climbing ECC error counts, since a GPU quietly accumulating correctable ECC errors can run slower with zero crash and zero log entry, which matches this symptom exactly. Once I've got the specific rank, the fix isn't really a software tuning problem — it's cordoning that node for hardware inspection and either continuing on the remaining capacity if the job's elastic, or restarting without that node, rather than trying to tune the training job around a hardware fault.

Looks only at aggregate cluster-wide metrics instead of per-rank step timing to find the specific slow GPU
Assumes a straggler would necessarily produce a visible error or crash somewhere in the logs
Doesn't consider thermal throttling or climbing ECC error counts as silent, non-crashing causes of a slow GPU
Attempts to fix a hardware-level straggler issue purely through software/training-configuration tuning
Doesn't propose instrumenting compute-time-versus-wait-time per rank as the actual diagnostic method

Correctly explains why nvidia-smi utilization can't distinguish real compute from barrier-wait time

questions.title: An NCCL Collective Hangs Indefinitely With No Timeout Error
questions.prompt: A multi-node training job stops making progress — no crash, no error, no log output — and sits indefinitely with GPUs at or near idle. The NCCL watchdog timeout, which should turn a hang into an explicit error, never fires. Walk through what could cause a genuine deadlock to hang past the point where the watchdog should have caught it, and how you'd actually debug a stuck job with almost no log signal.
questions.modelAnswer: If the watchdog timeout never fires despite the job genuinely being stuck, the most likely explanation is that the watchdog itself is configured with a timeout longer than how long the team has actually been waiting, or the hang is happening somewhere the watchdog doesn't monitor at all — NCCL's watchdog specifically covers NCCL collective operations, and a hang that's actually stuck in Python-level code before ever reaching a collective call (a deadlock in a data loader with multiple worker processes, a lock contention issue in application code, or a rank stuck waiting on a non-NCCL resource like a distributed filesystem read) would never trigger an NCCL-specific timeout at all, because NCCL's watchdog has no visibility into code that never calls into it. I'd check this first and cheaply: attach to one of the stuck processes (via `py-spy dump` on the process ID, which doesn't require the process to cooperate or be instrumented in advance) and get an actual Python-level stack trace for every thread, which immediately tells you whether the process is sitting inside a `torch.distributed` collective call (genuinely an NCCL-level hang) or stuck somewhere else entirely (a different kind of bug masquerading as a distributed-training hang). If it is genuinely stuck inside a collective, the classic cause is a rank mismatch in the number or order of collective calls across ranks — one rank, due to a conditional branch in the code that doesn't execute identically on every rank (a rank-0-only logging block that includes a collective call other ranks don't make, or a conditional checkpoint-save path with slightly different logic per rank), ends up calling a different sequence of collectives than its peers, and when ranks disagree about which collective they're participating in, the result isn't an error, it's every rank waiting forever for a peer that's never going to show up to that specific call — this is a genuine application-level deadlock, not a network issue, and NCCL's watchdog not firing on it specifically happens when the watchdog's own timeout was set generously (sometimes deliberately, to tolerate legitimately slow but not stuck collectives like a large checkpoint save) longer than anyone's actually been willing to wait before investigating. The fix for a rank-mismatch deadlock is finding and removing the rank-conditional collective call via careful code review guided by the `py-spy` stack traces across multiple ranks (comparing which collective, if any, each rank is stuck on), and the preventive fix is a stricter, shorter watchdog timeout in non-production/validation runs specifically so this class of bug surfaces fast during development rather than silently hanging for however long it takes someone to notice in a real multi-day run.
questions.professionalAnswer: If the watchdog genuinely should have fired and didn't, my first question isn't 'why didn't NCCL catch this,' it's 'is this actually an NCCL-level hang at all' — because NCCL's watchdog only has visibility into NCCL collective calls, and a hang stuck somewhere earlier, in a data loader deadlock across worker processes, a lock in application code, or a rank blocked on a slow filesystem read, would never trigger it, since the code never got far enough to call into NCCL in the first place. That's cheap to check first: `py-spy dump` against one of the stuck process IDs gives you an actual Python-level stack trace without needing the process to cooperate, and it immediately tells you whether you're really inside a `torch.distributed` collective call or stuck somewhere else entirely pretending to be a distributed-training problem. If it is genuinely stuck inside a collective, the classic cause I've seen is a rank-conditional code path — something like a rank-0-only logging block that happens to include a collective call the other ranks never make, or slightly different conditional logic per rank around a checkpoint save — which means the ranks disagree about which collective they're even participating in, and when that happens nobody errors out, every rank just waits forever for a peer that's never coming to that specific call. That's a genuine application-level deadlock, not a network problem, and the reason the watchdog didn't catch it is usually that its timeout was deliberately set generous enough to tolerate a legitimately slow collective, like a big checkpoint save, which ends up being longer than anyone actually waited before investigating. My fix is comparing py-spy stack traces across multiple ranks to see exactly which collective each one thinks it's stuck on, finding the rank-conditional call causing the mismatch, and removing it — and for prevention, I'd run a much stricter, shorter watchdog timeout specifically in validation/dev runs so this exact bug class surfaces fast during development instead of silently hanging in a real multi-day production run.

Doesn't use a non-invasive stack-trace tool (py-spy or equivalent) to check where the process is actually stuck
Assumes the watchdog not firing proves the hang isn't real, rather than considering a too-generous timeout
Misses rank-conditional collective calls (a branch that only some ranks execute) as a classic deadlock cause
Treats this purely as a network/infrastructure issue when it's actually an application-level logic bug
Doesn't propose comparing stack traces across multiple ranks to diagnose a rank-mismatch collective deadlock

Proposes a non-invasive stack-trace tool to inspect the stuck process without prior instrumentation
Identifies rank-conditional collective calls as a classic application-level deadlock cause
Explains why a generous watchdog timeout can let this hang persist well past when anyone expects it
Proposes comparing traces across multiple ranks to pinpoint the specific mismatched collective

questions.title: Training Throughput Is Fine on nvidia-smi But the Job Is Still Twice as Slow as Expected
questions.prompt: A training job's nvidia-smi shows sustained ~95% GPU utilization across all nodes, yet wall-clock throughput is roughly half of what the team's capacity-planning math predicted for this model and cluster size. Walk through how you'd reconcile 'the GPU looks busy' with 'the job is still too slow,' and what you'd actually check.
questions.modelAnswer: High nvidia-smi utilization answering 'is a kernel running' and capacity-planning math answering 'how much useful FLOPs/s is actually happening' are two different questions, and this exact gap — looks busy, isn't fast — is precisely why model FLOPs utilization (MFU) exists as a separate metric from raw GPU utilization. I'd start by computing the actual achieved MFU for this run (measured tokens/sec, converted to achieved FLOPs/s via the model's known parameter count, divided by the GPU's theoretical peak FLOPs/s) and compare it against the MFU the original capacity-planning estimate assumed — if the capacity plan assumed, say, 40% MFU and the job is actually running at 20%, that gap directly accounts for roughly the 2x slowdown being observed, and now the question becomes why achieved MFU is half of what was assumed, which is a much more specific, answerable question than 'why is nvidia-smi lying to me' (it isn't lying, it's just answering a different question than the one that matters here). With that reframing, I'd check the usual MFU-killers in order of how cheap they are to rule out: first, whether the GPU is spending its 'busy' time on memory-bound operations (attention, elementwise ops, normalization) rather than the large matrix multiplies that actually drive FLOPs, which would show up as high GPU_UTIL but low PIPE_TENSOR_ACTIVE in DCGM metrics specifically, a different and more precise signal than nvidia-smi's utilization number; second, whether activation checkpointing is enabled and recomputing more than strictly necessary, since checkpointing deliberately trades extra compute for memory savings, and a checkpointing granularity that's more aggressive than the memory budget actually requires directly lowers achieved MFU in exchange for memory headroom nobody's using; third, whether the actual sequence lengths or batch composition in production training data differ from what the capacity-planning estimate assumed, since a capacity estimate built on an average sequence length that turns out to be shorter than the real data's average length would predict a higher MFU than what padding or variable-length overhead actually delivers. The key reframing I'd push the team toward is that 'the GPU looks busy' was never actually in tension with 'the job is slow' — nvidia-smi utilization measures occupancy, not efficiency, and the real diagnostic work starts once you compute and compare achieved MFU against the assumed MFU, not when you stare harder at a dashboard that was never designed to answer this question.
questions.professionalAnswer: The thing I'd clear up first is that nvidia-smi utilization and the capacity-planning math are answering two completely different questions, so there isn't actually a contradiction here that needs reconciling — there's a gap between 'is the GPU doing something' and 'is the GPU doing useful FLOPs at the rate we assumed,' and that second question is what model FLOPs utilization (MFU) is for. I'd compute the actual achieved MFU for this run directly from measured throughput and the model's known parameter count, and compare it against whatever MFU the original capacity estimate assumed — if the plan assumed 40% and reality is 20%, that gap alone explains roughly the 2x slowdown, and now I've got a specific, answerable question instead of a vague one. From there I'd check the usual suspects in order of cheapest first: whether DCGM's PIPE_TENSOR_ACTIVE metric is actually low despite high GPU_UTIL, meaning the GPU is busy on memory-bound work like attention or normalization rather than the big matmuls that drive real FLOPs; whether activation checkpointing is set more aggressively than the actual memory budget requires, since checkpointing is a deliberate compute-for-memory trade that directly costs MFU; and whether the real training data's sequence-length distribution differs from whatever average the original capacity estimate assumed, since padding or variable-length overhead on shorter-than-assumed sequences eats into achieved throughput in a way a simple average-case estimate wouldn't have predicted. The actual fix for the team's confusion here is mostly reframing the question — nvidia-smi was never built to answer 'is this efficient,' only 'is this occupied,' and the real diagnostic work starts the moment you put a number on achieved MFU and compare it to the assumed one, not from staring at a utilization graph that looks fine.
commonMistakes: Treats nvidia-smi's high utilization number as proof the GPU is being used efficiently
Doesn't compute or compare achieved MFU against the capacity plan's assumed MFU
Misses DCGM's PIPE_TENSOR_ACTIVE as the more precise signal for distinguishing compute-bound from memory-bound busy time
Doesn't consider activation checkpointing granularity as a deliberate, quantifiable MFU cost
Doesn't check whether real training data's sequence-length distribution matches the capacity plan's assumption
Concludes there's a contradiction between the dashboards instead of recognizing they measure different things
keyPoints: Correctly distinguishes GPU occupancy (nvidia-smi) from compute efficiency (MFU)
Computes and compares achieved MFU against the capacity plan's assumed MFU to reframe the problem
Uses DCGM PIPE_TENSOR_ACTIVE to distinguish compute-bound from memory-bound GPU busy time
Considers activation-checkpointing granularity as a real, quantifiable MFU cost
Considers a mismatch between assumed and real sequence-length distribution as a plausible cause

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes GPU occupancy from compute efficiency (MFU)
Proposes computing and comparing achieved vs. assumed MFU
Identifies concrete, checkable causes of low MFU (tensor activity, checkpointing, sequence length)
Correctly reframes rather than treating this as a dashboard contradiction

questions.title: A Feature-Store Skew Bug Causes a Production Fraud Model to Quietly Underperform
questions.prompt: Three months after deployment, a fraud model's production precision has drifted down by several points from its launch-week numbers, with no retraining, no code deploy, and no infrastructure change in that window. Walk through how you'd investigate a regression with literally nothing that changed, and what class of bug this pattern usually points to.
questions.modelAnswer: 'Nothing changed in our code or infrastructure' is a claim about our systems, not about the world the model is scoring, and a three-month gradual drift with a static model and static code almost always means something about the input distribution or an upstream data source changed instead — the model and the pipeline code are a fixed function, but the data flowing through that function evolved. I'd start by checking for data drift directly: comparing the distribution of each input feature between launch week and now using a concrete statistical test (population stability index or a similar divergence measure) rather than eyeballing summary statistics, since a meaningful shift in even one or two heavily-weighted features (a change in the mix of transaction types, a new payment method becoming more common, a shift in customer demographics using the product) can degrade a model trained on the old distribution without anything in the ML pipeline itself being 'broken.' If feature distributions look stable, I'd check for a slower-burning version of training/serving skew: an upstream data source that feeds a feature's definition changing its own behavior silently — a third-party data provider changing how it codes a field, a database column's semantics quietly shifting due to an upstream team's unrelated change, or a feature that depends on a join against a reference table that's gone stale (a merchant category table that hasn't been refreshed, so a growing share of merchants fall into a fallback 'unknown' bucket that didn't exist at this scale during launch week) — none of which show up as a deploy or a code change on our side because the drift originates upstream of our own pipeline, which is exactly why 'nothing changed' can be true from our perspective and still be the wrong frame for diagnosing this. I'd also check the label side, not just the features: for fraud specifically, if the ground-truth labeling process itself changed (a different chargeback window, a policy change in which disputes count as confirmed fraud), a model's measured precision against today's labels can degrade even if the model's actual scoring behavior hasn't changed at all, because what's being measured as 'correct' shifted under it. Given the three-month timeline, I'd specifically check whether this coincides with any known seasonal or business-cycle pattern (a fraud model's input distribution often does shift with seasonal purchasing behavior) that a model trained on a different season's data would be expected to handle somewhat worse, which would point toward a retraining cadence problem rather than a one-off bug.
questions.professionalAnswer: The claim 'nothing changed' is true about our code and infrastructure, but it's not actually a claim about the thing that matters, which is the data the model is scoring — a static model plus a static pipeline plus a gradual regression almost always means the input distribution moved under a fixed function, not that the function broke. My first move is a real statistical drift check, PSI or something similar, comparing each input feature's distribution between launch week and now, rather than eyeballing summary stats, because a meaningful shift in even one or two heavily-weighted features is enough to degrade a model that was trained on the old distribution, with nothing in our own pipeline needing to be broken at all. If features look stable, I'd look for a slower, upstream version of training/serving skew — a third-party data provider quietly changing how it codes a field, a reference table a feature joins against going stale so a growing share of records fall into a fallback bucket that barely existed at launch — because none of that shows up as a deploy on our side, it originates upstream of anything we'd call a 'change,' which is exactly why the premise of 'nothing changed' needs to be challenged rather than accepted. I'd also check the label side specifically for fraud, because if the ground-truth labeling process itself shifted — a different chargeback window, a policy change in what counts as confirmed fraud — precision against today's labels can drop even if the model's actual behavior is completely unchanged, since what's being measured as 'correct' moved, not the model. And given it's been three months, I'd specifically check whether this lines up with a seasonal pattern, because a fraud model trained on one season's purchasing behavior is a very plausible and very boring explanation for a gradual precision drop, and it would point toward a retraining-cadence fix rather than treating this as a one-off bug to hunt down.
commonMistakes: Accepts 'nothing changed' at face value and searches only for a code/infrastructure cause
Doesn't run a concrete statistical drift test on input feature distributions over the relevant window
Misses upstream data-source changes (third-party provider, stale reference table) as a source of skew our own deploys wouldn't show
Doesn't consider that the ground-truth labeling process itself might have changed, confounding the precision measurement
Overlooks seasonal/business-cycle shifts as a plausible, boring explanation for a gradual regression
Treats this as a one-off bug to patch rather than considering it might point to a missing retraining cadence
keyPoints: Correctly reframes 'nothing changed' as a claim about our systems, not about the data distribution
Proposes a concrete statistical drift test (PSI or similar) on input features over the relevant time window
Considers upstream/third-party data-source drift as a skew source invisible to our own deploy history
Considers a shift in the ground-truth labeling process as a possible confound on the precision metric
Considers seasonality as a plausible explanation pointing toward a retraining-cadence fix

Proposes a concrete statistical drift test rather than eyeballing summary stats

questions.title: A Resharded Checkpoint Loads Successfully but Training Resumes With Visibly Worse Behavior
questions.prompt: After a node failure, a 128-GPU job's checkpoint was successfully loaded and resharded onto 96 GPUs via torch.distributed.checkpoint, with no errors during the load. Training resumes, but the loss is visibly higher than it was right before the checkpoint was taken, and gradually recovers over the next several hundred steps rather than continuing smoothly. Walk through what's actually going on and whether this is a bug or expected behavior.
questions.modelAnswer: The first thing I'd establish is whether this is actually a bug at all, because a visible loss bump immediately after a resume, followed by gradual recovery, is a known and often expected consequence of a few legitimate mechanisms, not automatically evidence of data loss or corruption — successfully loading with no errors only confirms the checkpoint's tensors deserialized and resharded correctly, it says nothing about whether every piece of optimizer state that affects training dynamics was captured and restored. The most common legitimate cause is optimizer state that's sensitive to the exact world size: if the training setup uses any form of learning-rate or batch-size scaling tied to world size (even something as simple as a global batch size computed from per-GPU batch size times world size), going from 128 to 96 GPUs changes the effective global batch size unless per-GPU batch size was deliberately adjusted to compensate, and a smaller or larger effective batch than what the optimizer's momentum and learning-rate schedule were tuned for produces exactly this kind of transient instability — not a bug in the checkpoint mechanism, but an expected consequence of resuming at a different scale without re-tuning for it. A second legitimate cause is data loader state: if the data loader's own shuffling/sharding state isn't part of what's checkpointed and resharded (many setups checkpoint model and optimizer state but treat the data loader as resumable only approximately, restarting from roughly the same epoch position rather than the exact sample), resuming on a different GPU count necessarily reshards the data differently across the new rank count, and a few hundred steps of mild instability while the model readjusts to a genuinely different data traversal order is a real, if mild, cost of this kind of recovery, not corruption. To distinguish 'expected transient from scale change' from 'an actual bug in the resharding,' I'd check two things concretely: whether the effective global batch size before and after the resume actually matches (if per-GPU batch size wasn't adjusted when going from 128 to 96 GPUs, that's your answer, and the fix is adjusting per-GPU batch size or the learning rate to compensate for the real change in effective batch size); and whether the optimizer state's key statistics (a spot-check of a few parameters' momentum values immediately after load, compared against what they were right before the checkpoint was taken on the original 128-GPU job) actually match what's expected, which would rule out a genuine DCP resharding bug versus a real, expected consequence of resuming at a different scale. If the global batch size matches and optimizer state checks out correctly, but there's still a loss bump, I'd suspect the data loader state is the more precise culprit, and the gradual-recovery-over-hundreds-of-steps pattern, specifically its gradualness rather than an instant return to normal, is consistent with either of these legitimate causes rather than pointing at a data-corruption bug, which would typically look more like a sharp spike or ongoing instability rather than a smooth recovery.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first question isn't 'what's broken,' it's 'is this actually a bug' — because a loss bump right after a resume that gradually recovers over a few hundred steps is a known, often legitimate thing, not automatic proof the checkpoint mechanism did something wrong. Loading with no errors only tells you the tensors deserialized and resharded correctly, it tells you nothing about whether everything that affects training dynamics got restored in a way that matches the new 96-GPU configuration. The most likely legitimate cause is that effective global batch size changed — if this setup computes global batch size from per-GPU batch size times world size, going from 128 to 96 GPUs shrinks the effective batch unless someone deliberately compensated for it, and resuming with a smaller effective batch than what the optimizer's momentum and schedule were actually tuned for produces exactly this kind of transient instability, with no bug involved at all. The other real candidate is data loader state — if the loader's own shuffle/shard position isn't part of what got checkpointed and resharded, resuming on a different GPU count necessarily reshards the remaining data differently, and a brief rough patch while the model adjusts to a genuinely different data traversal order is a real, if minor, cost of that kind of recovery. To actually tell the difference between 'expected consequence of the scale change' and 'a real resharding bug,' I'd check whether the effective global batch size before and after the resume actually matches, and I'd spot-check a few parameters' optimizer momentum values right after load against what they were right before the checkpoint was taken — if both check out, this is very likely the legitimate transient I'd expect from a scale change, not corruption, and the gradual-recovery shape itself is consistent with that rather than with a genuine data-corruption bug, which usually looks more like a sharp spike or sustained instability instead of a smooth, gradual recovery.
commonMistakes: Assumes a successful checkpoint load with no errors rules out any issue with what was restored
Jumps straight to 'this is a bug' without first checking whether effective global batch size changed with GPU count
Doesn't check whether data loader shuffle/shard state was actually part of what got checkpointed and resharded
Doesn't spot-check actual optimizer state values after load against pre-checkpoint values to confirm correctness
Treats the gradual-recovery pattern as equally consistent with corruption as with a legitimate transient, missing the distinguishing shape
Recommends re-architecting the checkpoint system before confirming whether this is even a real bug
keyPoints: Correctly questions whether this is a genuine bug before assuming so
Identifies effective-global-batch-size change with GPU count as the most likely legitimate cause
Considers data loader shard/shuffle state as a second plausible legitimate cause
Proposes concrete checks (batch size match, optimizer value spot-check) to distinguish bug from expected transient
Correctly reads the gradual-recovery shape as more consistent with a legitimate transient than with corruption

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly questions whether this is genuinely a bug before assuming so
Identifies effective-batch-size change as the most likely legitimate cause
Considers data loader state as an additional plausible legitimate cause
Proposes concrete, correct diagnostic checks to distinguish bug from expected behavior

questions.title: An Autoscaler Fails to Scale an Inference Fleet Even Though Requests Are Clearly Queuing
questions.prompt: Your Kubernetes HPA is configured to scale a vLLM deployment on CPU utilization, and under a real traffic spike, requests visibly queue and p99 latency spikes, but the HPA never triggers a scale-out event. Walk through why this specific signal choice fails here and how you'd actually fix the autoscaling configuration, not just restart it.
questions.modelAnswer: This isn't a malfunctioning autoscaler, it's a correctly-functioning autoscaler watching the wrong signal — CPU utilization on a GPU-bound inference pod stays low under heavy load because the CPU's job in this pipeline is mostly tokenization, request handling, and light orchestration, while the actual work (the forward pass) happens entirely on the GPU, so a pod can be fully saturated at the GPU level, visibly queuing requests and blowing its latency SLO, while its CPU utilization barely moves, and the HPA, doing exactly what it's configured to do, correctly observes that CPU usage hasn't crossed its scaling threshold and takes no action. The fix isn't to restart or re-tune the existing CPU-based rule, it's to replace the scaling signal entirely with one that actually tracks inference load: queue depth (the number of requests currently waiting for a free serving slot, which vLLM or the router in front of it can expose as a custom metric) is the most direct signal, since it's measuring the actual symptom users are experiencing, but GPU utilization itself (exposed via DCGM and scraped into Prometheus, then surfaced to the HPA via the Prometheus adapter or a custom metrics API) or in-flight request count are reasonable alternatives if queue depth isn't readily available as a clean metric. Implementing this requires more than flipping a config value: Kubernetes' HPA doesn't natively understand GPU or application-level metrics the way it understands CPU/memory out of the box, so I'd need the Prometheus adapter (or an equivalent custom/external metrics API) wired up to expose the chosen metric to the HPA, a `HorizontalPodAutoscaler` resource rewritten to reference that custom metric instead of CPU, and a target value for that metric chosen based on actual proven per-replica capacity (how much queue depth or GPU utilization one replica can sustain while still meeting the latency SLO, established via load testing, not guessed) — this is also the point where I'd push back on any pressure to just lower the CPU threshold as a quick fix, since CPU utilization has no real relationship to GPU saturation for this workload and tuning that threshold further wouldn't actually fix the underlying signal mismatch, it would just change when the wrong metric happens to coincidentally cross some number.
questions.professionalAnswer: This autoscaler isn't broken, it's just watching a signal that has almost nothing to do with what's actually happening — CPU on a GPU-serving pod mostly handles tokenization and light request orchestration, while the real work is the GPU forward pass, so a pod can be completely saturated at the GPU level, visibly queuing requests and blowing its latency target, while CPU utilization barely twitches, and the HPA is correctly doing nothing because the metric it's told to watch genuinely hasn't crossed its threshold. So my fix isn't to restart the HPA or nudge the CPU threshold down, it's to replace the signal entirely — queue depth is the most direct one, since it's measuring the actual symptom, with GPU utilization via DCGM or in-flight request count as reasonable alternatives if queue depth isn't cleanly exposed yet. The real work here is plumbing, not configuration: Kubernetes' HPA doesn't understand GPU or application-level metrics natively the way it understands CPU out of the box, so I'd need the Prometheus adapter wired up to expose whichever metric I pick as a custom metric, rewrite the HorizontalPodAutoscaler to target that instead of CPU, and set the actual target value from real load-tested per-replica capacity — how much queue depth or GPU utilization one replica can sustain while still hitting the latency SLO — not a guessed number. And I'd specifically push back on just lowering the CPU threshold as a stopgap, because CPU utilization has basically no real relationship to GPU saturation for this workload, so tuning that number further doesn't fix anything, it just changes when an irrelevant metric happens to cross some arbitrary line.

Proposes lowering the CPU utilization threshold as a fix instead of replacing the scaling signal entirely
Doesn't recognize that Kubernetes HPA needs a custom/external metrics pipeline (e.g. Prometheus adapter) for GPU-level signals
Picks a target value for the new metric without basing it on actual load-tested per-replica capacity
Doesn't propose queue depth, GPU utilization, or in-flight request count as concrete alternative signals
Assumes restarting the autoscaler or the deployment alone would resolve the underlying signal mismatch

Proposes a concrete, correct alternative signal (queue depth, GPU utilization, or in-flight requests)

questions.title: A Multi-Tenant GPU Fleet Shows Rising Costs With No Corresponding Growth in Useful Work
questions.prompt: Finance flags that GPU spend across your multi-tenant ML platform grew 35% over a quarter while the number of models in production and total served requests both grew only about 8%. Walk through how you'd actually find where that extra spend is going, rather than assuming it's simply 'more usage.'
questions.modelAnswer: A 35% cost increase against an 8% increase in actual output (models in production, requests served) means the cost-per-unit-of-work went up, not just the volume of work, and that gap is exactly what I'd chase first, because it points at the spend hiding in GPUs that aren't producing proportional output rather than in legitimate growth. I'd start with a per-namespace or per-team breakdown of cost versus utilization, specifically looking for teams whose GPU allocation grew faster than their actual utilization or output did — a common and boring cause is a team that requested more GPU capacity for a legitimate reason (an upcoming launch, a bigger model) and then either delayed that work or it didn't fully materialize, leaving the capacity allocated and billed but running well below the utilization that originally justified it. Second, I'd check whether any team shifted its workload mix toward a more expensive GPU tier (moving from a mid-range GPU to a frontier-class one for marginal quality gains) without a corresponding review of whether that upgrade was actually justified by the output growth it enabled, since a 35%-cost-for-8%-output gap is exactly what you'd see if a chunk of the fleet silently got more expensive per unit without producing more useful output per unit. Third, I'd specifically check for zombie or abandoned capacity — experiments, prototyping sessions, or training jobs left running (intentionally kept 'just in case' or simply forgotten) that consume dedicated or reserved capacity without contributing to either the production model count or the served-request count, since neither of those output metrics would ever surface this kind of waste; this is where I'd pull actual DCGM utilization data per namespace and flag any namespace with sustained low utilization relative to its allocated/billed capacity, converting that gap into a dollar figure so it's immediately actionable rather than just a percentage nobody prioritizes. Fourth, I'd check whether reserved or committed capacity (an annual or multi-year GPU commitment) grew ahead of actual demand as a forecasting decision, which is a legitimate business tradeoff (locking in capacity and pricing ahead of expected growth) but needs to be distinguished clearly from waste in the report to finance, since conflating 'we deliberately over-provisioned for a growth bet' with 'we're wasting money on idle GPUs' would lead to the wrong corrective action being taken for each.
questions.professionalAnswer: The core signal here is that cost-per-unit-of-work went up, not just total cost, since output only grew 8% against a 35% cost increase — so I'm not looking for 'more usage,' I'm looking for spend that isn't producing proportional output, and that's a fundamentally different investigation. My first cut is a per-team cost-versus-utilization breakdown, specifically hunting for teams whose allocated GPU capacity grew faster than their actual utilization or output did — the boring, common version of this is a team that requested capacity for something that got delayed or didn't fully materialize, and the capacity just kept running and billing anyway. Second, I'd check for a quiet shift toward a more expensive GPU tier somewhere in the fleet — moving to a frontier-class GPU for a marginal quality gain, without the output growth to justify the cost delta, is exactly the kind of thing that produces this specific gap between spend growth and output growth. Third, and this is usually where the real money is, I'd hunt for zombie capacity — experiments or training jobs left running, intentionally or just forgotten, that never show up in either the production-model count or the served-request count because they're not actually serving anything, which is exactly why those two output metrics on their own would never catch this. I'd pull DCGM utilization per namespace and convert any sustained gap between allocated capacity and actual utilization into a dollar number, because a percentage doesn't get prioritized the way a dollar figure does. And finally, I'd check whether some of this is actually a deliberate forecasting decision — reserved capacity locked in ahead of an expected growth curve — because that's a legitimate business tradeoff, not waste, and I'd be careful to separate that out clearly in the report to finance so the corrective action for 'we bet on growth that hasn't landed yet' doesn't get confused with the corrective action for 'we have idle GPUs nobody's using.'

Looks only at aggregate fleet cost instead of a per-team/per-namespace breakdown against utilization
Doesn't consider a shift toward a more expensive GPU tier as a source of rising cost-per-unit-of-work
Misses zombie/abandoned capacity as a cause invisible to production-model-count and request-count metrics
Reports utilization gaps as raw percentages rather than converting them into actionable dollar figures
Conflates legitimate deliberate over-provisioning (reserved capacity for forecasted growth) with actual waste
keyPoints: Correctly reframes the problem around cost-per-unit-of-work rather than total cost alone
Proposes a per-team/per-namespace cost-versus-utilization breakdown as the core investigative method
Considers a shift toward more expensive GPU tiers as a plausible contributing cause
Identifies zombie/abandoned capacity as a likely, metric-invisible cause
Distinguishes deliberate reserved-capacity forecasting decisions from genuine waste in the final reporting

questions.title: A Real Incident Was Missed Because the On-Call Engineer Had Muted a 'Noisy' Alert Channel
questions.prompt: A genuine multi-hour accuracy degradation in a production model went unnoticed for most of a day because the on-call engineer had muted the alert channel it fired into, citing weeks of false-positive noise from that same channel. Walk through how you'd handle the immediate incident, the postmortem, and the structural fix, without treating this as simply 'the on-call engineer made a mistake.'
questions.modelAnswer: The immediate incident response is the easy, mechanical part — confirm the degradation's scope and duration, roll back or mitigate via whatever fast path exists (a model rollback via registry alias, a feature killswitch, whatever's appropriate to this specific degradation), and communicate impact to stakeholders — but the harder and more important part of this is resisting the instinct to close this out as 'an engineer made a mistake by muting a channel,' because that framing stops the investigation exactly one step too early and sets up the same failure to recur with a different engineer next time. The postmortem needs to establish why muting that channel was a locally reasonable decision given the information the engineer actually had: if the channel had genuinely been producing weeks of false positives with no action taken on any of them, muting it wasn't negligence, it was a rational response to an alert that had already, in practice, stopped being a useful signal — the real failure happened earlier, when that channel's false-positive rate crossed the point where it should have been fixed or demoted, and nobody did either, leaving an individual engineer to make an ad hoc, under-informed call about a channel they didn't have the context or authority to actually fix. I'd write the postmortem's timeline to include that earlier failure explicitly — when did this channel's false-positive rate become a known problem, who knew about it, why wasn't it addressed — rather than starting the timeline at 'engineer muted channel,' because a timeline that starts there implicitly blames the symptom instead of the cause. The structural fix has two parts: first, an immediate, concrete decision about this specific alert — either fix its false-positive rate by improving the underlying signal (likely moving from a raw-metric threshold to an SLO-burn-rate-based rule, which is generally far less noisy), or formally demote it to a non-paging channel if it's not actually worth someone's attention at 3am, rather than leaving it in the ambiguous state that led an engineer to mute it unilaterally; second, a standing process change — a periodic audit of every paging alert's actual action rate (what fraction of firings led to a real human action), with a default policy that any alert below some threshold gets automatically flagged for fixing or demotion rather than silently tolerated until an incident forces the conversation. I'd deliver all of this as a blameless postmortem specifically because assigning blame to the individual engineer here would actively make the platform less safe going forward, not more — it would teach every other on-call engineer to keep tolerating noisy channels rather than escalating them, since escalating got a colleague blamed for an outcome that was really a structural failure finally surfacing through them.
questions.professionalAnswer: The mechanical incident response here is the straightforward part — confirm scope and duration, mitigate with whatever rollback or killswitch path fits this specific degradation, communicate impact — the real work is in not letting this get closed out as 'an engineer made a bad call muting a channel,' because that framing is both wrong and actively counterproductive. If that channel had genuinely been producing weeks of false positives with zero real action taken on any of them, muting it was a locally rational response to an alert that had already stopped functioning as a useful signal in practice — the actual failure happened earlier, when the false-positive rate crossed the point where someone should have fixed or demoted that alert, and nobody did, which left an individual engineer holding an under-informed, ad hoc decision they didn't have the context or standing to actually resolve properly. I'd make sure the postmortem's timeline starts there, not at 'engineer muted channel,' because starting the timeline at the mute implicitly blames the symptom instead of the real cause, and a blameless postmortem that still manages to anchor on the individual's action hasn't actually done its job. The structural fix is two things: fix or formally demote this specific alert now — usually by moving it from a raw-threshold rule to an SLO-burn-rate-based one, which tends to be far less noisy by design — and put in place a standing audit of every paging alert's actual action rate, so an alert that's crossed the 'nobody ever acts on this' line gets automatically flagged for a fix or a demotion instead of being silently tolerated until it causes exactly this kind of incident. And I'd keep this explicitly blameless, not as a nicety, but because blaming the individual here would teach every other on-call engineer the wrong lesson — that escalating a chronically noisy channel gets you blamed when the structural failure it was hiding finally surfaces, which is exactly the incentive that produces the next version of this same incident.

Fails to investigate why the channel had been producing weeks of false positives in the first place
Starts the incident timeline at the point the channel was muted rather than at the earlier structural failure
Treats this as resolved once the immediate incident is mitigated, without a structural fix to the alert itself
Doesn't propose a standing audit mechanism (alert action-rate review) to catch the next chronically noisy alert
Conducts a blame-oriented rather than blameless postmortem, risking a chilling effect on future escalation

Proposes a concrete fix for this specific alert (burn-rate-based rule or formal demotion)
