questions.title: A Model Rollback via Registry Alias Leaves the Fleet in an Inconsistent State
questions.prompt: After rolling back a bad model by reassigning the 'champion' alias to the previous version, some serving replicas are still returning predictions consistent with the bad version for several minutes, causing confusing, inconsistent behavior for users hitting different replicas. Walk through what's actually happening and how you'd fix both the immediate inconsistency and the underlying design gap.
questions.modelAnswer: An alias reassignment being 'instant' refers to the registry's own metadata update — the pointer itself flips immediately — but that's a completely different thing from every serving replica actually noticing the pointer moved and reloading the model it now points to, and the gap between those two is almost certainly what's causing several minutes of inconsistent behavior across replicas. If replicas resolve the `champion` alias only at startup, or on a polling interval (checking the registry every N minutes rather than being pushed a notification), then any replica that already loaded the bad version before the rollback will keep serving it until its next poll interval happens to land, or until it's restarted — which means the actual rollback timeline isn't 'instant,' it's 'as fast as the slowest replica's next poll,' and if that polling interval is, say, 5 minutes, a user population split across replicas at different points in their poll cycle sees exactly the inconsistent, confusing behavior described. The immediate fix is to force the issue rather than wait for replicas to notice on their own schedule: a rolling restart of every replica serving this model, which forces each one to re-resolve the alias fresh on startup, is the fastest way to guarantee consistency across the fleet right now, and I'd do this immediately rather than waiting for the normal poll cycle to catch up on its own, since the whole point of an emergency rollback is to stop the bad behavior as fast as possible, not within whatever interval the polling happens to be configured for. The underlying design gap is that alias resolution was built around a polling model without anyone deciding what an acceptable propagation-time SLO for a rollback actually is, and I'd fix that properly rather than just living with 'rolling restart whenever this happens': either move to a push-based notification (the registry actively notifies serving infrastructure of an alias change via a webhook or a pub/sub event, triggering an immediate reload rather than waiting for a poll), or at minimum shorten the polling interval specifically for the alias resolution check (which is cheap to check frequently, unlike reloading a whole model) while keeping the actual model reload less frequent, so a rollback's propagation time becomes bounded by a short, deliberate interval instead of accidentally being tied to the much longer interval of a routine health check. I'd also make sure the rollback runbook itself documents the rolling-restart step explicitly as part of 'how to roll back,' rather than assuming alias reassignment alone is sufficient, since the gap between 'the registry says it's rolled back' and 'every replica is actually serving the rolled-back version' is exactly the kind of thing that's invisible until an incident exposes it.
questions.professionalAnswer: The thing to untangle here is that 'alias reassignment is instant' is true only about the registry's own metadata — the pointer itself flips right away — but that's a separate question from whether every serving replica has actually noticed and reloaded, and that gap is almost certainly the whole story. If replicas only check the alias at startup or on a periodic poll rather than getting pushed a notification, any replica that already loaded the bad version keeps serving it until its next poll happens to land or it gets restarted, which means the real rollback timeline isn't instant at all, it's bounded by whatever that polling interval is — and a user population hitting different replicas at different points in that cycle is exactly the inconsistent experience described. My immediate fix is to force it: a rolling restart across every replica serving this model, which makes each one re-resolve the alias fresh right now instead of waiting for its normal poll cycle, because the entire point of an emergency rollback is stopping the bad behavior as fast as possible, not whenever the existing polling cadence happens to catch up. The real underlying gap, though, is that nobody ever decided what an acceptable rollback-propagation-time SLO actually is — alias resolution was just built around a convenient polling interval with no one asking whether that interval is fast enough for an emergency. I'd fix that properly rather than treating 'remember to do a rolling restart' as the permanent answer: either move the registry to push notifications on alias change so serving infrastructure reloads immediately, or at minimum decouple the alias-check interval from the full-model-reload interval, since checking 'did the alias change' is cheap and can run frequently even if actually reloading a model stays less frequent. And I'd make sure the rollback runbook spells out the rolling-restart step explicitly, rather than assuming alias reassignment by itself is the whole rollback, because the gap between 'the registry says we rolled back' and 'every replica is actually serving the rolled-back version' is exactly the kind of thing nobody notices until it causes an incident.
commonMistakes: Assumes alias reassignment being 'instant' means every serving replica picks it up immediately
Doesn't investigate how replicas actually resolve the alias (startup-only, polling interval, or push notification)
Treats the inconsistent behavior as a one-off fluke rather than a predictable consequence of the resolution mechanism
Doesn't propose an immediate forcing mechanism (rolling restart) to resolve the current incident quickly
Fixes only the immediate incident without addressing the underlying polling/propagation-time design gap
Doesn't propose defining an explicit rollback-propagation-time SLO or decoupling alias-check frequency from model-reload frequency
keyPoints: Correctly distinguishes registry metadata update speed from actual replica-level propagation speed
Identifies the specific resolution mechanism (polling interval, likely) causing the delay
Proposes a rolling restart as the correct immediate fix to force consistency now
Proposes a structural fix (push notification or decoupled, faster alias-check interval) for the underlying gap
Recommends documenting the rolling-restart step explicitly in the rollback runbook

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes registry update speed from replica propagation speed
Proposes a correct, fast immediate fix (rolling restart)
Proposes a sound structural fix for the propagation-time gap
Recommends codifying the fix into the rollback runbook

questions.title: A Quantized Model Passes Its Perplexity Check but Fails Badly on a Specific Downstream Task
questions.prompt: A newly quantized model passes its standard perplexity regression check (within 1% of the full-precision model) and ships to production, but within days, users report the model is unusually bad at a specific capability: following numbered-list formatting instructions. Walk through how this could happen despite a passing perplexity check, and how you'd fix both the immediate problem and the validation gap that let it ship.
questions.modelAnswer: Perplexity is a population-average, token-level metric computed over a broad sample of held-out text, and it can stay essentially unchanged while a narrow, specific capability degrades sharply, precisely because that capability's failure only affects a small fraction of total tokens in any broad sample — a model that gets numbered-list formatting wrong doesn't predict every token worse, it predicts a small, specific subset of tokens (the ones involved in list-item numbering and formatting) much worse, and that narrow effect gets averaged away by the vastly larger number of unrelated tokens the perplexity check also measures, which is exactly why a 1%-perplexity-regression gate can and did pass something with a real, user-visible capability regression. The mechanistic reason quantization specifically can cause this kind of narrow failure is that certain learned behaviors — a numbered-list formatting instruction being followed consistently is a fairly precise, possibly narrowly-represented behavior in the model's weights — can depend on a small number of specific weights or activation patterns being preserved with enough precision, and a quantization scheme calibrated on a general text sample may simply not have 'seen' enough examples of this specific behavior during calibration to preserve it well, especially if the calibration dataset happened to under-represent structured/formatted output relative to how often it actually occurs in real usage. The immediate fix is operational: roll back to the full-precision (or a less aggressively quantized) version for traffic until a corrected quantization pass is validated, since users are experiencing this right now and the fix to the validation process doesn't un-degrade what's already shipped. The deeper fix is to recalibrate the quantization using a calibration dataset that actually represents the real distribution of production use cases, including structured-output requests like numbered lists, rather than a generic text sample, and to re-validate specifically against a task-level eval suite covering the product's actual core capabilities (instruction-following formats, in this case) rather than relying on perplexity as the only pre-ship gate. The validation-gap fix, which is the part that actually prevents the next version of this exact bug, is making a task-specific eval suite — covering the handful of capabilities this specific product genuinely depends on — a standing, mandatory gate for any quantization change, run and compared before-and-after on real task performance, not just perplexity, before any quantized model is allowed to replace the production version; I'd specifically include the capability that just broke in that suite going forward, but I'd also push the team to think about what other narrow-but-important capabilities might be similarly exposed, rather than treating this as a one-off patch to perplexity's known blind spot.
questions.professionalAnswer: The mechanism here is exactly what perplexity's known limitation predicts: it's a population-average metric over broad held-out text, so a capability that only affects a small, specific subset of tokens — like correctly formatting numbered lists — can degrade sharply while barely moving the overall average, because the vastly larger number of unrelated tokens in that broad sample swamps the narrow effect. The reason quantization specifically tends to hit this kind of behavior is that something like consistent list-formatting is a fairly precise, possibly narrowly-represented pattern in the model's weights, and a quantization calibration pass run on generic text may simply not have included enough examples of that specific structured-output pattern to preserve it well, especially if the calibration set under-represents how often real usage actually needs it. My immediate move is operational, not a validation-process fix — roll back to full precision, or a less aggressive quantization, for traffic right now, because users are experiencing this today and no amount of improving the validation process retroactively fixes what already shipped. The actual fix is recalibrating quantization against a dataset that genuinely represents real production usage, including structured-output requests, and re-validating specifically against a task-level eval that covers this product's real core capabilities, not just perplexity. But the part I'd insist on past just patching this one case is making a task-specific eval suite a standing, mandatory gate for every future quantization change — run before and after on real task performance, not just perplexity — and I'd put the capability that just broke into that suite permanently, while also pushing the team to think about what other narrow but important behaviors might be similarly exposed, rather than treating this as a one-off fix to a known perplexity blind spot and moving on.
commonMistakes: Assumes a passing perplexity check should have caught any real capability regression
Doesn't explain the specific mechanism by which a narrow capability can degrade while the population average stays flat
Fixes only the immediate production issue without addressing the validation-process gap that let it ship
Recalibrates quantization without first mitigating the immediate user-facing problem via rollback
Proposes only reacting to this specific capability rather than building a standing task-level eval gate going forward
Doesn't consider that the calibration dataset's composition might not represent real production usage
keyPoints: Correctly explains why a population-average metric can hide a narrow capability regression
Explains the specific quantization mechanism (calibration-set representativeness) causing this
Proposes an immediate rollback to address the user-facing problem first
Proposes recalibrating quantization against a more representative calibration set
Proposes a standing task-level eval gate for future quantization changes, not just a one-off fix

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why perplexity can miss this specific regression
Explains the quantization-specific mechanism causing the narrow failure
Proposes an appropriate immediate mitigation (rollback) before a long-term fix
Proposes a standing structural fix (task-level eval gate) to prevent recurrence

questions.title: One Team's Runaway Training Job Starves the Shared Platform for Everyone Else
questions.prompt: A research team kicks off an experimental training job that, due to a bug, repeatedly crashes and restarts in a tight loop, each time briefly acquiring and holding a large chunk of shared GPU scheduling and data-loading infrastructure before crashing again. Within an hour, unrelated teams' inference services and other training jobs are experiencing severe degradation platform-wide. Walk through why a single team's bug was able to cause this, and what you'd actually fix.
questions.modelAnswer: A single team's bug causing platform-wide degradation is the textbook symptom of missing bulkhead isolation, and the specific mechanism here — a crash-loop repeatedly acquiring and releasing a large resource allocation — is a particularly nasty version of it, because each individual acquisition might look fine in isolation while the aggregate churn (rapid, repeated allocation and deallocation at scale) stresses shared infrastructure (a scheduler, a shared data-loading service, a shared metadata store) in a way a single long-running job never would. I'd investigate this in two parts: first, why the crash-loop itself wasn't caught and stopped quickly — a job that crashes and restarts in a tight loop should trip a `backoffLimit`-style circuit breaker well before an hour of damage accumulates, and if it didn't, that's either a missing or misconfigured restart-limit on this specific job type, or a gap in whatever's supposed to detect and halt a crash-looping job platform-wide rather than relying on the submitting team to notice their own job is unhealthy; second, and more fundamentally, why this team's crash-loop was able to degrade unrelated teams' services at all, which is a resource-isolation failure regardless of how the crash-loop started — if the scheduler, the data-loading infrastructure, or whatever shared resource got stressed doesn't have its own capacity limits or quotas per team/namespace, then any single tenant's pathological behavior, buggy or not, can consume a disproportionate, unbounded share of a resource everyone else also depends on. The concrete fixes are: a restart-limit (or a Volcano/Kubernetes-level crash-loop circuit breaker) that halts a repeatedly-failing job automatically after a small number of attempts rather than letting it loop for an hour; per-team or per-namespace quotas on the specific shared resource that got stressed (the scheduler's request-processing rate, the data-loading service's concurrent-connection limit, whatever it actually was), so that even an unbounded crash loop from one team can only ever consume its own quota's worth of that resource, not the whole shared pool; and, if the shared resource in question doesn't currently support per-tenant quotas at all, treating that as the real platform gap to close, since the research team's bug was the trigger here but it wasn't really the root cause — the root cause is that the platform's shared infrastructure had no bulkhead protecting one tenant's pathological behavior from affecting every other tenant, and a different bug from a different team would have found the same gap eventually.
questions.professionalAnswer: The headline fact here — one team's bug degrading everyone else platform-wide — is the signature of missing bulkhead isolation, and the specific shape of this bug, a tight crash-loop repeatedly grabbing and releasing a big chunk of shared infrastructure, is a nasty version of it because the churn itself, not just the size of any single allocation, is what stresses a shared scheduler or data-loading service in a way a normal long-running job never would. I'd split the investigation into two real questions. First: why didn't anything stop the crash-loop itself within minutes — a job that keeps crashing and restarting should trip some kind of restart-limit circuit breaker well before an hour goes by, and if it didn't, that's either a missing or misconfigured backoff limit on this job type, or a bigger gap in whatever's supposed to detect a platform-wide crash-looping job automatically rather than relying on the team that submitted it to notice. Second, and this is the one I'd actually spend more time on: why was this team's misbehavior able to touch unrelated teams' services at all, because that's a resource-isolation failure independent of how the crash-loop started — if the stressed shared resource has no per-team quota or capacity limit, any single tenant's pathological behavior, intentional or buggy, can eat an unbounded share of something everyone else also needs. My concrete fixes are a real restart-limit/circuit-breaker on crash-looping jobs so this stops within minutes next time, not an hour; per-team quotas on whichever specific shared resource got stressed, so even an unbounded crash loop from one team is capped at its own share rather than the whole pool; and if that shared resource genuinely has no per-tenant quota mechanism today, I'd treat that as the actual platform gap this incident exposed — the research team's bug was the trigger, but the real root cause is that the shared infrastructure had no bulkhead protecting everyone else from one tenant's pathological behavior, and some other team's bug would have found the exact same hole eventually.
commonMistakes: Treats the research team's bug as the root cause rather than the trigger that exposed a missing bulkhead
Doesn't investigate why the crash-loop itself wasn't automatically halted within a short window
Proposes fixing only the specific bug in this team's job without addressing the shared-resource isolation gap
Doesn't identify which specific shared resource lacked per-team quotas or capacity limits
Assumes a single long-running large allocation would stress shared infrastructure the same way a crash-loop's rapid churn does
Recommends manual monitoring/escalation as the fix instead of an automated restart-limit and quota mechanism
keyPoints: Correctly identifies missing bulkhead/resource-isolation as the real root cause, not just this team's bug
Investigates why the crash-loop itself wasn't automatically halted sooner
Identifies the specific shared resource that lacked per-tenant quotas or capacity limits
Proposes both an automated restart-limit fix and a per-tenant quota fix as distinct, necessary pieces
Frames this as exposing a platform gap that any team's future bug could have found

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies missing bulkhead isolation as the real root cause
Investigates and proposes a fix for the crash-loop not being halted automatically
Proposes a concrete per-tenant quota/capacity-limit fix for the stressed shared resource

questions.title: System Design: A Unified Platform for Training, Serving, and Governing Several Frontier-Scale Models
questions.prompt: Meridian AI runs three frontier-scale model families in production simultaneously (a general-purpose chat model, a code-specialized model, and a domain-specific model for a regulated industry customer), each retrained on its own cadence, each served to different customer segments with different latency/cost requirements, and all subject to an external audit requirement that can ask 'exactly which model version, trained on which data, served this specific customer request on this date.' Design the end-to-end platform spanning training infrastructure, serving infrastructure, and governance, as a staff/principal engineer would present it to other senior stakeholders.
commonMistakes: Treats all three model families as needing identical serving/isolation infrastructure rather than tailoring to each one's actual risk profile
Reconstructs audit lineage after the fact from scattered logs instead of capturing it synchronously at training and serving time
Uses a single shared registry alias across all three model families instead of per-family lifecycle management
Doesn't account for the gang-scheduling fairness needed to prevent one model family's retraining cadence from starving another
Treats the audit requirement as a reporting feature to add later rather than a core design constraint shaping the whole architecture
Fails to make the audit-chain query capability a standing, tested health check rather than something only exercised during a real audit
keyPoints: Tailors serving/isolation architecture to each model family's actual risk and compliance profile, not a uniform policy
Captures full lineage (code, data, config, run ID) synchronously at training time, not reconstructed later
Uses per-model-family registry governance and alias lifecycle rather than one shared global policy
Designs gang-scheduling fair-share to prevent cross-model-family starvation on the shared training fleet
Builds a concrete, automatic audit-chain resolution capability spanning request log, registry, and lineage
Makes the lineage-completeness gate a hard requirement specifically for the regulated-industry model family

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Designs training infrastructure with correct multi-tenant fairness and lineage capture
Designs registry/governance architecture tailored per model family's risk profile
Designs serving infrastructure with appropriate isolation tradeoffs
Designs a concrete, working audit/lineage-chain architecture satisfying the stated requirement
Identifies real failure modes and tradeoffs with concrete mitigations

deepDive.heading: Clarify requirements and constraints
deepDive.content: Three model families with independent retraining cadences means the platform has to support concurrent, isolated training runs sharing a common GPU fleet rather than one training pipeline serving one model. Different customer segments with different latency/cost requirements means serving infrastructure can't be one-size-fits-all — the regulated-industry customer likely has stricter data-handling and auditability requirements than the general chat product, which pushes toward some degree of infrastructure or at least logical separation for that specific model family. The audit requirement — 'exactly which model version, trained on which data, served this request' — is the single hardest constraint in this design, because it has to be satisfiable after the fact, for any historical request, which means lineage has to be captured at write time end-to-end rather than reconstructed later from scattered logs, and it has to survive model retraining, redeployment, and infrastructure changes without gaps.

deepDive.heading: Training infrastructure
deepDive.content: All three model families train on a shared GPU fleet managed by gang-scheduling (Volcano or Kubeflow's equivalent) with per-team/per-model-family queues and weighted fair-share, so the regulated-industry model's retraining cadence can't be starved by the chat model's larger, more frequent runs, and vice versa. Each training run is anchored to a run ID that ties together: the exact git commit of the training code, a versioned and immutable snapshot of the training data (not a live query against a mutable table), the exact container image digest, and the full hyperparameter configuration — captured automatically as part of the training job's startup, not as a manual step someone might skip. Checkpointing uses torch.distributed.checkpoint for fault tolerance on the larger runs, with checkpoint cadence derived from the fleet's actual expected failure rate rather than a round-number guess, and every checkpoint is tagged with the same run ID so a checkpoint can always be traced back to the exact code/data/config that produced it.

deepDive.heading: Model registry and governance
deepDive.content: Every training run that completes successfully registers a candidate model version in a central registry (MLflow or equivalent), with the registry entry storing the run ID — which transitively ties to code, data, and config — plus the evaluation results that justified promotion. Promotion to serving uses alias-based lifecycle management (a 'champion' alias per model family, not a shared global alias across families), reassigned only after a staged comparison: offline evaluation against a fixed holdout set specific to that model family's actual use case, shadow deployment against real traffic, and a canary rollout with real monitoring — the regulated-industry model's promotion criteria are stricter (likely requiring a compliance sign-off step the other two don't need), which the registry's governance workflow has to support as a per-model-family policy, not a single platform-wide rule.

deepDive.heading: Serving infrastructure
deepDive.content: Rather than one shared serving fleet for all three model families, I'd separate serving infrastructure primarily along the regulated-industry boundary: that model family gets dedicated serving infrastructure (its own node pool, its own data-handling path) to satisfy its stricter requirements and to keep its audit trail cleanly separable from the other two, while the chat model and code model can reasonably share a more cost-optimized, heterogeneous fleet with model-aware, capacity-aware load balancing, continuous batching via vLLM or similar, and autoscaling on queue depth or GPU utilization rather than CPU. Each model family's serving layer logs, for every single request, the exact model version (resolved alias target at the moment of serving, not just the alias name) and a reference back to that version's run ID — this logging has to happen at the serving layer itself, synchronously with serving the request, not reconstructed afterward from deployment history, because deployment history alone can't answer 'which version served this specific request' once an alias has moved multiple times.

deepDive.heading: Audit and lineage architecture
deepDive.content: The audit requirement is satisfied by a chain of four links that all have to hold for any historical request: the request log (model version + timestamp + customer), the model version's registry entry (run ID), the run's captured lineage (code commit, data snapshot, config), and an immutable, append-only audit log of every registry-affecting action (registration, promotion, rollback) so the history of which version was aliased as champion at any past moment is itself auditable, not just the current state. I'd store this audit log in write-once object storage (object-lock enabled) specifically because a log that could be edited after an incident provides no real guarantee to an external auditor, and I'd build a single query tool that, given a request ID or a timestamp-plus-customer, walks all four links automatically and produces the full chain, rather than requiring a human to manually cross-reference the registry, the logs, and the data versioning system under audit pressure.

deepDive.heading: Failure modes and tradeoffs
deepDive.content: The most likely failure mode in this design is a gap in the lineage chain — a run that was promoted before the automatic lineage capture was in place, or a hotfix deployed outside the normal promotion workflow during an incident — and I'd address this by making the serving layer refuse to serve a request under a model version that lacks a complete lineage record, treating 'can't prove what this is' as a hard gate for the regulated-industry model family specifically (the chat/code models could reasonably have a softer policy, logging a warning rather than blocking, if the business is willing to accept that risk tier for those products). A second real tradeoff is cost versus isolation: fully separate serving infrastructure per model family is the safest design for the regulated customer but the most expensive; sharing infrastructure between the chat and code models is the right cost tradeoff specifically because neither carries the regulated customer's audit stakes, and I'd present this as a deliberate, named tradeoff to stakeholders rather than a uniform policy applied without justification.

deepDive.heading: Cost and operational considerations
deepDive.content: Training cost is managed primarily through the gang-scheduling queue's fair-share weights and a chargeback model attributing GPU cost per model family's namespace, making each family's retraining cost visible to the team responsible for it. Serving cost is managed through capacity planning grounded in proven per-replica throughput under each model family's actual latency SLO, with headroom sized for the specific failure modes each family needs to tolerate (the regulated model family likely needs more headroom for failover given its stricter uptime expectations). Operationally, I'd run the audit-chain query tool as a standing, automated health check — periodically sampling real served requests and confirming the full lineage chain resolves cleanly — rather than only exercising it reactively when an actual external audit arrives, because discovering a lineage gap during a live audit is a far worse position than discovering and fixing it during a routine internal check.

Accounts for owned hardware's real operational overhead, including headcount, honestly
Includes a flexibility/being-wrong cost category with a concrete scenario-based estimate
Specifies the concrete utilization/stage conditions under which owned hardware would become the right call
Recommends sizing committed capacity to a conservative, proven baseline rather than an optimistic forecast

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly splits training and inference into distinct demand-shape-driven sub-decisions
Builds a sound TCO model using utilization-adjusted effective cost as the real comparison basis
Honestly accounts for operational overhead and flexibility cost of owned hardware
Specifies concrete conditions for revisiting the decision rather than treating it as permanent

deepDive.heading: Clarify requirements and constraints
deepDive.content: The decision has to be split into at least two separate sub-decisions, because training and inference have genuinely different demand shapes that shouldn't share one answer: training demand here is described as bursty and growing, which favors flexible, elastic capacity that can scale down between large runs, while inference demand is steadier, which is exactly the shape that benefits most from a committed, amortized-cost capacity model. I'd also clarify the real planning horizon and risk tolerance with leadership before building the model — a 3-year horizon with owned hardware assumes GPU generations and model architectures stay useful for that long, which is a real bet given how fast both GPU hardware and model efficiency are moving, and I'd want leadership to explicitly own that assumption rather than have it buried inside a spreadsheet.

deepDive.heading: Core TCO model structure
deepDive.content: I'd build the model around four cost categories for each option (on-demand cloud, reserved/committed cloud, owned/colocated hardware): the GPU compute cost itself (hourly on-demand rate, reserved/committed discount rate, or amortized purchase price over an assumed useful life); the operational overhead cost, which is usually underestimated for the owned-hardware option specifically — power, cooling, colocation fees, networking equipment, and crucially the headcount needed to actually run physical infrastructure (hardware procurement, failure replacement, firmware/driver management), none of which exists for the cloud options; the utilization-adjusted effective cost, which is the category that most TCO comparisons get wrong by comparing list prices instead of cost-per-actually-used-GPU-hour, since owned hardware sitting at 50% utilization costs twice its sticker price per useful hour; and the flexibility cost, a real but harder-to-quantify category capturing the cost of being wrong about future capacity needs — owned hardware that turns out to be the wrong generation or the wrong quantity in 18 months is a sunk cost, while cloud capacity can be adjusted, and I'd assign this a rough dollar value via a scenario analysis (what does being 30% wrong on demand cost under each option) rather than leaving it out of the model just because it's uncomfortable to estimate.

deepDive.heading: Splitting the training and inference decisions
deepDive.content: For inference specifically, steadier demand with a growing but roughly forecastable floor makes a reserved/committed cloud capacity tier for the baseline load the right default, sized to the proven, load-tested utilization floor (not peak), with on-demand or spot capacity layered on top specifically for burst above that floor — this gets most of the committed-capacity discount without the risk of over-committing to a number that turns out wrong. For training, the bursty, growing-but-less-predictable demand argues against owned hardware as the primary strategy at this company's current scale (180 engineers is a meaningful but not yet massive organization, and the operational overhead of owned hardware has a real fixed-cost floor that's easier to justify at a larger scale with more predictable utilization) — I'd recommend a reserved capacity commitment sized to a conservative baseline of expected training throughput, with on-demand/spot bursting above that for the largest or least-predictable runs, rather than either pure on-demand (currently too expensive at this volume) or owned hardware (too operationally heavy and too risky a multi-year bet at this company's stage).

deepDive.heading: When owned hardware actually becomes correct
deepDive.content: I'd present the specific conditions under which the recommendation would flip toward owned hardware, rather than presenting 'rent, don't buy' as a permanent answer: if sustained utilization (not peak, not burst, the actual floor) across both training and inference consistently exceeds roughly 70-80% of a would-be owned fleet's capacity for a meaningful stretch (sufficient to amortize the operational overhead), and if the company has or is willing to build the operational capability to run physical infrastructure reliably, owned hardware's lower marginal compute cost starts to outweigh its overhead and flexibility costs. I'd frame this as a decision to revisit on a defined cadence (annually, or triggered by a specific utilization threshold being sustained) rather than a one-time choice, since the right answer is explicitly a function of utilization and company stage, both of which change.

deepDive.heading: Governance and operational considerations
deepDive.content: Whatever mix is chosen, I'd insist on a chargeback/cost-attribution system that makes both training and inference cost visible per team, so the decision's actual outcome (are we hitting the utilization assumptions the model was built on) is measurable going forward rather than a one-time analysis nobody revisits. I'd also build in an explicit review cadence tied to the reserved-capacity commitment terms — if the committed cloud tier is a 1-year reservation, the utilization data needs to be reviewed well before renewal, not reactively after a renewal deadline has already passed and locked in another year of a possibly-wrong assumption.

deepDive.heading: Failure modes and tradeoffs
deepDive.content: The biggest risk in this kind of model is treating the owned-hardware option's purchase price as the dominant number and underweighting operational overhead and utilization-adjustment, which is the single most common way these analyses mislead leadership into an expensive mistake — I'd present the utilization-adjusted effective cost number as the headline figure for every option, not the sticker price, specifically to prevent that framing error. A second real risk is committing to reserved cloud capacity sized to a demand forecast that turns out wrong in either direction — underestimating growth leaves the company paying on-demand premiums above the committed tier more than planned, while overestimating leaves paid-for, unused committed capacity sitting idle — and I'd size the commitment to a conservative, already-proven baseline rather than an optimistic growth projection specifically to bias the error in the cheaper direction (slightly more on-demand bursting, not idle paid capacity).

questions.title: Design Fault-Tolerant Training Infrastructure for a 1,000+ GPU Cluster
questions.prompt: Design the fault-tolerance architecture for a sustained, multi-week pretraining run across more than 1,000 GPUs, covering checkpoint strategy, failure detection, and recovery, grounded in the actual math of failure rates at this scale rather than a generic 'add checkpoints' answer.
questions.modelAnswer: The design has to start from the actual expected failure rate at this scale, because 'checkpoint periodically' without that math produces either wasted compute from checkpointing too often or unacceptable recomputation loss from checkpointing too rarely. At even a conservative 1-2% annualized per-GPU failure rate, a 1,000+ GPU fleet running continuously should expect something like 10-20 individual GPU failures over a year of cumulative fleet-time, which for a multi-week run translates to a real, non-negligible probability of at least one failure during the run — the exact math (failure rate x GPU-count x run-duration-as-a-fraction-of-a-year) should drive the checkpoint interval decision directly: I'd target a checkpoint cadence such that the expected recomputation cost from a failure between checkpoints (failure probability per interval x cost of redoing that interval's work) is small relative to the checkpoint's own write cost, rather than picking a round number like 'every hour' without that calculation. Checkpointing itself uses torch.distributed.checkpoint so each rank saves and loads only its own shard in parallel with resharding metadata, which both makes individual checkpoint writes fast enough to checkpoint at the derived cadence without meaningfully hurting throughput, and lets the job resume on a different GPU count if the failed capacity isn't replaced immediately. Failure detection operates at two layers: NCCL's own watchdog timeout catches a hung collective and turns it into an explicit, actionable error rather than an indefinite hang, while a separate node-level health-check layer (monitoring Xid errors in the driver log, ECC error counts, and DCGM thermal/health metrics) catches degrading-but-not-yet-crashed hardware before it causes a hang or a straggler pattern at all, which matters because the straggler case — a GPU running correctly but slower — doesn't trigger NCCL's watchdog and needs this separate detection layer to catch at all. Recovery uses torch.distributed.elastic with an `--nnodes` range and a meaningful `--max-restarts` budget, so a detected failure triggers automatic cordon-and-drain of the bad node, re-formation of the process group with remaining healthy nodes, and resumption from the last checkpoint — with the floor of the nnodes range set well above a token minimum, since training at a small fraction of the intended scale is rarely worth continuing versus pausing for replacement capacity. The rank-0/coordination role specifically should sit on more stable, less-likely-to-be-reclaimed capacity than ordinary worker ranks, since losing the coordination point is a more disruptive failure than losing one worker even under elastic's own recovery model, and gang-scheduling at the queue level (ensuring the job's full allocation is available together, with an autoscaler provisioning any shortfall) prevents the job from being left in a partially-scheduled, partially-functional state after a failure and subsequent re-acquisition of capacity.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd ground the whole design in the actual failure-rate math rather than picking a checkpoint interval that sounds reasonable, because at even a conservative 1-2% annualized per-GPU failure rate, a cluster over 1,000 GPUs should expect something like 10-20 failures a year across the fleet, and for a multi-week run that's a real, calculable probability of hitting at least one failure during the run — I'd size the checkpoint cadence so the expected cost of recomputing work lost between checkpoints stays small relative to the cost of writing a checkpoint itself, derived from that real failure-rate math, not a round number like 'every hour.' Checkpointing uses torch.distributed.checkpoint specifically because each rank only saves and loads its own shard in parallel, which keeps checkpoint writes cheap enough to actually hit the derived cadence without eating into throughput, and lets the job resume on a different GPU count if replacement capacity isn't instantly available. On detection, I'd run two layers: NCCL's watchdog catches a hung collective and turns it into a real error instead of an infinite hang, but that layer alone misses a straggler — a GPU that's degraded but still technically responding — so I'd pair it with node-level health monitoring (Xid errors, ECC counts, DCGM thermal signals) specifically to catch that slower-but-not-crashed failure mode the watchdog can't see at all. Recovery runs through torch.distributed.elastic with a real nnodes range and restart budget, so a detected failure triggers an automatic cordon-and-drain, re-forms the process group with whoever's left, and resumes from the last checkpoint — and I'd set the floor of that nnodes range well above some token minimum, because training at a small fraction of intended scale usually isn't worth continuing versus just pausing for replacement capacity to arrive. I'd also keep rank-0's coordination role on more stable capacity than ordinary workers specifically because losing the coordination point is a worse failure than losing one worker even under elastic's own model, and I'd pair all of this with gang-scheduling at the queue level so the job never ends up stuck half-allocated after a failure and a subsequent attempt to get capacity back.
commonMistakes: Picks a checkpoint cadence by intuition or convention instead of deriving it from actual failure-rate math
Relies solely on NCCL's watchdog for failure detection, missing the straggler/degraded-hardware case it can't catch
Checkpoints using a naive gather-to-one-rank approach instead of torch.distributed.checkpoint's parallel sharded save
Sets torch.distributed.elastic's nnodes floor too low, allowing the job to limp along at an unproductive fraction of scale
Places rank-0's coordination role on equally volatile capacity as ordinary workers
Doesn't pair elastic recovery with gang-scheduling, risking the job getting stuck partially allocated after a failure
keyPoints: Derives checkpoint cadence from actual fleet-scale failure-rate math, not an arbitrary interval
Uses torch.distributed.checkpoint for fast, parallel, resharding-capable checkpoint writes
Layers NCCL watchdog detection with node-level health monitoring to catch stragglers and degrading hardware
Uses torch.distributed.elastic with a sensible nnodes range and restart budget for automatic recovery
Protects the rank-0 coordination role with more stable capacity placement
Pairs elastic recovery with gang-scheduling to avoid partial-allocation deadlock

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Derives checkpoint cadence from real failure-rate math
Correctly designs multi-layer failure detection (watchdog + node health)
Correctly designs elastic recovery with sound nnodes/restart configuration
Addresses rank-0 placement and gang-scheduling as distinct, necessary pieces

questions.title: Design the Network Fabric Topology for a Frontier-Scale Training Cluster
questions.prompt: Design the physical network topology — not the software stack on top of it — for a new cluster intended to support frontier-scale pretraining runs using thousands of GPUs across many racks. Explain the specific topology choice and why a cheaper alternative would be a mistake here.
questions.modelAnswer: The topology choice has to be driven by the actual communication pattern of large-scale distributed training, which is dominated by collective operations (all-reduce, all-gather, reduce-scatter) that, depending on the parallelism strategy, can require any GPU to communicate with any other GPU, not just its physically nearby neighbors — this rules out a cheaper, oversubscribed tree topology from the start, because oversubscription means the aggregate bandwidth available when traffic crosses between branches of the tree is less than the sum of what each branch could produce individually, and for a workload where cross-rack, cross-branch communication is the normal case rather than the exception, that oversubscription becomes the actual bottleneck on every single training step, not an occasional congestion event. The correct topology is a fat-tree (or an equivalent leaf-spine design) built to be non-blocking, meaning a 1:1 oversubscription ratio at every layer — enough spine-switch capacity that the worst-case bisection bandwidth (the total bandwidth available between any two halves of the cluster, split in the worst possible way) matches what a fully non-blocking design would provide, rather than a cheaper design that saves on spine switches at the cost of bisection bandwidth that only shows up as a problem once the cluster is running real multi-rack collective traffic. Within this fat-tree, I'd use InfiniBand NDR (or an equivalent lossless, RDMA-capable fabric) rather than plain Ethernet specifically because training collectives are latency- and loss-sensitive in a way that makes InfiniBand's credit-based, natively lossless flow control and GPUDirect RDMA's ability to write directly into GPU memory (skipping a host-RAM copy) materially better-suited than standard TCP/IP Ethernet, where a single dropped packet mid-collective can stall every participating GPU until retransmission completes — this isn't a marginal preference, it's the difference between a collective that completes predictably and one that occasionally stalls the entire job on a single lost packet. Intra-node, GPUs connect via NVLink, giving each GPU far higher bandwidth to its node-mates than any inter-node link provides, which is why parallelism strategies with the most latency-sensitive communication pattern (tensor parallelism specifically) should be scoped to stay within a node wherever possible, with the fat-tree fabric handling the comparatively more latency-tolerant inter-node traffic (pipeline parallelism's activation-passing, and the data-parallel dimension's gradient all-reduce). The mistake I'd flag explicitly to anyone proposing a cheaper, oversubscribed design to save on switch costs is that the savings are real and immediate on the budget line, but the cost shows up later as training runs that take meaningfully longer wall-clock time due to communication-bound steps, which, multiplied across a multi-week run on an expensive GPU fleet, almost always costs far more in wasted GPU-hours than the switch-cost savings were worth — I'd present this tradeoff explicitly with real numbers rather than let a hardware-budget decision get made without visibility into its training-throughput cost.
questions.professionalAnswer: The design has to follow the actual communication pattern, and large-scale training's collectives routinely need any GPU to talk to any other GPU across the whole cluster, not just nearby neighbors — which immediately rules out a cheaper oversubscribed tree, because oversubscription means less aggregate bandwidth is available exactly when traffic has to cross between branches, and for this workload that's not an edge case, it's every single training step. So the topology has to be a non-blocking fat-tree or leaf-spine design, with enough spine capacity that worst-case bisection bandwidth — the real bandwidth available between any two halves of the cluster split the worst possible way — matches what a fully non-blocking design provides, because a cheaper design that cuts spine capacity to save switch cost only reveals that cost once real multi-rack collective traffic is actually running. Within that fat-tree, I'd specifically use InfiniBand rather than plain Ethernet, not as a marginal preference but because training collectives are latency- and loss-sensitive enough that InfiniBand's native lossless flow control and GPUDirect RDMA's direct-to-GPU-memory writes matter a lot — a single dropped packet on plain TCP/IP Ethernet mid-collective can stall every participating GPU until it's retransmitted, which is a real, recurring cost at this scale, not a rare event. Intra-node, NVLink gives GPUs far more bandwidth to their node-mates than any inter-node link can match, which is why I'd keep the most latency-sensitive parallelism strategy, tensor parallelism, scoped within a node wherever possible, letting the fat-tree fabric carry the more latency-tolerant traffic instead — pipeline parallelism's activation passing, and the data-parallel gradient all-reduce. And the thing I'd push back on hardest if someone proposed cutting spine capacity to save on the switch budget is that the savings are real and visible on the hardware line item, but the cost shows up later as communication-bound training steps that stretch out wall-clock time on a multi-week run across an expensive GPU fleet, and that almost always costs far more in wasted GPU-hours than the switch savings were worth — I'd insist on making that tradeoff visible with real numbers rather than letting it get decided purely as a hardware line-item question.
commonMistakes: Proposes an oversubscribed tree topology to save on switch cost without accounting for bisection-bandwidth impact
Chooses plain Ethernet over InfiniBand/RDMA without accounting for training collectives' latency/loss sensitivity
Doesn't scope latency-sensitive tensor parallelism to stay within NVLink-connected node boundaries
Treats the network topology purely as a hardware-budget decision without quantifying its training-throughput cost
Assumes bisection bandwidth only matters for the largest jobs, missing that it affects every collective-heavy training step
Doesn't explain why oversubscription's cost only becomes visible under real multi-rack collective traffic, not benchmarks run within one rack
keyPoints: Correctly identifies the collective communication pattern as the driver of topology choice
Specifies a non-blocking fat-tree/leaf-spine design with real bisection-bandwidth reasoning
Correctly justifies InfiniBand/RDMA over plain Ethernet for this workload's latency/loss sensitivity
Correctly scopes tensor parallelism to NVLink-connected intra-node boundaries
Quantifies the training-throughput cost of a cheaper, oversubscribed design rather than treating it as free

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies collective communication pattern as the topology driver
Specifies a correct non-blocking fat-tree design with bisection-bandwidth reasoning
Correctly justifies InfiniBand/RDMA choice over Ethernet
Quantifies/communicates the real cost of a cheaper alternative

questions.title: Design a Gang-Scheduling and Fair-Share Queue Architecture for Competing Research Teams
questions.prompt: Design the scheduling architecture for a shared 2,000-GPU cluster used by five research teams with very different job sizes and priorities — one team runs occasional massive 500+ GPU jobs, several run frequent small 8-32 GPU experiments, and one team has a contractual priority guarantee for a customer-facing deadline. Explain how you'd actually structure queues, fairness, and preemption so no team can starve another.
questions.modelAnswer: The core design tension is that gang scheduling's all-or-nothing placement requirement (a job's pods are placed only once enough capacity exists for all of them simultaneously) interacts badly with naive fair-share if left unaddressed, because a single 500-GPU job and dozens of 8-32 GPU jobs have fundamentally different admission requirements, and a scheduler that doesn't account for that can let many small jobs partially consume capacity in a way that leaves the large job permanently unable to find a contiguous 500-GPU window, even if the cluster's total free capacity would technically be enough. I'd structure this with per-team queues (Volcano's Queue resource or an equivalent), each with a `weight` setting its proportional share of the cluster when multiple queues want capacity simultaneously, and a separate `capability` ceiling on each queue so no single team, even one with a high weight, can consume the entire cluster and starve everyone else outright regardless of relative priority. For the team running occasional massive jobs, I'd give their queue a reservation mechanism — not a permanent dedicated allocation, since that wastes capacity between their large runs, but a scheduler-level priority that lets their job's gang-scheduled admission preempt or wait for a specific, computed window of capacity to free up, with the small-job teams' queues configured to respect a soft capacity ceiling that leaves room for this periodically, rather than being allowed to fill 100% of the cluster whenever the large job isn't currently running. For the team with a contractual priority guarantee, I'd implement this as a distinct priority class above the normal fair-share weighting — not just a higher weight, but an actual preemption right, so their critical jobs can preempt lower-priority jobs from other teams' queues (returning that capacity, with the preempted jobs re-queued rather than killed outright, so they resume rather than lose all progress) specifically during the contractual deadline window, reverting to normal fair-share weighting outside that window so the priority guarantee doesn't become a permanent, unbounded claim on the cluster. I'd also implement a starvation-prevention backstop independent of all of the above: any job that's been pending longer than a defined threshold gets an automatically escalating priority boost, so even in a worst-case scenario where the weight/capability configuration has an edge case, no job can wait indefinitely — this is a deliberately crude, defensive layer on top of the more precise weight/capability/preemption design, specifically because fairness configurations have edge cases and a hard floor on wait time catches whatever the more precise rules miss.
questions.professionalAnswer: The thing that makes this hard is that gang scheduling's all-or-nothing admission for the 500-GPU jobs doesn't play nicely with naive fair-share unless I design for it explicitly — a bunch of small jobs can easily fragment the cluster's free capacity in a way that technically leaves enough total GPUs free but never a contiguous 500-GPU window, starving the large job even though the numbers look fine on paper. So I'd set up per-team queues with both a weight, for proportional share when multiple teams want capacity at once, and a separate capability ceiling, so no team, even a high-weight one, can ever claim the whole cluster and starve everyone else outright. For the team running occasional massive jobs, I wouldn't give them a permanent dedicated allocation since that wastes capacity between runs, but I would give their queue a reservation mechanism that lets a 500-GPU gang-scheduled request get priority access to a specific, computed capacity window, with the smaller teams' queues configured with a capability ceiling that leaves room for that periodically rather than letting them fill 100% of the cluster by default. For the team with the contractual deadline, that's a real priority class with actual preemption rights, not just a bigger weight — their critical jobs can preempt lower-priority work from other queues during the specific deadline window, with preempted jobs requeued rather than killed so they resume instead of losing all their progress, and that priority class reverts to normal fair-share behavior once the deadline window closes, so the contractual guarantee doesn't quietly become a permanent claim on the cluster. And underneath all of that, I'd put in a blunt, defensive backstop — any job pending past some threshold gets an automatic priority escalation — specifically because weight/capability/preemption configurations have edge cases, and I'd rather catch whatever those miss with a crude hard floor than discover a starved job three days later.
commonMistakes: Uses only proportional weighting without a capability ceiling, letting a high-weight team consume the entire cluster
Doesn't account for gang scheduling's all-or-nothing admission fragmenting capacity against the large-job team's needs
Gives the contractual-priority team a permanently elevated weight instead of a time-bounded preemption right
Kills preempted jobs outright instead of requeuing them to resume, wasting their prior progress
Doesn't include a starvation-prevention backstop independent of the weight/capability/preemption configuration
Gives the large-job team a permanent dedicated reservation, wasting capacity between their infrequent runs
keyPoints: Correctly addresses gang-scheduling fragmentation risk against the occasional large-job team's needs
Uses both weight and capability ceilings per queue to prevent any single team from starving others
Implements the contractual priority as a time-bounded preemption right, not a permanent weight increase
Requeues rather than kills preempted jobs to preserve their progress
Adds an independent starvation-prevention backstop as a defensive layer

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly addresses gang-scheduling fragmentation risk for the large-job team
Designs sound per-queue weight/capability fairness preventing starvation
Correctly scopes the contractual priority guarantee as time-bounded preemption
Adds a defensive starvation-prevention backstop

questions.title: Design a Multi-Model Serving Architecture Under a Hard Monthly Cost Ceiling
questions.prompt: Design the serving architecture for three models (a large general-purpose model, a mid-sized specialized model, and a small, high-volume classifier) that together must stay under a fixed monthly GPU spend ceiling set by finance, while each still meeting its own latency SLO. Explain how you'd actually allocate capacity and what you'd be willing to sacrifice to stay under the ceiling.
questions.modelAnswer: A hard cost ceiling means this design can't start from 'what capacity would each model ideally want' and add them up — it has to start from the ceiling and allocate down, which means explicitly deciding which model's SLO is most flexible before an incident forces that decision under pressure. I'd first establish each model's actual proven per-replica capacity via load testing against its own latency SLO, then size a minimum viable fleet for each based on its traffic volume, and only then check whether the sum fits under the ceiling — if it doesn't, which is the realistic case given that a ceiling was imposed specifically because current spend exceeds it, the allocation decisions I'd make, in order of preference, are: first, apply compression (quantization, and distillation if the volume justifies the engineering cost) to the large general-purpose model specifically, since it's almost certainly the most expensive per-replica and the one where a moderate compression-driven cost reduction buys the most absolute savings; second, consider whether the large model's workload and the specialized model's workload can share a heterogeneous GPU pool with capacity-aware load balancing rather than each having fully dedicated, separately-sized capacity, since pooling reduces the total headroom needed across both compared to each maintaining its own separate buffer; third, for the small high-volume classifier specifically, check whether it even needs GPU serving at all, since a sufficiently small, high-volume classification model is sometimes cheaper to serve on CPU or a much smaller/cheaper accelerator than to occupy GPU capacity that the larger models need more. If after all of that the numbers still don't fit, the actual tradeoff decision — which I'd bring to stakeholders explicitly rather than making unilaterally — is which model's latency SLO gets relaxed: I'd argue for protecting the general-purpose model's SLO most strongly if it's customer-facing and differentiating, and treating the specialized or classifier model's SLO as the one with headroom to relax first, but that's a product decision informed by engineering constraints, not purely an engineering call, and I'd present the actual dollar cost of hitting all three SLOs simultaneously versus the savings from relaxing one, so the tradeoff is made with real numbers rather than as an abstract engineering preference. Whatever allocation is chosen, I'd implement it with capacity reserved per model (not a shared pool with no guardrails, which risks one model's traffic spike silently starving another's capacity) but with the pools sized using the headroom-minimization techniques above rather than each model getting its naively-calculated ideal allocation, and I'd build the cost-ceiling check into the deployment pipeline itself — any capacity change for any of the three models gets validated against the aggregate ceiling before it ships, rather than discovering a ceiling breach after the fact in a monthly finance review.
questions.professionalAnswer: A hard ceiling means I can't size each model's ideal capacity independently and hope the sum works out — I have to start from the ceiling and allocate down, which means somebody has to decide in advance which model's SLO has the most flexibility, rather than that decision getting made under pressure during an incident. My first step is proving each model's real per-replica capacity against its own SLO via load testing, sizing a minimum viable fleet for each from actual traffic volume, and then checking the sum against the ceiling — and if it doesn't fit, which is the likely case given that a ceiling usually gets imposed because current spend already exceeds it, my levers in order are: compress the large general-purpose model first, since it's almost certainly the most expensive per replica and buys the most absolute savings per unit of engineering effort; look at pooling the large and specialized models onto one heterogeneous GPU fleet with capacity-aware load balancing instead of each keeping separate dedicated headroom, since pooled headroom is smaller than the sum of two separate buffers; and specifically check whether the small high-volume classifier even needs a GPU at all, because a model that small is sometimes genuinely cheaper to run on CPU or a smaller accelerator than to tie up GPU capacity the bigger models need more. If none of that closes the gap, the real decision is which model's SLO gets relaxed, and that's not something I'd decide unilaterally — I'd bring it to stakeholders with the actual dollar cost of hitting all three SLOs versus the savings from relaxing one, and argue for protecting whichever model is most customer-facing and differentiating, but make sure that's a product call made with real numbers, not an engineering assumption nobody questioned. And whatever the final allocation is, I'd build the cost-ceiling check directly into the deployment pipeline so any future capacity change for any of the three models gets validated against the aggregate ceiling automatically, instead of someone discovering a breach in a monthly finance review after it's already happened.
commonMistakes: Sizes each model's capacity independently and only checks the aggregate ceiling after the fact
Treats compression, pooling, and CPU-serving-for-small-models as interchangeable rather than sequencing them by impact/cost
Relaxes a model's SLO unilaterally as an engineering decision instead of bringing the real tradeoff to stakeholders
Uses a fully shared, unguarded capacity pool across all three models, risking one model starving another's traffic spike
Doesn't build the cost-ceiling check into the deployment pipeline, discovering breaches only in a later finance review
Assumes the large general-purpose model's SLO must always be protected without checking whether that's actually the right product call
keyPoints: Sizes capacity top-down from the ceiling rather than bottom-up from each model's ideal allocation
Sequences cost-reduction levers (compression, pooling, right-sizing to CPU) by actual impact and cost
Brings the real SLO-relaxation tradeoff to stakeholders with concrete dollar numbers rather than deciding unilaterally
Designs capacity pools with guardrails preventing one model's traffic from silently starving another's
Builds the cost-ceiling check into the deployment pipeline as an automated gate

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Designs a correct top-down, ceiling-first capacity allocation approach
Sequences cost-reduction levers soundly by actual impact and cost
Correctly frames the SLO-relaxation tradeoff as a stakeholder decision with real numbers
Builds the ceiling constraint into an automated deployment-pipeline gate

questions.title: Design a Feature Store Architecture for 40 Teams Sharing Features With Governance
questions.prompt: Design a feature-store architecture for an organization where 40 ML teams increasingly want to discover and reuse each other's computed features, but currently each team builds and owns its features independently with no shared visibility, leading to duplicated work and inconsistent definitions of similar-sounding features. Explain the governance model, not just the storage/serving mechanics.
questions.modelAnswer: The storage and serving mechanics (an offline store for training-time history, an online key-value store for low-latency serving, materialization jobs connecting them, point-in-time joins to prevent leakage) are close to solved problems at this point and shouldn't be the hard part of this design — the actual hard problem, and the reason 40 teams haven't already solved this themselves, is governance: who's allowed to register a feature, who's responsible when it breaks, and how a team discovering an existing feature can trust it enough to reuse it rather than rebuilding their own version, which is exactly the duplicated-work pattern described. I'd design a central feature registry (built on top of whatever Feast-equivalent handles the storage mechanics) with mandatory metadata at registration time: an owning team, a plain-language description of what the feature actually means (not just its name, since 'similar-sounding features with inconsistent definitions' is explicitly the current failure mode), its freshness/staleness characteristics, and a versioning scheme that treats any change to the feature's underlying logic as a new version rather than a silent mutation of the existing one — this versioning requirement is the single most important governance rule, because the described problem (inconsistent definitions hiding behind similar names) is exactly what happens when a feature's logic can change without a name or version change signaling that it happened. I'd make feature discovery genuinely usable, not just technically possible, by requiring the registry to support search by business meaning and by entity type, not just by exact name, since a team looking for 'does something like average order value already exist' needs to find it even if it's named slightly differently by its original owner. For reuse trust specifically, I'd implement a lightweight 'adoption' mechanism — when a team reuses another team's feature, that creates a visible dependency relationship in the registry, so the owning team knows who's relying on their feature before they make a breaking change, and a breaking change to a feature with active downstream adopters requires a notice period and a new major version rather than an in-place mutation, borrowing the same discipline a platform team would apply to any shared library with multiple consumers. For ownership and support, each registered feature needs a clear, enforced on-call or support contact (not just a name field nobody checks), and I'd build a lightweight review step for any feature intended to be shared platform-wide (versus one team's private, unlisted feature) so a feature entering the shared catalog has at least a basic quality bar — a clear description, a point-in-time-correct implementation, no known freshness surprises — before 40 teams start building on something nobody vetted. The organizational piece underneath all of this is that governance only works if using the shared registry is actually easier than not using it, so I'd invest in making registration, search, and the online/offline split as close to zero-marginal-effort as possible for an individual team, since a governance process that adds friction without adding enough value just gets bypassed, which would recreate the exact siloed, duplicated-work problem this design is supposed to fix.
questions.professionalAnswer: The storage and serving side of a feature store is honestly the easy part at this point — offline store for history, online key-value store for serving, materialization connecting them, point-in-time joins to avoid leakage, that's all well-trodden. The actual hard problem, and the reason 40 teams haven't solved this on their own already, is governance: who can register something, who's on the hook when it breaks, and how another team can trust a feature enough to actually reuse it instead of just rebuilding their own version, which is exactly the duplication this whole effort is trying to kill. I'd build a central registry that requires real metadata at registration — an owning team, a plain-language description of what the feature actually means, its freshness characteristics, and crucially a versioning rule that treats any change to the feature's logic as a new version, never a silent in-place mutation — because 'similar-sounding features with inconsistent definitions' is literally what happens when a feature's logic can drift without any name or version signal announcing it. I'd make discovery actually usable by supporting search on meaning and entity type, not just exact feature name, since someone looking for 'does an average-order-value feature already exist somewhere' needs to find it even if whoever built it first called it something slightly different. For trust specifically, I'd add a lightweight adoption mechanism — reusing another team's feature creates a visible dependency the owning team can see, so they know who depends on them before they change anything, and a breaking change to a feature with real downstream adopters needs a notice period and a new major version, the same discipline you'd expect from any shared library with multiple consumers. I'd also require a real, checked support contact per feature, and a basic review gate before a feature enters the shared, platform-wide catalog versus staying a team's private thing, so the 40 teams aren't building on something nobody ever vetted for correctness or freshness surprises. And underneath everything, the real organizational test is whether using the registry is actually easier than not using it — if registering and discovering a feature adds friction without clearly paying for itself, teams will just quietly go back to building their own, which recreates exactly the siloed problem this whole design exists to solve.
commonMistakes: Focuses primarily on storage/serving mechanics while treating governance as an afterthought
Allows a feature's underlying logic to change without a version bump, enabling the exact inconsistent-definition problem described
Builds a registry that only supports exact-name search, missing semantic/entity-type discovery needs
Doesn't implement a dependency-visibility mechanism, letting an owning team break a feature with no awareness of downstream adopters
Requires no review or quality bar for a feature entering the shared platform-wide catalog
Designs a governance process heavy enough that teams are incentivized to bypass it and keep building privately
keyPoints: Correctly identifies governance, not storage/serving mechanics, as the actual hard problem
Makes versioning on any logic change mandatory to prevent silent definition drift
Designs genuinely usable discovery (semantic/entity-type search, not just exact name)
Implements a dependency-visibility/adoption mechanism protecting downstream consumers from breaking changes
Requires a basic quality/review gate for features entering the shared catalog
Explicitly designs for low marginal friction so the governance process doesn't get bypassed

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies governance as the core design problem, not storage mechanics
Designs mandatory versioning preventing silent definition drift
Designs genuine discoverability and dependency-visibility mechanisms
Addresses adoption/friction as a real design constraint, not an afterthought

questions.title: Design a Model Registry and Lifecycle Governance Architecture for a Regulated ML System
questions.prompt: Design the model registry and promotion-governance architecture for a healthcare company's diagnostic-assistance model, which is subject to regulatory review requiring documented evidence of what was validated before any version reached production, and requiring the ability to prove, for any point in the past, exactly which model version was live. Explain the architecture, not just 'use MLflow.'
questions.modelAnswer: Naming a tool isn't an architecture, and the regulatory requirement here — documented evidence of validation before production, plus provable historical point-in-time knowledge of which version was live — demands specific structural guarantees that a default registry setup doesn't provide out of the box. For 'documented evidence of what was validated before any version reached production,' I'd require the promotion workflow itself to be gated on an explicit, recorded approval step, not just a passing automated test: every promotion needs an attached validation report (the specific evaluation results, who reviewed them, and an explicit sign-off, potentially from a compliance role distinct from the engineering team that built the model) stored immutably alongside the registry entry, with promotion to the production alias technically blocked — not just discouraged by process — until that sign-off record exists, enforced via the registry's own access controls or a wrapping approval-gate service rather than relying on everyone remembering to follow the process correctly every time. For 'prove exactly which version was live at any point in the past,' the critical architectural requirement is that alias history itself has to be versioned and immutable, not just the current alias state — a registry that only stores 'champion currently points to version 7' with no record of what it pointed to last month is structurally unable to answer this regulatory question, so I'd build (or require, if evaluating a vendor registry) an append-only, timestamped log of every alias reassignment, separate from and in addition to the registry's live current-state view, specifically so a query for 'what was in production on March 3rd' is a simple lookup against that immutable history rather than a reconstruction effort from scattered deployment logs. I'd extend this same immutability requirement to the model's full lineage — the training data snapshot, code commit, and configuration that produced each version — captured at training time and never mutable afterward, since 'what was validated' is meaningless if the thing that was validated can't be definitively reconstructed later. For serving-side proof, every production request needs to log the resolved model version (not just the alias name, since aliases move) alongside the request, so a specific past prediction can be tied back to the specific version that produced it, which is the serving-layer half of the same provability requirement. I'd also design rollback to go through the exact same governed promotion path as a forward promotion — a rollback to a previous version still requires its own recorded justification and sign-off in a regulated context, rather than being treated as an emergency bypass of the normal governance, because an un-governed emergency rollback path is exactly the kind of gap a regulatory audit would flag, and I'd make sure the architecture supports a fast emergency mitigation (serving-side traffic redirection) that's immediately reversible, while still requiring the registry-level rollback's paperwork to be completed promptly afterward rather than skipped because it happened during an emergency.
questions.professionalAnswer: Saying 'use MLflow' isn't an architecture for this — the actual regulatory requirements demand specific structural guarantees that a default setup doesn't give you for free. For 'documented evidence of validation before production,' I'd make the promotion workflow itself hard-gated on an explicit, recorded sign-off, not just a passing test suite — every promotion needs an attached validation report with the actual results and an explicit approval, ideally from a compliance role separate from the team that built the model, stored immutably with the registry entry, and I'd enforce that the production alias literally can't move until that sign-off record exists, through access controls or a wrapping approval service, rather than trusting everyone to remember the process every single time. For 'prove exactly which version was live at any point in the past,' the key architectural piece is that alias history has to be its own immutable, timestamped, append-only log, separate from the registry's current-state view — a registry that only knows what the alias points to right now, with no record of what it pointed to last month, structurally can't answer a regulator's question about March 3rd, and I don't want that answer to require digging through scattered deployment logs under audit pressure.
